docs.title: Welcome
docs.text:
Introduction to the [PHP 8] language by example

created by Anthropic’s AI Claude at the request of Serge Tahé - October 2026

|Version française|

This course teaches the PHP 8 language by example: console scripts, all commented line by line with their results reproduced, then web services and a web application. It is the PHP 8.5 rewrite of the course Introduction au langage PHP 7 par l'exemple (2019): none of its scripts uses a deprecated feature.

After setting up the working environment (Laragon, PHP 8.5, VS Code, Composer), it presents the basics of the language (types and strict typing, arrays, strings, functions, files, JSON), classes (typed properties, readonly, enumerations, property hooks), interfaces, exceptions, traits, layered applications and their tests with PHPUnit; then the MySQL and PostgreSQL databases with PDO, network functions (TCP, HTTP, SMTP, POP3, IMAP), web services (JSON, sessions, authentication, HTTPS) and XML document processing.

A common thread runs through the whole course: the calculation of French income tax, built in 13 versions, from a simple script up to an MVC web application answering in JSON, XML or HTML, with its console client, its tests, a Redis cache and e-mails sent to the administrator.

Prerequisite: having already programmed in some language.

All of Claude and Serge Tahé's courses

docs.title: 23. Application exercise – version 12
docs.text: In this chapter we will write a web application that follows the MVC (Model-View-Controller) architecture. The application will be able to deliver its responses in three formats: JSON, XML, HTML. There is a jump in complexity between what we are about to do now and what has been done previously. We will reuse most of the concepts seen so far and we will detail all the steps leading to the final application.

docs.title: 23.1. MVC architecture
docs.text:
We will implement the so-called MVC (Model – View – Controller) architectural pattern as follows:

The processing of a client request will proceed as follows:

  • 1 - request: the requested URLs will be of the form [http://machine:port/contexte/main.php?action=uneAction&param1=v1&param2=v2&…]. The [Main controller] will use the [action] parameter of the URL to "route" the request to the secondary controller responsible for processing this action. The rest of the URL [param1=v1&param2=v2&…] consists of optional parameters that will be passed to the action. The C of MVC is here the chain [Main controller, Controller / Action]. If no controller can process the requested action, the server will respond that the requested action is invalid;
  • 2 - processing:
    • the chosen action [2a] can use the parameters that the [Main controller] has passed to it. These can come from several sources: the path [/param1/param2/…] of the URL, the parameters [param1=v1&param2=v2] of the URL, parameters posted by the browser with its request;
    • while processing the user's request, the action may need the [métier] layer [2b]. Once the client's request has been processed, it can call for various responses. A classic example is: an error response if the request could not be processed correctly, a confirmation response otherwise;
    • the [Controller / Action] will return its response [2c] to the main controller along with a state code. These state codes will uniquely represent the state the application is in. They will be either success codes or error codes;
  • 3 - response:
    • depending on whether the client has requested a JSON, XML or HTML response, the [Main controller] will instantiate [3a] the appropriate response type and ask it to send the response to the client. The [Main controller] will pass it the response and the state code provided by the [Controller / Action] that was executed;
    • if the desired response is of type JSON or XML, the selected response will format the response of the [Controller / Action] it was given and send it [3c]. The client able to use this response can be a PHP console script or a JavaScript script hosted in an HTML page;
    • if the desired response is of type HTML, the selected response will choose [3b] one of the HTML views [Vuei] using the state code it was given. This is the V of MVC. A state code corresponds to a single view. This view V will display the response of the [Controller / Action] that was executed. It dresses the data of this response with HTML, CSS, JavaScript. This data is called the view model. This is the M of MVC. The client is then most often a browser.

Now, let us clarify the link between the MVC web architecture and the layered architecture. Depending on the definition given to the model, these two concepts are related or not. Let us take a single-layer MVC web application:

Above, the [Controller / Action] components each incorporate part of the [métier] and [dao] layers. In the [web] layer we do have an MVC architecture, but the application as a whole does not have a layered architecture. Here there is only one layer that does everything.

Now, let us consider a multi-layer web architecture:

The [web] layer can be implemented without following the MVC pattern. We then do have a multi-layer architecture, but the web layer does not implement the MVC pattern.

For example, in the .NET world the [web] layer above can be implemented with ASP.NET Core MVC, and we then have a layered architecture with an MVC-type [web] layer. Once this is done, we can replace this ASP.NET Core MVC layer with an ASP.NET Core [Razor Pages] layer while keeping the rest (business, DAO, driver) identical. We then have a layered architecture with a [web] layer that is no longer of the MVC type.

In MVC, we said that the model M was that of the view V, i.e. the set of data displayed by the view V. Another definition of the model M of MVC is given:

Many authors consider that what lies to the right of the [web] layer forms the model M of MVC. To avoid ambiguity, we can speak of:

  • the domain model when referring to everything to the right of the [web] layer;
  • the view model when referring to the data displayed by a view V.

docs.title: 23.2. Project tree
docs.text:
We adopt for the project a tree structure reflecting the MVC pattern. In [VS Code], the folder [scripts-web/impots/version-12] contains the following elements:

scripts-web/impots/version-12
├── Controllers
│   ├── AfficherCalculImpotController.php
│   ├── AuthentifierUtilisateurController.php
│   ├── CalculerImpotController.php
│   ├── FinSessionController.php
│   ├── InitSessionController.php
│   ├── InterfaceController.php
│   ├── ListerSimulationsController.php
│   └── SupprimerSimulationController.php
├── Data
│   ├── .htaccess
│   ├── config.json
│   └── logs.txt
├── Entities
│   ├── Action.php
│   ├── ControllerResult.php
│   ├── ResponseType.php
│   └── Simulation.php
├── Responses
│   ├── HtmlResponse.php
│   ├── InterfaceResponse.php
│   ├── JsonResponse.php
│   ├── ParentResponse.php
│   └── XmlResponse.php
├── Tests
│   ├── vue-authentification.php
│   ├── vue-calcul-impot.php
│   ├── vue-erreurs.php
│   └── vue-liste-simulations.php
├── Views
│   ├── logo.jpg
│   ├── v-authentification.php
│   ├── v-bandeau.php
│   ├── v-calcul-impot.php
│   ├── v-erreurs.php
│   ├── v-liste-simulations.php
│   ├── v-menu.php
│   ├── vue-authentification.php
│   ├── vue-calcul-impot.php
│   ├── vue-erreurs.php
│   └── vue-liste-simulations.php
├── index.php
└── main.php
  • [main.php] is the main controller of our MVC pattern. It is the C of MVC;
  • the [Controllers] folder contains the secondary controllers. Each one processes a particular action. This action is indicated in the URL, for example […/main.php?action=authentifier-utilisateur]. With this action, the main controller [main.php] will select a secondary controller, here [AuthentifierUtilisateurController], to process the requested action. These controllers are also part of the C of MVC;
  • the [Responses] folder contains the classes responsible for sending the response to the client. There is one class per desired response type:
    • [JsonResponse]: for a JSON response;
    • [XmlResponse]: for an XML response;
    • [HtmlResponse]: for an HTML response;
  • the [Views] folder contains the HTML views when an HTML response is desired. This is the V of MVC. They are activated by the [HtmlResponse] class, which passes them the data to display. This data is the view model. Depending on the terminology adopted for the M, this data may be the M of MVC;
  • the [Tests] folder contains test versions of the views, which make it possible to fine-tune their visual appearance;
  • the [Entities] folder contains classes and enumerations used by the various controllers;
  • the [Data] folder contains the configuration file [config.json] and the log file [logs.txt]. As in the previous versions, the [.htaccess] file from version 8 forbids [Apache] from serving its files: the configuration contains passwords.

The PHP 7 course copied into the version 12 folder the classes of the [métier] and [dao] layers ([Model] folder) and the utilities ([Utilities] folder). We do not copy them: as in the previous versions, these classes are loaded from the folders of versions 5, 8, 9 and 11 where they were written.

Using this tree structure, we can describe the processing path of an action requested by a client:

  • [main.php] receives the request;
  • after performing a few preliminary checks (is the action one of the accepted actions?), it passes the request on to the secondary controller responsible for processing this action;
  • the secondary controller does what it has to do. In its work, it may need the [métier] and [dao] layers as well as the entities of the [Entities] folder. It returns its response to the main controller [main.php] that activated it;
  • depending on the response type [JSON, XML, HTML] desired by the client, the main controller [main.php] activates one of the responses of the [Responses] folder;
  • the responses [JsonResponse, XmlResponse] send the JSON or XML response respectively to the client;
  • the [HtmlResponse] response uses one of the views of the [Views] folder to send an HTML response to the client;
  • the various elements have access to the [Logger] class of version 9 to write logs to the file [Data/logs.txt]. The following are logged:
    • the requested action;
    • the response of its controller. It is recorded in JSON format regardless of the type [JSON, XML, HTML] requested;
  • in the event of a fatal error (HTTP status 500 Internal Server Error), the main controller [main.php] sends an email to the administrator using the [SendAdminMail] class of version 9.

docs.title: 23.3. The application's actions
docs.text:
The client passes the action to be executed to the web server in the form of an [action] parameter in the URL [/main.php?action=xxx]. The PHP 7 course listed the allowed actions in the configuration file, each one associated with the class name of its controller. We use an enumeration (PHP 8.1), the [Action] enumeration of the [Entities] folder:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// espace de noms
namespace Application;

// les actions acceptées par l'application : la valeur d'un cas est le nom de l'action dans l'URL
enum Action: string
{
    case InitSession = "init-session";
    case AuthentifierUtilisateur = "authentifier-utilisateur";
    case CalculerImpot = "calculer-impot";
    case ListerSimulations = "lister-simulations";
    case SupprimerSimulation = "supprimer-simulation";
    case FinSession = "fin-session";
    case AfficherCalculImpot = "afficher-calcul-impot";

    // l'action exige-t-elle que le type de la session (json, xml, html) soit connu ?
    public function exigeTypeSession(): bool
    {
        return $this !== self::InitSession;
    }

    // l'action exige-t-elle que l'utilisateur soit authentifié ?
    public function exigeAuthentification(): bool
    {
        return match ($this) {
            self::InitSession, self::AuthentifierUtilisateur => false,
            default => true,
        };
    }
}

Comments

  • line 9: the [Action] enumeration is a backed enumeration (backed enum): each of its cases has a value, here of type [string]. We encountered enumerations in the chapter on classes;
  • line 11: [init-session] starts a session of tax calculation simulations. This action indicates the type of responses desired [JSON, XML, HTML];
  • line 12: once the session type is set, the client will have to authenticate with the [authentifier-utilisateur] action. As long as it is not authenticated, all other actions are forbidden except [init-session];
  • line 13: once authenticated, the client can perform a series of tax calculations with the [calculer-impot] action;
  • line 14: at any time, the client can ask to see the list of simulations it has performed with the [lister-simulations] action;
  • line 15: it can delete some of them with the [supprimer-simulation] action;
  • line 16: the client ends its simulation session with the [fin-session] action. From that point on, it will have to authenticate again if it wants to use the application;
  • line 17: in the HTML application, the [afficher-calcul-impot] action requests the display of the form used to calculate the tax;
  • lines 20-23: an enumeration can have methods. In a method, [$this] designates the enumeration case on which the method is called. The [exigeTypeSession] method tells whether the action can only be executed when the session type is known: this is the case for all actions except [init-session]. The cases of an enumeration are unique objects: they are compared with the [===] operator;
  • lines 26-32: the [exigeAuthentification] method tells whether the action can only be executed by an authenticated user: this is the case for all actions except [init-session] and [authentifier-utilisateur]. The [match] expression accepts several values, separated by commas, in the same branch.

These rules, which were written in the main controller of the PHP 7 course, are thus grouped together with the definition of the actions.

Comments

  • line 2: the JSON file describing the MySQL database [dbimpots-2019], the one from version 8. The path is relative to the [version-12] folder;
  • lines 3-33: the PHP files of the application. It first contains the classes already written:
    • the entities [ExceptionImpots, TaxAdminData, Database] and the [Utilitaires] class of version 5;
    • the [dao] and [métier] layers of versions 8 and 9;
    • the utilities [Logger] and [SendAdminMail] of version 9 and [XmlUtilitaires] of version 11;
    • then the classes of version 12, which we are going to present. The PHP 7 file also contained the absolute paths of the third-party libraries ([C:/myprograms/laragon-lite/www/vendor/autoload.php]): the [Composer] class loader is now loaded directly by [main.php], with a relative path;
  • lines 34-39: the user allowed to use the application;
  • lines 40-48: the mail details of the application administrator. The mail is sent to the [Mailpit] server, which listens on port 1025 (see version 9);
  • line 49: the path of the log file;
  • lines 50-54: the details of the [Redis] server, which serves as [application]-scope memory (see version 10);
  • lines 55-59: associations [HTML view => array of the state codes leading to this view]. They are presented a little further on;
  • line 60: the view [vue-erreurs.php] is displayed in an HTML session every time an abnormal error occurs:
    • a JSON or XML application is usually queried with a programmed client. The latter passes the server parameters that may be missing or incorrect. All the controllers handle these cases and return error codes to the client. All possible error cases must be handled;
    • with an HTML application, it is a little different. When used normally, the web application uses only part of the possible use cases of the JSON and XML clients. Let us take an example: the [calculer-impot] action expects three posted parameters (sent by a POST): [marié, enfants, salaire]. With a JSON client that allows URLs to be typed by hand, the [calculer-impot] action can be requested with a GET rather than a POST, or with a POST without any posted parameter when three are required, etc. The JSON server must handle all these cases. With a web application, the [calculer-impot] action will be requested from a web form where neither of the two previous cases will be possible: the [calculer-impot] action will be requested with a POST and the three parameters [marié, enfants, salaire]. However, the user can reproduce certain errors by typing URLs into the browser themselves. For safety, this case must be handled;
    • the view [vue-erreurs.php] will be displayed every time a secondary controller returns a state code incompatible with the web application, i.e. a state code absent from the [vues] key of the configuration file. We opt for this solution for teaching purposes. Another possible option would be to redisplay the view currently displayed in the client's browser so that the user has the impression that the server does not respond to their hand-made URLs.

Compared with the configuration file of the PHP 7 course, the keys [rootDirectory] (the root folder is now known to [main.php]), [actions] (replaced by the [Action] enumeration) and [types] (replaced by the [ResponseType] enumeration presented later) have disappeared.

docs.title: 23.5.1. The [curl] tool
docs.text:
The PHP 7 course used the graphical tool [Postman] to query the various URLs of the web application. We use the command-line tool [curl], presented in the chapter on web services. It allows us:

  • to use any URL: they are made by hand;
  • to query the web server with a GET, POST, PUT, OPTIONS… (options [-X] and [-d]);
  • to specify the parameters of the GET (in the URL) or of the POST (options [-d] and [--data-urlencode]);
  • to set the HTTP headers of the request (option [-H]);
  • to receive a response in JSON, XML, HTML format;
  • to have access to the HTTP headers of the response (option [-i]);
  • to manage the session cookie like a browser: the option [-c cookies.txt] saves in the file [cookies.txt] the cookies sent by the server, the option [-b cookies.txt] sends them back to the server.

Since we make the queried URLs by hand, we will be able to test all the possible error cases and see how the server reacts. Remember that in a [PowerShell] terminal, you must type [curl.exe] rather than [curl]. All the commands of this chapter are typed in a terminal opened in any working folder, where [curl] creates the file [cookies.txt].

To post a parameter whose name contains accented characters, such as [marié], we will use the option [--data-urlencode "marié=oui"], which encodes the name and the value of the parameter ([mari%C3%A9=oui]). In the URL, we will write the encoded name ourselves: [num%C3%A9ro] for [numéro].

docs.title: 23.5.2. The Symfony / Serializer library
docs.text:
The PHP 7 course used the [Symfony / Serializer] library to serialize into JSON and XML the server's responses, which may contain [Simulation] objects. It had two advantages: the same API for JSON and XML; the serialization of objects with private attributes, exposed through getters.

We do not use it in this version, even though it is installed in the course's [vendor] folder:

  • our [Simulation] class is a [readonly] class with public attributes (see next section). The [json_encode] function directly serializes the public attributes of an object: JSON serialization no longer requires a library;
  • for XML, we have the [XmlUtilitaires] class of version 11, which produces XML documents of the same form as those of version 11, which the XML clients already know how to use. We just have to give it an array, after transforming the [Simulation] objects into associative arrays;
  • the server never has to deserialize JSON or XML into objects, which was the other advantage put forward by the PHP 7 course.

The [Symfony / Serializer] library would therefore only add one more dependency here. It remains a good choice when documents must be deserialized into typed objects or when many formats must be handled.

docs.title: 23.6. The application's entities
docs.text:
The [Entities] folder contains two enumerations, [Action] (already presented) and [ResponseType] (presented with the server's responses), and two classes. The [Simulation] class encapsulates the elements of a tax calculation simulation:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// espace de noms
namespace Application;

// une simulation de calcul d'impôt : un objet immuable
final readonly class Simulation
{
    // les attributs sont publics : ils ne peuvent pas être modifiés (readonly) mais
    // ils sont lus directement, sans getters, et sérialisés par [json_encode]
    public function __construct(
        // les paramètres du calcul
        public string $marié,
        public int $enfants,
        public int $salaire,
        // le résultat du calcul
        public int $impôt,
        public int $surcôte,
        public int $décôte,
        public int $réduction,
        public float $taux,
    ) {
    }
}

Comments

  • line 9: the class is [readonly] (PHP 8.2): all its attributes are read-only. A simulation is an immutable object: once built, it no longer changes;
  • lines 13-24: the attributes are declared and initialized through constructor parameter promotion (PHP 8.0). They are typed: [string] for the marital status, [int] for the other parameters and the amounts, [float] for the tax rate;
  • the attributes are public: since they are read-only, it is no longer necessary to protect them with getters. The PHP 7 [Simulation] class derived from the [BaseEntity] class, had eight untyped [protected] attributes and eight getters.

The second class, [ControllerResult], represents the result that a secondary controller returns to the main controller:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// espace de noms
namespace Application;

// le résultat rendu par un contrôleur secondaire au contrôleur principal
final readonly class ControllerResult
{
    public function __construct(
        // le code de statut HTTP de la réponse
        public int $statusCode,
        // l'état de l'application après l'exécution de l'action
        public int $état,
        // la réponse proprement dite : un message, une liste de messages, une simulation...
        public mixed $réponse,
        // des entêtes HTTP à ajouter à la réponse
        public array $headers = [],
    ) {
    }
}
  • line 13: the HTTP status code of the response to be sent to the client;
  • line 15: the state the application is in after the action has been executed;
  • line 17: the actual response. Its type depends on the action: a message, a list of error messages, a simulation, a list of simulations. The [mixed] type (PHP 8.0) accepts any value;
  • line 19: the HTTP headers to be added to the response. It is an optional parameter.

In the PHP 7 course, the controllers returned the array [[$statusCode, $état, $content, $headers]]. An object with named, typed attributes is safer: you cannot get the order of the elements wrong.

docs.title: 23.7. The application's utilities
docs.text:
The application uses three utilities already presented:

  • the [Logger] class of version 9 makes it possible to log events to a text file;
  • the [SendAdminMail] class of version 9 makes it possible to send an email to the application administrator;
  • the [XmlUtilitaires] class of version 11 makes it possible to obtain the XML document of an array.

docs.title: 23.8. The [métier] and [dao] layers
docs.text:
The classes and interfaces of the [métier] and [dao] layers have all been defined and used in previous versions:

ClassRoleExceptionImpotsThe class of the exceptions thrown by the [dao] layer. Version 5, [Entities] folderInterfaceServerDaoInterface implemented by the server's [dao] layer. Version 8, [Dao] folderServerDaoImplementation of the [InterfaceServerDao] interface: the tax data is read from the database. Version 8ServerDaoWithSessionClass derived from [ServerDao]: the tax data can be supplied to the constructor. Version 9, [Dao] folderInterfaceServerMetierInterface implemented by the server's [métier] layer. Version 8, [Metier] folderServerMetierImplementation of the [InterfaceServerMetier] interface: the tax calculation. Version 8

The application being written therefore uses many elements already presented and used:

  • the [métier] and [dao] layers;
  • the utilities [Logger], [SendAdminMail] and [XmlUtilitaires];
  • the entities [ExceptionImpots, TaxAdminData, Database].

We will focus on the [web] layer of the application:

docs.title: 23.9.1. Introduction
docs.text:
The main controller [main.php] is configured by the file [Data/config.json]. Let us recall its position in our MVC architecture:

The main controller [main.php] is the 1st element of the MVC architecture to process the client's request. It has several roles:

  • it first performs the basic checks:
    • does its configuration file exist and is it valid?
    • it loads all the project's dependencies. This amounts to loading all the elements of the MVC architecture;
    • has the requested action been specified? If so, is it valid?
  • if the requested action is valid, it selects [2a] the secondary controller that will process it and passes it the information it needs: the application configuration, the HTTP request, the session;
  • it retrieves [2c] the secondary controller's response. Depending on the response type (JSON, XML, HTML) requested by the client, it selects [3a] the response (JsonResponse, XmlResponse, HtmlResponse) responsible for sending the response to the client and passes it all the information it needs (the HTTP request, the session, the application configuration, the secondary controller's response).

docs.title: 23.9.2. [main.php] - 1
docs.text:
The beginning of the main controller [main.php] is as follows:

<?php

// respect strict des types déclarés des paramètres et des résultats des fonctions
declare(strict_types=1);

// espace de noms
namespace Application;

// dépendances Symfony
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Session\Session;

// les erreurs de PHP ne sont pas envoyées au client (elles vont dans le journal du serveur web)
ini_set("display_errors", "0");

// le dossier racine de l'application : les chemins du fichier de configuration sont relatifs à ce dossier
const ROOT_DIRECTORY = __DIR__;
// chemin du fichier de configuration
const CONFIG_FILENAME = ROOT_DIRECTORY . "/Data/config.json";

// l'autoloader de Composer (Symfony, Predis)
require_once ROOT_DIRECTORY . "/../../../vendor/autoload.php";

// on récupère la configuration
$fileContents = is_readable(CONFIG_FILENAME) ? file_get_contents(CONFIG_FILENAME) : false;
if ($fileContents === false) {
    sendConfigError(131, "Le fichier de configuration [config.json] n'existe pas");
}
try {
    $config = json_decode($fileContents, true, flags: JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR);
} catch (\JsonException) {
    sendConfigError(132, "Le fichier de configuration [config.json] n'a pu être exploité correctement");
}

Comments

  • lines 10-12: the main controller uses the following classes of Symfony's [HttpFoundation] library:
    • [Request]: the HTTP request being processed;
    • [Response]: the HTTP response to the client;
    • [Session]: the web application's session;
  • line 15: the errors detected by PHP are not included in the document sent to the client: they would corrupt the JSON or XML responses. They are still recorded in the web server's error log (Apache's [error.log] file). During development, this line can be commented out: PHP errors then appear in the responses received by [curl] or the browser. This is a debugging aid. The PHP 7 script also changed the error reporting level with [error_reporting(E_ALL && !E_WARNING && !E_NOTICE)], an expression that was in fact wrong (the bitwise operators [&] and [~] were needed): on the contrary, we want to ignore no error;
  • line 18: the root folder of the application, that of the [main.php] script. The paths in the configuration file are relative to this folder. The constant is defined in the [Application] namespace: it is therefore visible to the classes of this namespace, in particular to the controller that will calculate the tax;
  • line 20: the path of the configuration file;
  • line 23: we load the [Composer] class loader, which makes the Symfony and Predis classes available. It is loaded before the configuration is read: the error response sent if reading fails uses Symfony's [Response] class. The PHP 7 script used an absolute path here;
  • lines 26-29: we read the configuration file. If it does not exist or cannot be read, an error response with state [131] is sent to the client by the [sendConfigError] function;
  • lines 30-34: we decode the JSON of the configuration file. With the [JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR] option, the [json_decode] function throws a [JsonException] exception if the JSON is invalid. We then send an error response with state [132]. Since PHP 8.0, the [catch] clause can omit the exception variable when it is not used: [catch (\JsonException)];

Here we have a configuration file that exists and is syntactically correct. We should also test that the keys expected in this file are indeed present. We will consider that this is part of the developer's normal debugging work.

The [sendConfigError] function is defined at the end of the script:

// --------------------------------------------------------------------------
// erreur sur le fichier de configuration : réponse JSON 500 puis fin du script
// les classes de l'application ne sont pas encore chargées : on utilise directement [Response]
function sendConfigError(int $état, string $message): never
{
    $json = json_encode(["action" => "", "état" => $état, "réponse" => $message], JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE);
    $response = new Response($json, Response::HTTP_INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR);
    $response->headers->set("Content-Type", "application/json; charset=utf-8");
    $response->send();
    exit;
}
  • line 124: the return type [never] (PHP 8.1) indicates that the function never returns control to the caller: it always ends with [exit] or with an exception. A code analyzer such as the [PHP Intelephense] extension of [VS Code] then knows that the code following a call to [sendConfigError] is executed only if the configuration could be read;
  • line 126: all the responses made by the web application will have three keys:
    • [action]: the action requested by the client (unknown here);
    • [état]: the state of the application after this action has been executed;
    • [réponse]: the web server's response;
  • line 127: since the application's classes are not loaded yet, we build a Symfony response directly, with the status [500 Internal Server Error];
  • line 128: the response is a JSON document encoded in UTF-8;
  • line 129: the response is sent to the client.

docs.title: 23.9.3. [curl] tests - 1
docs.text:
We are going to check the server's behavior when the configuration file is missing or incorrect. Let us rename [Data/config.json] to [Data/config2.json] and then request the URL of the main controller:

> curl -i "http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/impots/version-12/main.php"
HTTP/1.0 500 Internal Server Error
Date: Thu, 01 Oct 2026 16:51:52 GMT
Server: Apache/2.4.58
X-Powered-By: PHP/8.5.11
Cache-Control: no-cache, private
Connection: close
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8

{"action":"","état":131,"réponse":"Le fichier de configuration [config.json] n'existe pas"}
  • line 1: the [-i] option asks [curl] to display the HTTP headers of the response;
  • line 2: the server returned the status [500 Internal Server Error];
  • line 8: the response is a JSON document;
  • line 10: the JSON document of the response. It is indeed the one we expected.

Let us give the file back its name [config.json], then make it syntactically incorrect, for example by deleting everything after its second line. We no longer display the HTTP headers:

> curl "http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/impots/version-12/main.php"
{"action":"","état":132,"réponse":"Le fichier de configuration [config.json] n'a pu être exploité correctement"}

This first test showed us that we can send any type of request to the server under test and that we get the whole response: HTTP headers and the document following these headers. Let us not forget to restore the contents of the [config.json] file.

docs.title: 23.9.4. [main.php] – 2
docs.text:
We resume the study of the main controller [main.php]:

// on inclut les dépendances de l'application
foreach ($config["dependencies"] as $dependency) {
    require_once ROOT_DIRECTORY . "/$dependency";
}

// la requête courante
$request = Request::createFromGlobals();
// la session - démarrée après le chargement des classes : elle contient des objets [Simulation]
$session = new Session();
$session->start();

// création du fichier des logs
try {
    $logger = new Logger(ROOT_DIRECTORY . "/" . $config["logsFilename"]);
} catch (ExceptionImpots) {
    // erreur 500 - réponse JSON sans logs
    $content = [
        "action" => "",
        "état" => 133,
        "réponse" => "Le fichier de logs [{$config["logsFilename"]}] n'a pu être créé",
    ];
    (new JsonResponse())->send($request, $session, $config, Response::HTTP_INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, $content);
    exit;
}

Comments

  • lines 37-39: we include all the application's dependencies. We have already encountered this code several times;
  • line 42: we encapsulate all the information of the client's request in the Symfony [Request] object;
  • lines 44-45: we start a new session or retrieve the existing session if the client sent a session cookie. The session is started after the application's classes have been loaded: it will contain [Simulation] objects, and the [Simulation] class must be known when PHP rebuilds the session's objects;
  • lines 48-59: we try to create the [Logger] object that will allow us to log events to the file [Data/logs.txt]. This creation may fail: the [Logger] constructor then throws an [ExceptionImpots] exception;
  • lines 52-56: the error response, with state [133]. The message uses the log file name given in the configuration and not the full path: the latter would reveal the server's folder organization to the client;
  • line 57: the response is sent by a [JsonResponse] object, without a log since it could not be created. The application's classes are now loaded: we can use them;
  • line 58: we stop the script.

All the responses sent to the client implement the following [InterfaceResponse] interface, from the [Responses] folder:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// espace de noms
namespace Application;

// dépendances Symfony
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Session\Session;

// l'interface implémentée par les trois types de réponse [JsonResponse, XmlResponse, HtmlResponse]
interface InterfaceResponse
{
    // envoi de la réponse au client
    // Request $request : la requête en cours de traitement
    // Session $session : la session de l'application web
    // array $config : la configuration de l'application
    // int $statusCode : le code HTTP de statut de la réponse
    // array $content : la réponse du serveur, le tableau [action, état, réponse]
    // array $headers : les entêtes HTTP à ajouter à la réponse
    // ?Logger $logger : le journal de l'application (null s'il n'a pu être créé)
    public function send(
        Request $request,
        Session $session,
        array $config,
        int $statusCode,
        array $content,
        array $headers = [],
        ?Logger $logger = null
    ): void;
}
  • lines 23-31: the [InterfaceResponse] interface has a single method [send] to send the response to the client;
  • lines 16-22: the meaning of the various parameters of the [send] method;
  • lines 27-29: the parameters [$statusCode], [$content] and [$headers] contain the result of the secondary controller and the keys [action, état] added by the main controller. However, the response may need other information. So it is given the first three parameters, which give it access to all the information concerning the request, the session, the configuration;
  • line 30: the response needs the [Logger] because it is going to log the response sent to the client. The type [?Logger] indicates that the parameter can be [null]: this is the case when the log could not be created. In the PHP 7 signature, the parameters [Request $request = NULL] and [Logger $logger = NULL] were implicitly nullable: this notation has been deprecated since PHP 8.4. Moreover, declaring an optional parameter before required parameters has been deprecated since PHP 8.0.

The [JsonResponse] class implements the [InterfaceResponse] interface as follows:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// espace de noms
namespace Application;

// dépendances Symfony
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Session\Session;

// une réponse JSON
final class JsonResponse extends ParentResponse
{
    #[\Override]
    public function send(
        Request $request,
        Session $session,
        array $config,
        int $statusCode,
        array $content,
        array $headers = [],
        ?Logger $logger = null
    ): void {
        // sérialisation JSON : [json_encode] sérialise aussi les attributs publics des objets [Simulation]
        $json = json_encode($content, self::JSON_OPTIONS);
        // envoi de la réponse par la classe parent
        $this->sendResponse($statusCode, $json, "application/json", $headers);
        // log
        $logger?->write("réponse=$json");
    }
}

Comments

  • line 13: the class extends the abstract class [ParentResponse], which implements the [InterfaceResponse] interface. All response types extend this class. It is this parent class that sends the response to the client. It is because this code is common to all response types that it has been factored out into a parent class. Our [JsonResponse] class is not Symfony's [JsonResponse] class: it is in the [Application] namespace and we do not import the Symfony class;
  • line 15: the [Override] attribute (PHP 8.3) indicates that the [send] method implements a method of a parent class or of an interface. If this were not the case (a typo in the name, for example), PHP would report an error;
  • line 26: the response [$content] is serialized to JSON. The options of [json_encode] are defined once and for all in the parent class. The [json_encode] function serializes a [Simulation] object as a JSON object whose keys are the names of its public attributes;
  • line 28: we ask the parent class to send the response to the client, specifying the document type [application/json];
  • line 30: we log the JSON response. The nullsafe operator [?->] calls the [write] method only if [$logger] is not [null].

The code of the parent class [ParentResponse] is as follows:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// espace de noms
namespace Application;

// dépendances Symfony
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;

// la classe parent des trois types de réponse : elle factorise ce qui leur est commun
// elle est abstraite : la méthode [send] de l'interface est implémentée par les classes filles
abstract class ParentResponse implements InterfaceResponse
{
    // les options de [json_encode] utilisées par toutes les réponses
    protected const int JSON_OPTIONS = JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE | JSON_UNESCAPED_SLASHES
        | JSON_PRESERVE_ZERO_FRACTION | JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR;

    // envoi effectif de la réponse au client
    // $statusCode : le code HTTP de statut de la réponse
    // $body : le corps de la réponse, selon les cas une chaîne JSON, XML ou HTML
    // $contentType : le type du document envoyé (application/json, application/xml, text/html)
    // $headers : les entêtes HTTP à ajouter à la réponse
    protected function sendResponse(int $statusCode, string $body, string $contentType, array $headers): void
    {
        // la réponse Symfony
        $response = new Response($body, $statusCode, $headers);
        // le type du document envoyé, codé en UTF-8
        $response->headers->set("Content-Type", "$contentType; charset=utf-8");
        // envoi des entêtes HTTP puis du corps de la réponse
        $response->send();
    }

    // log de la réponse en JSON, quel que soit le type de la réponse envoyée
    protected function log(?Logger $logger, array $content): void
    {
        $logger?->write("réponse=" . json_encode($content, self::JSON_OPTIONS));
    }

    // rend la donnée [$data] dans laquelle les objets (des simulations) ont été remplacés
    // par le tableau associatif de leurs attributs publics
    protected static function toArray(mixed $data): mixed
    {
        return match (true) {
            is_object($data) => self::toArray(get_object_vars($data)),
            is_array($data) => array_map(self::toArray(...), $data),
            default => $data,
        };
    }
}

Comments

  • line 13: the class is abstract: it cannot be instantiated. It implements the [InterfaceResponse] interface without defining the [send] method, which will be defined by the child classes. In the PHP 7 course, [ParentResponse] was an ordinary class that the child classes extended while also implementing the interface;
  • line 16: the [json_encode] options common to all responses. Since PHP 8.3, a class constant can be typed:
    • [JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE]: accented characters are written as they are and not in the form [\u00e9];
    • [JSON_UNESCAPED_SLASHES]: the [/] character is not encoded as [\/];
    • [JSON_PRESERVE_ZERO_FRACTION]: a real number is always written with a decimal point (a zero rate is written [0.0]);
    • [JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR]: a serialization error throws a [JsonException] exception;
  • line 24: the [sendResponse] method sends the response to the client. Note that the body [$body] of the response is of type [string] and therefore ready to be sent;
  • line 27: the constructor of the Symfony [Response] class receives the body, the status and the headers of the response;
  • line 29: the type of the document sent, encoded in UTF-8;
  • line 31: sending the response to the client;
  • line 35: the [log] method logs the response in JSON. It will be used by the XML and HTML responses;
  • lines 42-49: the static method [toArray] returns the data [$data] in which objects have been replaced by the associative array of their public attributes. It will be used by the XML response:
    • the expression [match (true)] chooses the first branch whose condition is true;
    • line 45: an object is replaced by the array of its attributes, returned by the [get_object_vars] function. Called outside the object's class, it returns only its public attributes. The attributes may themselves be objects: so we call [toArray] again;
    • line 46: each element of an array is transformed by [toArray]. The syntax [self::toArray(...)] (PHP 8.1) creates an anonymous function (a [Closure]) from the [toArray] method: this is the first-class callable syntax. With a single array, the [array_map] function preserves the array's keys;
    • line 47: the other values (strings, numbers) are returned as they are.

docs.title: 23.9.5. [curl] tests – 2
docs.text:
Let us modify the [config.json] file as follows: ["logsFilename": "Data"]. The log file is now [Data], which is a folder. Creating the file [Data] should therefore fail:

> curl -i "http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/impots/version-12/main.php"
HTTP/1.0 500 Internal Server Error
Date: Thu, 01 Oct 2026 16:51:52 GMT
Server: Apache/2.4.58
X-Powered-By: PHP/8.5.11
Cache-Control: max-age=0, private, must-revalidate
Set-Cookie: PHPSESSID=5c2f09b4ca8ff3ceb0601052072f6256; path=/
Cache-Control: no-cache, private
Connection: close
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8

{"action":"","état":133,"réponse":"Le fichier de logs [Data] n'a pu être créé"}
  • line 2: the status [500 Internal Server Error];
  • line 7: the session cookie: the session was started before the log was created;
  • line 12: the expected JSON response.

Let us restore the value [Data/logs.txt] of the [logsFilename] key.

docs.title: 23.9.6. [main.php] – 3
docs.text:
Let us continue the study of the main controller [main.php]:

// 1er log
$logger->write("---nouvelle requête");

// l'action demandée
$nomAction = strtolower(trim($request->query->getString("action")));
$logger->write("action [$nomAction] demandée");
// l'action est-elle l'un des cas de l'énumération [Action] ? (null sinon)
$action = Action::tryFrom($nomAction);
// vérifications préliminaires : un résultat d'erreur, ou null si l'action peut être exécutée
$erreur = match (true) {
    !$request->query->has("action") => [101, "paramètre [action] manquant"],
    $action === null => [102, "action [$nomAction] invalide"],
    $action->exigeTypeSession() && !$session->has("type")
        => [103, "pas de session en cours. Commencer par action [init-session]"],
    $action->exigeAuthentification() && !$session->has("user")
        => [104, "action demandée par utilisateur non authentifié"],
    default => null,
};
if ($erreur !== null) {
    // on prépare la réponse d'erreur sans l'envoyer
    [$état, $message] = $erreur;
    $résultat = new ControllerResult(Response::HTTP_BAD_REQUEST, $état, [$message]);
} else {
    // on exécute l'action à l'aide de son contrôleur secondaire
    $controller = match ($action) {
        Action::InitSession => new InitSessionController(),
        Action::AuthentifierUtilisateur => new AuthentifierUtilisateurController(),
        Action::CalculerImpot => new CalculerImpotController(),
        Action::ListerSimulations => new ListerSimulationsController(),
        Action::SupprimerSimulation => new SupprimerSimulationController(),
        Action::FinSession => new FinSessionController(),
        Action::AfficherCalculImpot => new AfficherCalculImpotController(),
    };
    $logger->write("contrôleur : " . $controller::class);
    $résultat = $controller->execute($config, $request, $session);
}

// la réponse au client : [action, état] puis la réponse du contrôleur
$content = ["action" => $nomAction, "état" => $résultat->état, "réponse" => $résultat->réponse];
// erreur fatale : on envoie un mail à l'administrateur
if ($résultat->statusCode === Response::HTTP_INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR) {
    // [SendAdminMail] intercepte toutes les exceptions et les logue lui-même
    (new SendAdminMail($config["adminMail"], $logger))
        ->send(json_encode($content, JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE | JSON_UNESCAPED_SLASHES | JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR));
}
// le type de la réponse est dans la session - JSON par défaut s'il n'a pas encore été fixé
$type = ResponseType::tryFrom($session->get("type", "")) ?? ResponseType::Json;
// l'objet [InterfaceResponse] du type demandé envoie la réponse au client
$type->response()->send(
    $request,
    $session,
    $config,
    $résultat->statusCode,
    $content,
    $résultat->headers,
    $logger
);
// fin
exit;

Comments

  • line 62: we log the fact that we have a new request. We could not do so earlier because we were not sure we had a valid log file;
  • line 65: the [action] parameter must be part of the URL in the form [main.php?action=uneAction]. It is then part of the URL parameters [$request->query]. Symfony's [getString] method returns the value of the parameter as a character string, or the empty string if the parameter is absent;
  • line 66: the requested action is logged;
  • line 68: the static method [tryFrom] of a backed enumeration returns the enumeration case whose value is [$nomAction], or [null] if no case has this value. The [from] method would do the same thing but would throw a [ValueError] exception in the second case;
  • lines 70-78: the preliminary checks. Their result [$erreur] is either an array [état, message] describing the first error encountered, or [null] if the action can be executed. The conditions are evaluated in order:
    • line 71: the [action] parameter is missing from the URL: state [101];
    • line 72: the action is unknown: state [102];
    • line 73: the application provides three response types (JSON, XML, HTML). This type is set by the [init-session] action, which places it in the session, associated with the [type] key. Apart from the [init-session] action, every action must take place with a [type] key in the session: state [103] otherwise;
    • line 75: apart from the [init-session] and [authentifier-utilisateur] actions, all actions must be performed after authentication. This is done using the [authentifier-utilisateur] action which, if authentication succeeds, puts a [user] key in the session: state [104] otherwise;
    • line 77: no error;
  • lines 79-82: if the requested action or its execution context is incorrect, we prepare the error response without sending it: status [400 Bad Request], state, list of errors (here with a single error). The destructuring [[$état, $message] = $erreur] assigns the two elements of the [$erreur] array in a single statement;
  • lines 85-93: we have a valid action. We instantiate the secondary controller that will process it. The PHP 7 course built the controller's class name from the configuration ([__NAMESPACE__ . $config["actions"][$action]]) and then instantiated it with [new $controller()]. The [match] expression on the cases of the [Action] enumeration is safer: the [VS Code] code analyzer checks the class names, and if a case is added to the enumeration without being added here, [match] will throw an [UnhandledMatchError] exception instead of instantiating some random class;
  • line 94: we log the name of the secondary controller, for checking during development. Since PHP 8.0, [$objet::class] gives the fully qualified class name of an object;
  • line 95: the secondary controller is executed. It returns a [ControllerResult] object. We will come back to the secondary controllers a little further on;
  • we then reach line 99 either because there was an error or after a controller has been executed. In both cases, the [$résultat] object contains everything needed to build the response to the client;
  • line 99: the response to the client is an array with three keys [action, état, réponse]. The [action] key will make it easier to follow the logs in the [logs.txt] file. The [état] key will have two roles:
    • it will allow JSON and XML clients to know the state in which the executed action has put the web application;
    • in the case of an HTML response, it will make it possible to choose the HTML view to be sent to the client browser;
  • lines 101-104: special case of the status code [500 Internal Server Error]. If a controller has set this status code, it means the application cannot work. This is for example the case of the tax calculation if the DBMS or the [Redis] server has not been started or no longer responds. We then send an email to the application administrator to warn them, with the [SendAdminMail] class of version 9;
  • line 107: we determine the type [JSON, XML, HTML] of the response. If the [init-session] action was executed successfully, this type is in the session, associated with the [type] key. If this is not the case, the session's [get] method returns the default value [""], [tryFrom] returns [null] and the [??] operator chooses the JSON type;
  • lines 109-117: the [response] method of the [ResponseType] enumeration, presented later, returns the [JsonResponse], [XmlResponse] or [HtmlResponse] object suited to the session type. Its [send] method sends the response to the client. Since the three classes implement the same [InterfaceResponse] interface, their [send] methods all have the same signature;
  • line 119: the main controller has finished its work. The PHP 7 script closed the log file here: our [Logger] class no longer has a [close] method.

docs.title: 23.9.7. [curl] tests – 3
docs.text:
We are going to test various error cases of the [action] parameter of the URL:

> curl "http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/impots/version-12/main.php"
{"action":"","état":101,"réponse":["paramètre [action] manquant"]}

> curl "http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/impots/version-12/main.php?action=x"
{"action":"x","état":102,"réponse":["action [x] invalide"]}

> curl "http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/impots/version-12/main.php?action=lister-simulations"
{"action":"lister-simulations","état":103,"réponse":["pas de session en cours. Commencer par action [init-session]"]}
  • lines 1-2: a request without the [action] parameter in the URL: state [101];
  • lines 4-5: a request with an invalid [action] parameter: state [102];
  • lines 7-8: a recognized action, but the session type (json, xml, html) has not yet been specified: state [103].

In these three cases, the [réponse] key is a list of errors, here with a single error.

docs.title: 23.10. The secondary controllers
docs.text:
Each action is executed by one of the controllers of the [Controllers] folder:

In the general architecture of the application above, the secondary controllers are at [2a]. Each controller implements the following [InterfaceController] interface:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// espace de noms
namespace Application;

// dépendances Symfony
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Session\Session;

// l'interface implémentée par tous les contrôleurs secondaires
interface InterfaceController
{
    // traitement de l'action demandée
    // array $config : la configuration de l'application
    // Request $request : la requête en cours de traitement
    // Session $session : la session de l'application web, que le contrôleur peut modifier
    // rend un objet [ControllerResult] : statut HTTP, état de l'application, réponse, entêtes HTTP
    public function execute(array $config, Request $request, Session $session): ControllerResult;
}

Comments

  • line 20: all the secondary controllers are executed via the [execute] method. This method is passed the information known to the main controller:
    • [array $config]: the application configuration;
    • [Request $request]: the HTTP request being processed;
    • [Session $session]: the current session of the web application;
  • the [execute] method returns a [ControllerResult] object: the HTTP status code of the response, the state the application is in at the end of the execution, the response to be sent to the client, the HTTP headers to be added to the response.

The PHP 7 method had a fourth parameter [array $infos = NULL], provided "as a precaution" and never used: we have removed it. Each secondary controller is called by the following code of the main controller:

    // on exécute l'action à l'aide de son contrôleur secondaire
    $controller = match ($action) {
        Action::InitSession => new InitSessionController(),
        Action::AuthentifierUtilisateur => new AuthentifierUtilisateurController(),
        Action::CalculerImpot => new CalculerImpotController(),
        Action::ListerSimulations => new ListerSimulationsController(),
        Action::SupprimerSimulation => new SupprimerSimulationController(),
        Action::FinSession => new FinSessionController(),
        Action::AfficherCalculImpot => new AfficherCalculImpotController(),
    };
    $logger->write("contrôleur : " . $controller::class);
    $résultat = $controller->execute($config, $request, $session);

docs.title: 23.11. The actions
docs.text:
We now review the various possible actions of the web service:

ActionRoleExecution contextinit-sessionUsed to set the type (json, xml, html) of the desired responsesGET request main.php?action=init-session&type=xCan be issued at any timeauthentifier-utilisateurAllows a user to log in or notPOST request main.php?action=authentifier-utilisateurThe request must have two posted parameters [user, password]Can only be issued if the session type (json, xml, html) is knowncalculer-impotPerforms a tax calculation simulationPOST request main.php?action=calculer-impotThe request must have three posted parameters [marié, enfants, salaire]Can only be issued if the session type is known and the user is authenticatedlister-simulationsAsks to see the list of simulations performed since the beginning of the sessionGET request main.php?action=lister-simulationsThe request accepts no other parameterCan only be issued if the session type is known and the user is authenticatedsupprimer-simulationDeletes a simulation from the list of simulationsGET request main.php?action=supprimer-simulation&numéro=xThe request accepts no other parameterCan only be issued if the session type is known and the user is authenticatedfin-sessionEnds the simulation sessionGET request main.php?action=fin-sessionTechnically, the old web session is deleted and a new session is createdCan only be issued if the session type is known and the user is authenticatedafficher-calcul-impotDisplays the tax calculation view (HTML application)GET request main.php?action=afficher-calcul-impotCan only be issued if the session type is known and the user is authenticated

All the secondary controllers proceed in the same way:

  • they check their parameters. These are found in the [$request->query] object for the parameters present in the URL and in the [$request->request] object for those that are posted (POST request);
  • a controller is similar to a function or method that checks the validity of its parameters. For the controller, however, it is a little more complicated:
    • the expected parameters may be missing;
    • the expected parameters are all character strings, whereas a function can set the type of its parameters. If the expected parameter is a number, then it must be checked that the parameter's string is indeed that of a number;
    • once it has been checked that the expected parameters are present and syntactically correct, it must be checked that they are valid in the current execution context. This context is present in the session. Authentication is an example of execution context: certain actions must only be processed once the client is authenticated. A key in the session indicates whether or not this authentication has taken place;
  • once the previous checks have been made, the secondary controller can do its work. This parameter-checking work is very important. We cannot accept that a client sends us anything at any moment in the life of the application. We must have full control over its life;
  • once its work is done, the secondary controller returns the [ControllerResult] object expected by the main controller that called it.

We are now going to review the various controllers or, what amounts to the same thing, the various actions that punctuate the life of the web application.

docs.title: 23.11.1. The [init-session] action
docs.text:
The [init-session] action is processed by the following [InitSessionController] controller:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// espace de noms
namespace Application;

// dépendances Symfony
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Session\Session;

// action [init-session] : fixe le type (json, xml, html) des réponses de la session
final class InitSessionController implements InterfaceController
{
    #[\Override]
    public function execute(array $config, Request $request, Session $session): ControllerResult
    {
        // on doit avoir un GET avec les seuls paramètres [action, type] dans l'URL
        if ($request->getMethod() !== "GET" || $request->query->count() !== 2) {
            $message = "méthode GET exigée avec les paramètres [action, type] dans l'URL";
            return new ControllerResult(Response::HTTP_BAD_REQUEST, 701, $message);
        }
        // le paramètre [type] doit être présent
        if (!$request->query->has("type")) {
            return new ControllerResult(Response::HTTP_BAD_REQUEST, 702, "paramètre [type] manquant");
        }
        // et valide : [tryFrom] rend null si la chaîne n'est la valeur d'aucun cas de l'énumération
        $type = strtolower(trim($request->query->getString("type")));
        if (ResponseType::tryFrom($type) === null) {
            return new ControllerResult(Response::HTTP_BAD_REQUEST, 703, "paramètre type [$type] invalide");
        }
        // on met le type de la session dans la session
        $session->set("type", $type);
        // réussite
        return new ControllerResult(Response::HTTP_OK, 700, "session démarrée avec type [$type]");
    }
}

Comments

  • we expect a request [GET main.php?action=init-session&type=xxx];
  • line 14: the class implements the [InterfaceController] interface. It is [final]: it cannot be derived from;
  • lines 20-23: we check that the request is a GET request with two parameters in the URL. If this is not the case, we return an error result to the main controller, with state [701]. Symfony's [getMethod] method returns the name of the HTTP method in upper case: it is no longer useful to convert it to lower case as the PHP 7 script did;
  • lines 25-27: we check that the [type] parameter is indeed present in the URL. If this is not the case, we return an error result with state [702];
  • line 29: we note the session type;
  • lines 30-32: we check that the session type is one of the terms (json, xml, html), i.e. the value of one of the cases of the [ResponseType] enumeration. If this is not the case, we return an error result with state [703];
  • line 34: the session type is put in the web application's session;
  • line 36: the controller has finished its work. We return a success result to the main controller, with state [700].

Each error case leads to an immediate [return]. The PHP 7 script used a boolean variable [$erreur] tested at each step: the code is now shorter and more readable. Let us recall what the main controller does with the response of the secondary controllers: it adds the keys [action] and [état] to the response and sends it by instantiating one of the classes [JsonResponse, XmlResponse, HtmlResponse] depending on the type (json, xml, html) of the current session.

In what follows, we will run [curl] tests in a [json]-type simulation session.

docs.title: 23.11.3. The [authentifier-utilisateur] action
docs.text:
The [authentifier-utilisateur] action is executed by the following [AuthentifierUtilisateurController] controller:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// espace de noms
namespace Application;

// dépendances Symfony
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Session\Session;

// action [authentifier-utilisateur] : authentifie l'utilisateur avec les paramètres postés [user, password]
final class AuthentifierUtilisateurController implements InterfaceController
{
    #[\Override]
    public function execute(array $config, Request $request, Session $session): ControllerResult
    {
        // on doit avoir un POST avec le seul paramètre [action] dans l'URL
        if ($request->getMethod() !== "POST" || $request->query->count() !== 1) {
            $message = "méthode POST requise, paramètre [action] dans l'URL, paramètres postés [user, password]";
            return new ControllerResult(Response::HTTP_BAD_REQUEST, 201, $message);
        }
        // on récupère les paramètres postés
        $erreurs = [];
        $état = 210;
        // user
        if (!$request->request->has("user")) {
            $état += 2;
            $erreurs[] = "paramètre [user] manquant";
        }
        // password
        if (!$request->request->has("password")) {
            $état += 4;
            $erreurs[] = "paramètre [password] manquant";
        }
        // erreurs ?
        if ($erreurs !== []) {
            return new ControllerResult(Response::HTTP_BAD_REQUEST, $état, $erreurs);
        }
        $user = trim($request->request->getString("user"));
        $password = trim($request->request->getString("password"));
        // l'utilisateur fait-il partie des utilisateurs autorisés ?
        $trouvé = array_any(
            $config["users"],
            fn(array $u): bool => $u["login"] === $user && hash_equals($u["passwd"], $password)
        );
        if (!$trouvé) {
            // échec : code 401 - le mot de passe n'est jamais renvoyé au client
            return new ControllerResult(Response::HTTP_UNAUTHORIZED, 221, "Echec de l'authentification [$user]");
        }
        // on note dans la session l'identifiant de l'utilisateur authentifié
        $session->set("user", $user);
        // réussite
        return new ControllerResult(Response::HTTP_OK, 200, "Authentification réussie [$user]");
    }
}

Comments

  • we expect a request [POST main.php?action=authentifier-utilisateur] with two posted parameters [user, password];
  • lines 20-23: we check that we have a POST request with a single parameter in the URL. If this is not the case, we return an error result with state [201];
  • line 26: the state for errors on the posted parameters starts from the value 210;
  • lines 28-31: we check the presence of the [user] parameter in the posted values. If it is not present, we note the error and add 2 to the state;
  • lines 33-36: we check the presence of the [password] parameter. If it is not present, we note the error and add 4 to the state. The state is therefore 212 if only [user] is missing, 214 if only [password] is missing, 216 if both are missing;
  • lines 38-40: if one of the posted values is missing, we return an error result whose response is the list of errors;
  • lines 41-42: the posted credentials;
  • lines 44-47: we check that the pair [[$user, $password]] is present in the [$config["users"]] array of the configuration file. The [array_any] function (PHP 8.4) returns [true] if at least one of the array's elements satisfies the condition expressed by the arrow function. The password is compared with the [hash_equals] function, whose execution time does not depend on the position of the first differing character: an attacker cannot guess the password character by character by measuring response times. The PHP 7 script used a [while] loop;
  • lines 48-51: if the user is not found, we return an error result with the HTTP status [401 Unauthorized] and state [221]. The PHP 7 message contained the password entered: a password must never be sent back to the client, nor written to the logs;
  • line 53: authentication has succeeded. We record this in the session by placing the [user] key in it, with the user's identifier as its value. It is the presence of this key that indicates a successful authentication;
  • line 55: we return a success result to the main controller, with state [200].

  • lines 1-2: before any authentication, we request a tax calculation. The [-d] option makes the request a POST. The main controller refuses the action: state [104];
