  • lines 31-46: the [Classe3] class extends the [Classe1] class and defines the method g of its parent class;
  • lines 40-44: the [Classe3] class also overrides the method f of its parent class;
  • lines 49-54: two objects of types [Classe2] and [Classe3] are created and their methods f and g are called;
  • line 57: an abstract class cannot be instantiated: we get an error (line 6 of the results).

docs.title: 5.19. Final classes
docs.text:
A final class is a class that cannot be derived. Consider the following script [classes-11.php]:

<?php

// respect strict des types déclarés des paramètres de fonctions
declare(strict_types=1);

// espace de noms
namespace Exemples;

// classe non dérivable
final class Classe1
{
}

// classe dérivée - provoque une erreur
class Classe2 extends Classe1
{
}

// code
new Classe2();

Results:

> php classes-11.php

Fatal error: Class Exemples\Classe2 cannot extend final class Exemples\Classe1 in .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/classes/classes-11.php on line 15
Stack trace:
#0 {main}

Comments

  • line 10: the keyword [final] makes the [Classe1] class a final class that cannot be derived;
  • line 15: the [Classe2] class extends the final class [Classe1], which is an error;
  • the error is reported as soon as the PHP interpreter loads the definition of the [Classe2] class: it is a fatal error that cannot be caught by a [try / catch]. The script is not executed.

Declaring a class [final] is good practice when it was not designed to be derived: this prevents other developers from relying on the internal details of the class.

docs.title: 5.20. Final methods
docs.text:
A final method is a method that cannot be overridden through derivation. Here is an example [classes-12.php]:

<?php

// respect strict des types déclarés des paramètres de fonctions
declare(strict_types=1);

// espace de noms
namespace Exemples;

// classe principale
class Classe1
{
    // cette méthode ne peut être redéfinie dans une classe dérivée
    final public function f(): int
    {
        return 1;
    }
}

// classe dérivée
class Classe2 extends Classe1
{
    // redéfinition interdite - provoque une erreur
    public function f(): int
    {
        return 2;
    }
}

// code
new Classe2();

Results:

> php classes-12.php

Fatal error: Cannot override final method Exemples\Classe1::f() in .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/classes/classes-12.php on line 23
Stack trace:
#0 {main}

Comments

  • line 13: the method f of the [Classe1] class is declared final by the keyword [final];
  • line 20: the [Classe2] class extends the [Classe1] class;
  • line 23: the method f of the parent class [Classe1] is overridden. This causes a fatal error, reported as soon as the [Classe2] class is loaded.

docs.title: 5.21. Static methods and attributes
docs.text:
A static method is a method bound to the class in which it is defined and not to the objects that are instances of the class. Thus, if class C declares a static method M, to use it you write:

  • [C::M] if you are outside the class;
  • [self::M] if you are inside the class.

Here is an example [classes-17.php]:

<?php

// respect strict des types déclarés des paramètres de fonctions
declare(strict_types=1);

class Classe1
{
    // méthode statique
    public static function say(string $message): void
    {
        print "$message\n";
    }

    // méthode statique utilisant une autre méthode statique de la classe
    public static function sayTwice(string $message): void
    {
        self::say($message);
        self::say($message);
    }
}

// test -------------------
Classe1::say("hello");
Classe1::sayTwice("bonjour");
// syntaxe des callables de première classe : [Classe1::say(...)] est une fonction
$dire = Classe1::say(...);
$dire("salut");
// que l'on peut passer à une autre fonction
array_map($dire, ["un", "deux"]);

Results:

> php classes-17.php
hello
bonjour
bonjour
salut
un
deux

Comments

  • line 9: the [say] method is declared static with the keyword [static];
  • line 17: inside the class, the static method [say] is called with the notation [self::say];
  • line 23: call of the static method [say] with the notation [Classe1::say];
  • line 26: the first-class callable syntax (PHP 8.1): writing [(...)] in place of the arguments of a call does not make the call but returns the function itself, in the form of a [Closure] object. The variable [$dire] then contains a function that is called like an ordinary function (line 27). The same syntax applies to functions ([strlen(...)]) and to an object's methods ([$p->identite(...)]);
  • line 29: such a function can be passed as a parameter to another function. The [array_map] function applies the function [$dire] to each of the elements of the array (lines 6-7 of the results).

Now consider the following code [classes-18.php]:

<?php

// respect strict des types déclarés des paramètres de fonctions
declare(strict_types=1);

class Classe1
{
    // attribut statique
    private static int $nbObjects = 0;

    public function __construct()
    {
        print "constructeur Classe1\n";
        self::$nbObjects++;
    }

    // méthode statique
    public static function say(): void
    {
        print self::$nbObjects . " objets de type [Classe1] ont été construits\n";
    }
}

// test -------------------
new Classe1();
new Classe1();
Classe1::say();

Results:

> php classes-18.php
constructeur Classe1
constructeur Classe1
2 objets de type [Classe1] ont été construits

Comments

  • line 9: we declare a static attribute that will count the number of instances of the [Classe1] class created. This is not an attribute that can belong to an instance of the class. Indeed, if two objects O1 and O2 are created, neither of them knows about the other. Having a counter in the instance makes no sense: when a new object is created, in which instance would a counter be incremented? A static attribute is an attribute of the class and not of an instance of the class;
  • lines 11-15: it is in the constructor that the objects created will be counted, since the creation of each new object causes the constructor to be executed;
  • line 14: note the notation [self::$nbObjects] to indicate that we are referring to a static attribute of the class in which the executed code is located;
  • lines 18-21: the role of the static method [say] is to display the number of objects created;
  • lines 25-27: two objects are created and the object counter is displayed.

docs.title: 5.22. Visibility between parent class and child class
docs.text:
Let us examine the following script [classes-19.php]:

<?php

// respect strict des types déclarés des paramètres de fonctions
declare(strict_types=1);

class SomeParent
{
    // attribut
    private int $attributeOfParent = 4;

    // méthode
    public function doTest(): void
    {
        // qui appelle ?
        print "parent :\n";
        var_dump($this);
        // affichage parent
        print "parent : attributeOfParent={$this->attributeOfParent}\n";
        print "parent : attributeOfChild={$this->attributeOfChild}\n";
    }
}

class SomeChild extends SomeParent
{
    // attribut
    private int $attributeOfChild = 14;

    // méthode
    #[\Override]
    public function doTest(): void
    {
        // affichage enfant
        print "child : attributeOfParent={$this->attributeOfParent}\n";
        print "child : attributeOfChild={$this->attributeOfChild}\n";
        // parent
        parent::doTest();
    }
}

// script principal
print "---------------------------test1\n";
(new SomeParent())->doTest();
print "---------------------------test2\n";
(new SomeChild())->doTest();

Comments

  • lines 6-21: the [SomeParent] class;
  • lines 23-38: the child class [SomeChild]. We can see that it extends the [SomeParent] class;
  • line 9: the [SomeParent] class has only one attribute;
  • lines 12-20: the purpose of the [SomeParent::doTest] method is to display two attributes:
    • [$attributeOfParent], which belongs to the [SomeParent] class;
    • [$attributeOfChild], which belongs to the [SomeChild] class;
  • lines 15-16: the identity of the caller is displayed: indeed, we are going to call the method in two different ways:
    • from the parent class [SomeParent];
    • from the child class [SomeChild];
  • lines 18-19: display of the two attributes;
  • line 26: the [SomeChild] class has only one attribute;
  • line 30: the purpose of the [SomeChild::doTest] method is to display two attributes:
    • [$attributeOfParent], which belongs to the [SomeParent] class;
    • [$attributeOfChild], which belongs to the [SomeChild] class;
  • lines 33-34: display of the two attributes;
  • line 36: call of the [doTest] method of the parent class, which will in turn display the two attributes;
  • line 42: the [SomeParent::doTest] method is called;
  • line 44: the [SomeChild::doTest] method is called.

In the 1st test, the visibility of both attributes is [private]. We can therefore expect the child class not to see the attribute of its parent class. That attribute would need at least [protected] visibility. But what about the child class's attribute? Is it visible in the parent class?

Here are the results of this 1st test:

> php classes-19.php
---------------------------test1
parent :
object(SomeParent)#1 (1) {
  ["attributeOfParent":"SomeParent":private]=>
  int(4)
}
parent : attributeOfParent=4

Warning: Undefined property: SomeParent::$attributeOfChild in .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/classes/classes-19.php on line 19
parent : attributeOfChild=
---------------------------test2

Warning: Undefined property: SomeChild::$attributeOfParent in .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/classes/classes-19.php on line 33
child : attributeOfParent=
child : attributeOfChild=14
parent :
object(SomeChild)#1 (2) {
  ["attributeOfParent":"SomeParent":private]=>
  int(4)
  ["attributeOfChild":"SomeChild":private]=>
  int(14)
}
parent : attributeOfParent=4

Fatal error: Uncaught Error: Cannot access private property SomeChild::$attributeOfChild in .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/classes/classes-19.php:19
Stack trace:
#0 .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/classes/classes-19.php(36): SomeParent->doTest()
#1 .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/classes/classes-19.php(44): SomeChild->doTest()
#2 {main}
  thrown in .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/classes/classes-19.php on line 19

Comments

  • lines 2-11: results of the 1st test, where the [SomeParent::doTest] method is called;
  • lines 3-7: we see that the object calling the method is of type [SomeParent];
  • line 8: display of the attribute [$attributeOfParent];
  • lines 10-11: we see that the attribute [SomeParent::$attributeOfChild] does not exist. It is therefore not displayed. In PHP 8, reading a non-existent attribute causes a [Warning]-level warning (it was a mere [Notice] in PHP 7);
  • lines 12-31: results of the 2nd test, where the [SomeChild::doTest] method is called;
  • lines 14-15: we see that the attribute [SomeChild::$attributeOfParent] does not exist. It is therefore not displayed. This is normal: the attribute [SomeParent::$attributeOfParent] is [private] and therefore not known in the child class;
  • line 16: display of the attribute [$attributeOfChild];
  • lines 17-31: we are in the [SomeParent::doTest] method called by the child class;
  • lines 18-23: we see that [$this] is of type [SomeChild] with two private attributes;
  • line 24: very surprisingly, [$this] of type [SomeChild] here sees the parent's private attribute [$attributeOfParent];
  • lines 26-31: just as surprisingly, [$this] of type [SomeChild] does not see its attribute [$attributeOfChild]: accessing it causes a fatal error.

This result is very surprising: although lines 18-23 indicate that [$this] is of type [SomeChild], this [$this] inside the [SomeParent::doTest] method behaves as if it were an instance of the [SomeParent] class and not of the [SomeChild] class. In fact, visibility is checked relative to the class in which the code is written (here [SomeParent]) and not relative to the class of the object.

Let us run a new test with the script [classes-20.php]. The attribute [$attributeOfParent] now has [protected] visibility:

<?php

// respect strict des types déclarés des paramètres de fonctions
declare(strict_types=1);

class SomeParent
{
    // attribut
    protected int $attributeOfParent = 4;

    // méthode
    public function doTest(): void
    {
        // qui appelle ?
        print "parent :\n";
        var_dump($this);
        // affichage parent
        print "parent : attributeOfParent={$this->attributeOfParent}\n";
        print "parent : attributeOfChild={$this->attributeOfChild}\n";
    }
}

class SomeChild extends SomeParent
{
    // attribut
    private int $attributeOfChild = 14;

    // méthode
    #[\Override]
    public function doTest(): void
    {
        // affichage enfant
        print "child : attributeOfParent={$this->attributeOfParent}\n";
        print "child : attributeOfChild={$this->attributeOfChild}\n";
        // parent
        parent::doTest();
    }
}

// script principal
print "---------------------------test1\n";
(new SomeParent())->doTest();
print "---------------------------test2\n";
(new SomeChild())->doTest();

Results:

> php classes-20.php
---------------------------test1
parent :
object(SomeParent)#1 (1) {
  ["attributeOfParent":protected]=>
  int(4)
}
parent : attributeOfParent=4

Warning: Undefined property: SomeParent::$attributeOfChild in .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/classes/classes-20.php on line 19
parent : attributeOfChild=
---------------------------test2
child : attributeOfParent=4
child : attributeOfChild=14
parent :
object(SomeChild)#1 (2) {
  ["attributeOfParent":protected]=>
  int(4)
  ["attributeOfChild":"SomeChild":private]=>
  int(14)
}
parent : attributeOfParent=4

Fatal error: Uncaught Error: Cannot access private property SomeChild::$attributeOfChild in .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/classes/classes-20.php:19
Stack trace:
#0 .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/classes/classes-20.php(36): SomeParent->doTest()
#1 .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/classes/classes-20.php(44): SomeChild->doTest()
#2 {main}
  thrown in .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/classes/classes-20.php on line 19

Comments

  • line 13: the [SomeChild] class now sees its parent's attribute [$attributeOfParent]. This is normal since it now has [protected] scope;
  • in the [SomeParent::doTest] method, the object [$this] is of type [SomeChild] (lines 16-21). It sees its parent's attribute [$attributeOfParent] (line 22) but still not its own private attribute [$attributeOfChild] (lines 24-29).

In the 3rd attempt [classes-21.php], the attribute [$attributeOfChild] also has [protected] scope:

<?php

// respect strict des types déclarés des paramètres de fonctions
declare(strict_types=1);

class SomeParent
{
    // attribut
    protected int $attributeOfParent = 4;

    // méthode
    public function doTest(): void
    {
        // qui appelle ?
        print "parent :\n";
        var_dump($this);
        // affichage parent
        print "parent : attributeOfParent={$this->attributeOfParent}\n";
        print "parent : attributeOfChild={$this->attributeOfChild}\n";
    }
}

class SomeChild extends SomeParent
{
    // attribut
    protected int $attributeOfChild = 14;

    // méthode
    #[\Override]
    public function doTest(): void
    {
        // affichage enfant
        print "child : attributeOfParent={$this->attributeOfParent}\n";
        print "child : attributeOfChild={$this->attributeOfChild}\n";
        // parent
        parent::doTest();
    }
}

// script principal
print "---------------------------test1\n";
(new SomeParent())->doTest();
print "---------------------------test2\n";
(new SomeChild())->doTest();

The execution results are as follows:

> php classes-21.php
---------------------------test1
parent :
object(SomeParent)#1 (1) {
  ["attributeOfParent":protected]=>
  int(4)
}
parent : attributeOfParent=4

Warning: Undefined property: SomeParent::$attributeOfChild in .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/classes/classes-21.php on line 19
parent : attributeOfChild=
---------------------------test2
child : attributeOfParent=4
child : attributeOfChild=14
parent :
object(SomeChild)#1 (2) {
  ["attributeOfParent":protected]=>
  int(4)
  ["attributeOfChild":protected]=>
  int(14)
}
parent : attributeOfParent=4
parent : attributeOfChild=14
  • line 23: this time, inside the parent, [$this] of type [SomeChild] (lines 16-21) sees the protected attribute [$attributeOfChild] of its own class [SomeChild].

What should we take away from these tests?

  • that [$this], an instance of a parent class, used in a method of the parent class sees:
    • the attributes and methods of the parent class whatever their visibility;
    • nothing of the attributes and methods of its child classes;
  • this is the expected behavior;
  • that [$this], an instance of a child class, used in a method of the child class sees:
    • the attributes and methods of the parent class if they have at least [protected] visibility. Those with [private] visibility are not seen;
    • the attributes and methods of the child class whatever their visibility;
  • this is the expected behavior;
  • that [$this], an instance of a child class, used in a method of the parent class sees:
    • the attributes and methods of the parent class whatever their visibility;
    • the attributes and methods of its own class only if they have at least [protected] visibility. Those with [private] visibility are not seen;
  • this is unexpected behavior, which is explained by the rule stated above: visibility depends on the class in which the code is written.

docs.title: 5.23. Enumerations (PHP 8.1)
docs.text:
A person has a gender: woman or man. How should this information be represented? In PHP 7, a string (["F"], ["H"]) or class constants were used. Nothing then prevented an incorrect value (["X"], ["femme"]...) from being passed. PHP 8.1 introduced enumerations (keyword [enum]): an enumeration is a type that has only a finite number of possible values, called cases. We define the enumeration [Genre] in the file [Genre.php]:

<?php

// respect strict des types déclarés des paramètres de fonctions
declare(strict_types=1);

// espace de noms
namespace Exemples;

// une énumération adossée à des chaînes de caractères (backed enum)
enum Genre: string
{
    case Femme = "F";
    case Homme = "H";

    // une énumération peut avoir des méthodes
    public function libelle(): string
    {
        return match ($this) {
            Genre::Femme => "Madame",
            Genre::Homme => "Monsieur",
        };
    }
}

Comments

  • line 10: the [Genre] enumeration. The [string] type after its name makes it a "backed" enumeration (backed enum): each case is associated with a scalar value, here a string. This value is useful for saving the case to a file or a database. Without this type, you have a pure enumeration whose cases have no associated value;
  • lines 12-13: the two cases of the enumeration and their values;
  • lines 16-22: an enumeration can have methods (as well as constants and static methods). In a method, [$this] designates the case on which the method is called;
  • lines 18-21: the [match] expression (PHP 8.0) compares its parameter with the values of each branch using the [===] operator and returns the value of the first matching branch. If no branch matches, an [UnhandledMatchError] error is thrown. Here, all the branches are provided for.

The enumeration is used by the script [classes-26.php]:

<?php

// respect strict des types déclarés des paramètres de fonctions
declare(strict_types=1);

require_once __DIR__ . "/Genre.php";
use Exemples\Genre;

// une personne avec un genre
final readonly class Personne
{
    public function __construct(
        public string $prenom,
        public string $nom,
        public Genre $genre,
    ) {
    }

    public function __toString(): string
    {
        return "{$this->genre->libelle()} $this->prenom $this->nom";
    }
}

// test
$p1 = new Personne("Paul", "Langevin", Genre::Homme);
$p2 = new Personne("Sylvie", "Lefur", Genre::Femme);
print "$p1\n$p2\n";
// un cas d'énumération a un nom et une valeur
print "nom={$p2->genre->name}, valeur={$p2->genre->value}\n";
// les cas sont des objets uniques : on les compare avec ===
print "p1 est un homme : " . var_export($p1->genre === Genre::Homme, true) . "\n";
// la liste des cas
foreach (Genre::cases() as $genre) {
    print "$genre->name ($genre->value) : {$genre->libelle()}\n";
}
// d'une valeur (lue dans un fichier, une base de données...) vers un cas
print "from('F') : " . Genre::from("F")->name . "\n";
print "tryFrom('X') : " . var_export(Genre::tryFrom("X"), true) . "\n";
try {
    Genre::from("X");
} catch (\ValueError $e) {
    print "Erreur : " . $e->getMessage() . "\n";
}
// le type [Genre] n'accepte que les cas de l'énumération
try {
    new Personne("Steve", "Boer", "H");
} catch (\TypeError $e) {
    print "Erreur : " . $e->getMessage() . "\n";
}

Results:

> php classes-26.php
Monsieur Paul Langevin
Madame Sylvie Lefur
nom=Femme, valeur=F
p1 est un homme : true
Femme (F) : Madame
Homme (H) : Monsieur
from('F') : Femme
tryFrom('X') : NULL
Erreur : "X" is not a valid backing value for enum Exemples\Genre
Erreur : Personne::__construct(): Argument #3 ($genre) must be of type Exemples\Genre, string given, called in .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/classes/classes-26.php on line 47

Comments

  • line 15: the attribute [genre] of the [Personne] class is of type [Genre];
  • line 21: call of the [libelle] method of the case stored in the attribute [genre];
  • line 26: a case is designated by the notation [Genre::Homme];
  • line 30: each case has an attribute [name], its name, and, for a backed enumeration, an attribute [value], its value (line 4 of the results);
  • line 32: each case is a unique object: cases are compared with the [===] operator;
  • line 34: the static method [cases] returns the list of the enumeration's cases (lines 6-7 of the results);
  • line 38: the static method [from] returns the case associated with a value. It is the reverse path of [value]: ["F"] is read from a database and the case [Genre::Femme] is obtained;
  • line 39: the [tryFrom] method returns [null] if the value does not correspond to any case;
  • line 41: the [from] method, on the other hand, throws a [ValueError] error (line 10 of the results);
  • line 47: the [Genre] type only accepts the cases of the enumeration, not their values: ["H"] is rejected (line 11 of the results). This is the whole point of enumerations: an incorrect value is detected immediately.

docs.title: 5.24. JSON encoding of a class
docs.text:
The [__toString] method is often present in a class: it is supposed to return a string representing the object that calls it. It can be tempting to make this string a JSON string. We now explore this path. The scripts are in the [scripts-console/classes/json] folder:

php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/classes/json
├── json-01.php
├── json-02.php
├── json-03.php
├── json-04.php
├── Personne.php
├── Personne2.php
├── Personne3.php
└── Personne4.php

We will use the following [Personne] class:

<?php

// respect strict des types déclarés des paramètres de fonctions
declare(strict_types=1);

class Personne
{
    // attributs
    private ?string $nom = null;
    private ?string $prénom = null;
    private ?int $âge = null;
    private ?array $enfants = null;

    // setter global
    public function setFromArray(array $arrayOfAttributes): static
    {
        // initialisation de certains attributs de la classe
        foreach ($arrayOfAttributes as $attribute => $value) {
            // on refuse les attributs non déclarés dans la classe
            if (!property_exists($this, $attribute)) {
                throw new \InvalidArgumentException("Attribut [$attribute] inconnu");
            }
            $this->$attribute = $value;
        }
        // on retourne l'objet
        return $this;
    }

    // getters
    public function getNom(): ?string
    {
        return $this->nom;
    }

    public function getPrénom(): ?string
    {
        return $this->prénom;
    }

    public function getÂge(): ?int
    {
        return $this->âge;
    }

    public function getEnfants(): ?array
    {
        return $this->enfants;
    }


    // __toString
    public function __toString(): string
    {
        // on identifie l'objet
        var_dump($this);
        // on récupère ses attributs
        $attributes = \get_object_vars($this);
        var_dump($attributes);
        // on rend la chaîne jSON des attributs
        return \json_encode($attributes, JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE);
    }
}

Comments

  • lines 9-12: the four attributes of the class. They are of nullable types ([?string] means [string] or [null]) and are initially [null];
  • lines 30-45: the getters that give the value of these attributes;
  • lines 15-27: a global setter that initializes the attributes from an associative array [$arrayOfAttributes] whose keys are identical to the names of the class's attributes;
  • line 20: the [property_exists] function checks that the attribute is declared in the class. Without this check, an unknown key would create a dynamic attribute, which has been deprecated since PHP 8.2;
  • line 23: the notation [$this->$attribute] designates the attribute whose name is the value of the variable [$attribute];
  • line 15: the method returns the current object [$this]. Its return type is [static]: "an object of the class on which the method was called". This makes it possible to chain calls: [(new Personne())->setFromArray([...])];
  • lines 52-61: the [__toString] method of the class;
  • line 57: the PHP function [get_object_vars] gives the values of the object's attributes in the form of an associative array [['nom'=>'nom1', 'prénom'=>'prénom1', 'âge'=>âge1, 'enfants'=>[...]]]. Called inside the class, it also returns the private attributes;
  • line 60: the JSON string of this array of attributes is returned. The [JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE] option asks for accented characters not to be transformed into [\u00e9] sequences.

Let us examine the script [json-01.php], which uses the [Personne] class:

<?php

// respect strict des types déclarés des paramètres de fonctions
declare(strict_types=1);

// classe Personne
require_once __DIR__ . "/Personne.php";

// instanciation du père
$père = new Personne();
// initialisation du père
$père->setFromArray([
    "nom" => "Bertholomé",
    "prénom" => "Dieudonné",
    "âge" => 58,
]);
// instanciation et initialisation enfant1
$enfant1 = (new Personne())->setFromArray([
    "nom" => "Bertholomé",
    "prénom" => "Sylvain",
    "âge" => 17,
]);
// instanciation et initialisation enfant2
$enfant2 = (new Personne())->setFromArray([
    "nom" => "Bertholomé",
    "prénom" => "Géraldine",
    "âge" => 12,
]);
// initialisation des enfants du père
$père->setFromArray([
    "enfants" => [$enfant1, $enfant2],
]);

// affichage des éléments du père
$enfant1 = $père->getEnfants()[0];
$enfant2 = $père->getEnfants()[1];
print "------------------------enfant1\n";
print "enfant1=$enfant1\n";
print "------------------------enfant2\n";
print "enfant2=$enfant2\n";
print "------------------------père\n";
print "père=$père\n";

Comments

  • lines 10-16: a [Personne] object [$père] is initialized with the [Personne::setFromArray] method;
  • lines 18-22: a [Personne] object [$enfant1] is initialized in the same way;
  • lines 24-28: a [Personne] object [$enfant2] is initialized;
  • line 31: the father's attribute [enfants] is initialized with an array of the two children;
  • lines 35-36: the father's two children are retrieved;
  • line 38: the [print] operation will try to transform the object [$enfant1] into a string. To do so, it uses the object's [__toString] method. We therefore hope to see the object's JSON string;
  • line 42: we do the same with the father.

The results are as follows:

> php json-01.php
------------------------enfant1
object(Personne)#2 (4) {
  ["nom":"Personne":private]=>
  string(11) "Bertholomé"
  ["prénom":"Personne":private]=>
  string(7) "Sylvain"
  ["âge":"Personne":private]=>
  int(17)
  ["enfants":"Personne":private]=>
  NULL
}
array(4) {
  ["nom"]=>
  string(11) "Bertholomé"
  ["prénom"]=>
  string(7) "Sylvain"
  ["âge"]=>
  int(17)
  ["enfants"]=>
  NULL
}
enfant1={"nom":"Bertholomé","prénom":"Sylvain","âge":17,"enfants":null}
------------------------enfant2
object(Personne)#3 (4) {
  ["nom":"Personne":private]=>
  string(11) "Bertholomé"
  ["prénom":"Personne":private]=>
  string(10) "Géraldine"
  ["âge":"Personne":private]=>
  int(12)
  ["enfants":"Personne":private]=>
  NULL
}
array(4) {
  ["nom"]=>
  string(11) "Bertholomé"
  ["prénom"]=>
  string(10) "Géraldine"
  ["âge"]=>
  int(12)
  ["enfants"]=>
  NULL
}
enfant2={"nom":"Bertholomé","prénom":"Géraldine","âge":12,"enfants":null}
------------------------père
object(Personne)#1 (4) {
  ["nom":"Personne":private]=>
  string(11) "Bertholomé"
  ["prénom":"Personne":private]=>
  string(10) "Dieudonné"
  ["âge":"Personne":private]=>
  int(58)
  ["enfants":"Personne":private]=>
  array(2) {
    [0]=>
    object(Personne)#2 (4) {
      ["nom":"Personne":private]=>
      string(11) "Bertholomé"
      ["prénom":"Personne":private]=>
      string(7) "Sylvain"
      ["âge":"Personne":private]=>
      int(17)
      ["enfants":"Personne":private]=>
      NULL
    }
    [1]=>
    object(Personne)#3 (4) {
      ["nom":"Personne":private]=>
      string(11) "Bertholomé"
      ["prénom":"Personne":private]=>
      string(10) "Géraldine"
      ["âge":"Personne":private]=>
      int(12)
      ["enfants":"Personne":private]=>
      NULL
    }
  }
}
array(4) {
  ["nom"]=>
  string(11) "Bertholomé"
  ["prénom"]=>
  string(10) "Dieudonné"
  ["âge"]=>
  int(58)
  ["enfants"]=>
  array(2) {
    [0]=>
    object(Personne)#2 (4) {
      ["nom":"Personne":private]=>
      string(11) "Bertholomé"
      ["prénom":"Personne":private]=>
      string(7) "Sylvain"
      ["âge":"Personne":private]=>
      int(17)
      ["enfants":"Personne":private]=>
      NULL
    }
    [1]=>
    object(Personne)#3 (4) {
      ["nom":"Personne":private]=>
      string(11) "Bertholomé"
      ["prénom":"Personne":private]=>
      string(10) "Géraldine"
      ["âge":"Personne":private]=>
      int(12)
      ["enfants":"Personne":private]=>
      NULL
    }
  }
}
père={"nom":"Bertholomé","prénom":"Dieudonné","âge":58,"enfants":[{},{}]}

Comments

  • lines 3-12: the object [$enfant1];
  • lines 13-22: the array of attributes of the object [$enfant1]. We do have them all;
  • line 23: we do have the JSON string of the object [$enfant1];
  • lines 24-45: same for the object [$enfant2];
  • lines 46-113: for the father it is a little different, since his attribute [enfants] is not [null] as it was for the children;
  • line 113: we see that in the father's JSON string, the children are empty objects [{}];
  • lines 80-112: we see that in the father's array of attributes, child 1 has remained an object, and likewise child 2. In other words, the expression [\get_object_vars($this)], where [$this] represents the father, is not recursive: if an attribute of the [Personne] class is itself an object, the expression [\get_object_vars($this)] does not try to obtain its array of attributes. Yet the [json_encode] function only encodes the public attributes of an object: the children, all of whose attributes are private, become empty JSON objects.

Things can be improved. We modify the [Personne] class into the following [Personne2] class:

    // __toString
    public function __toString(): string
    {
        // on récupère les attributs de l'objet
        $attributes = $this->getAttributes();
        $enfants = $attributes["enfants"];
        if ($enfants !== null) {
            $attributes["enfants"] = [$enfants[0]->getAttributes(), $enfants[1]->getAttributes()];
        }
        // on rend la chaîne jSON des attributs
        return \json_encode($attributes, JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE);
    }

    public function getAttributes(): array
    {
        return \get_object_vars($this);
    }
}

Comments

  • lines 64-67: the [getAttributes] method returns the array of attributes of the object that calls it;
  • lines 52-62: the [__toString] method;
  • line 55: the object's attributes are retrieved into the array [$attributes];
  • line 56: we know, from the previous example, that [$attributes["enfants"]] is an array of two objects of type [Personne2];
  • lines 57-59: the two objects are replaced by their array of attributes;
  • line 61: all that remains is to encode the constructed array of attributes in JSON.

The script [json-02.php] uses the [Personne2] class as follows:

<?php

// respect strict des types déclarés des paramètres de fonctions
declare(strict_types=1);

// classe Personne2
require_once __DIR__ . "/Personne2.php";

// instanciation du père
$père = new Personne2();
// initialisation du père
$père->setFromArray([
    "nom" => "Bertholomé",
    "prénom" => "Dieudonné",
    "âge" => 58,
]);
// instanciation et initialisation enfant1
$enfant1 = (new Personne2())->setFromArray([
    "nom" => "Bertholomé",
    "prénom" => "Sylvain",
    "âge" => 17,
]);
// instanciation et initialisation enfant2
$enfant2 = (new Personne2())->setFromArray([
    "nom" => "Bertholomé",
    "prénom" => "Géraldine",
    "âge" => 12,
]);
// initialisation des enfants du père
$père->setFromArray([
    "enfants" => [$enfant1, $enfant2],
]);

// affichage du père
print "------------------------père\n";
print "père=$père\n";

The script [json-02.php] is identical to the script [json-01.php] except that the [Personne2] class has replaced the [Personne] class and only the father is displayed. The execution results are as follows:

> php json-02.php
------------------------père
père={"nom":"Bertholomé","prénom":"Dieudonné","âge":58,"enfants":[{"nom":"Bertholomé","prénom":"Sylvain","âge":17,"enfants":null},{"nom":"Bertholomé","prénom":"Géraldine","âge":12,"enfants":null}]}

This time, we did get the children along with the father.

The previous solution is not satisfactory, because the children may themselves have children. We then run into the previous problem again. The [Personne3] class solves this problem as follows:

    // __toString
    public function __toString(): string
    {
        // on rend la chaîne jSON des attributs
        $attributes = [];
        $this->getRecursiveAttributes($attributes, $this, []);
        // chaîne jSON des attributs
        return \json_encode($attributes, JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE);
    }

    public function getAttributes(): array
    {
        return \get_object_vars($this);
    }

    private function getRecursiveAttributes(array &$attributes, mixed $value, array $keys): void
    {
        // analyse de la valeur [$value]
        // $keys est un tableau [key1, key2, .., keyn]
        // $value=$attributes[key1][key2]...[keyn]
        // si [$value] est un objet on utilise sa méthode [getAttributes]
        if (\is_object($value)) {
            // attributs de l'objet [$value]
            $objectAttributes = $value->getAttributes();
            // y a-t-il des clés ?
            if ($keys) {
                // dans [$attributes], on va remplacer $value par le tableau de ses attributs
                // il faut construire l'élément $attributes[key1][key2]...[keyn]
                // où $keys est le tableau [key1, key2, .., keyn]
                // on prend la référence du tableau [$attributes]
                $attribute = &$attributes;
                // on scanne le tableau des clés
                foreach ($keys as $key) {
                    // on prend la référence de l'attribut
                    $attribute = &$attribute[$key];
                }
                // ici $attribute et $attributes[key1][key2]...[keyn] sont identiques
                // ils partagent le même emplacement mémoire
                // l'objet [$value] est remplacé par son tableau d'attributs :
                // il faut écrire $attributes[key1][key2]...[keyn]=$objectAttributes
                // ce qui équivaut à $attribute = $objectAttributes
                $attribute = $objectAttributes;
            } else {
                // pas de clés - on est au début de l'exploration de l'objet
                // $objectAttributes représente les attributs de 1er niveau de la classe
                $attributes += $objectAttributes;
            }
            // peut-être que dans [$objectAttributes] il y a encore des objets
            // on explore les attributs de [$objectAttributes]
            $this->getRecursiveAttributes($attributes, $objectAttributes, $keys);
        } elseif (\is_array($value)) {
            // on a un tableau - on analyse chacun de ses éléments
            foreach ($value as $key => $élément) {
                // on rajoute la clé courante au tableau $keys
                $keys[] = $key;
                // on analyse $élément
                $this->getRecursiveAttributes($attributes, $élément, $keys);
                // on enlève du tableau $keys la clé qui vient d'être analysée
                \array_pop($keys);
            }
        }
    }
}

Comments

  • line 56: this time, the [__toString] method asks for the attributes of its class and asks for this to be done recursively: if an attribute is an object or an array of objects, then each object must be replaced by its array of attributes in the final array of attributes of the class;
  • lines 66-112: the [getRecursiveAttributes] method does this work. Its code has been commented. Writing a recursive function is often something complex. That is the case here. The reader will lose nothing if they do not understand it: we will see right after that PHP offers a much simpler solution. The recursive call takes place on lines 100 and 107;
  • the value of this code is that it was not written for the [Personne3] class alone. It is valid for any class whose attributes have objects of different types as values, as long as the classes used by the main class have, like it, the [getAttributes] method of lines 61-64.

The script [json-03.php] uses the [Personne3] class as follows:

<?php

// respect strict des types déclarés des paramètres de fonctions
declare(strict_types=1);

// classe Personne3
require_once __DIR__ . "/Personne3.php";

// instanciation du père
$père = new Personne3();
// initialisation du père
$père->setFromArray([
    "nom" => "Bertholomé",
    "prénom" => "Dieudonné",
    "âge" => 58,
]);
// instanciation et initialisation enfant1
$enfant1 = (new Personne3())->setFromArray([
    "nom" => "Bertholomé",
    "prénom" => "Sylvain",
    "âge" => 27,
]);
// instanciation et initialisation enfant2
$enfant2 = (new Personne3())->setFromArray([
    "nom" => "Bertholomé",
    "prénom" => "Géraldine",
    "âge" => 12,
]);
// initialisation des enfants du père
$père->setFromArray([
    "enfants" => [$enfant1, $enfant2],
]);
// instanciation et initialisation enfant11
$enfant11 = (new Personne3())->setFromArray([
    "nom" => "Bertholomé",
    "prénom" => "Gaëtan",
    "âge" => 2,
]);
// instanciation et initialisation enfant12
$enfant12 = (new Personne3())->setFromArray([
    "nom" => "Bertholomé",
    "prénom" => "Mathilde",
    "âge" => 1,
]);
// initialisation des enfants de enfant1
$enfant1->setFromArray([
    "enfants" => [$enfant11, $enfant12],
]);
// affichage du père
print "------------------------père\n";
print "père=$père\n";
  • lines 34-47: [$enfant1] is given two children.

The execution results are as follows:

> php json-03.php
------------------------père
père={"nom":"Bertholomé","prénom":"Dieudonné","âge":58,"enfants":[{"nom":"Bertholomé","prénom":"Sylvain","âge":27,"enfants":[{"nom":"Bertholomé","prénom":"Gaëtan","âge":2,"enfants":null},{"nom":"Bertholomé","prénom":"Mathilde","âge":1,"enfants":null}]},{"nom":"Bertholomé","prénom":"Géraldine","âge":12,"enfants":null}]}

We did retrieve the JSON strings of all the [Personne3] objects making up the father.

docs.title: 5.24.1. The [JsonSerializable] interface
docs.text:
There is a much simpler solution, provided by PHP: the predefined interface [JsonSerializable]. We will study interfaces in the next chapter. For now, just remember that a class that "implements" the [JsonSerializable] interface must define a method [jsonSerialize(): mixed]. When the [json_encode] function encounters an object of this class, it calls its [jsonSerialize] method and encodes the returned value in place of the object. And it does so at every level of the data tree. The [Personne4] class uses this interface:

<?php

// respect strict des types déclarés des paramètres de fonctions
declare(strict_types=1);

// la classe implémente l'interface prédéfinie [JsonSerializable]
class Personne4 implements \JsonSerializable
{
    // constructeur avec promotion des paramètres
    public function __construct(
        private string $nom,
        private string $prénom,
        private int $âge,
        // tableau d'objets [Personne4]
        private array $enfants = [],
    ) {
    }

    // ajoute un enfant et rend l'objet courant pour chaîner les appels
    public function ajouterEnfant(Personne4 $enfant): static
    {
        $this->enfants[] = $enfant;
        return $this;
    }

    // méthode de l'interface [JsonSerializable] :
    // rend la valeur que [json_encode] doit encoder à la place de l'objet
    #[\Override]
    public function jsonSerialize(): mixed
    {
        return \get_object_vars($this);
    }

    // __toString : la chaîne jSON de l'objet
    public function __toString(): string
    {
        return \json_encode($this, JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE | JSON_PRETTY_PRINT | JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR);
    }
}

Comments

  • line 7: the class implements the [JsonSerializable] interface;
  • lines 10-16: a constructor with parameter promotion replaces the global setter. The array of children is empty by default;
  • lines 20-24: adds a child and returns the current object (return type [static]) so that calls can be chained;
  • line 29: the method required by the interface. Its return type is [mixed] (PHP 8.0), which means "any type". Here it returns the array of the object's attributes. The children remain [Personne4] objects in it: [json_encode] will call their own [jsonSerialize] method. The recursion is done by PHP;
  • line 28: the [#[\Override]] attribute also applies to a method required by an interface;
  • line 37: [json_encode] is called directly on the object. Three options are combined with the [|] operator:
    • [JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE]: accented characters are written as they are;
    • [JSON_PRETTY_PRINT]: the JSON string is formatted over several lines, with indentation;
    • [JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR] (PHP 7.3): in case of error, [json_encode] throws a [JsonException] exception instead of returning [false]. This is important here: the [__toString] method must return a string and cannot return [false].

The script [json-04.php] uses the [Personne4] class:

<?php

// respect strict des types déclarés des paramètres de fonctions
declare(strict_types=1);

// classe Personne4
require_once __DIR__ . "/Personne4.php";

// le père, ses enfants et ses petits-enfants
$enfant1 = (new Personne4("Bertholomé", "Sylvain", 27))
    ->ajouterEnfant(new Personne4("Bertholomé", "Gaëtan", 2))
    ->ajouterEnfant(new Personne4("Bertholomé", "Mathilde", 1));
$père = (new Personne4("Bertholomé", "Dieudonné", 58))
    ->ajouterEnfant($enfant1)
    ->ajouterEnfant(new Personne4("Bertholomé", "Géraldine", 12));

// affichage du père : [json_encode] appelle [jsonSerialize] sur chaque objet rencontré
print "------------------------père\n";
print "père=$père\n";
// une chaîne jSON compacte, sans échappement des caractères accentués
print "------------------------json_encode\n";
print json_encode($enfant1, JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE | JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR) . "\n";
// décodage : on obtient un tableau associatif (2e paramètre à true), pas un objet [Personne4]
print "------------------------json_decode\n";
$data = json_decode((string) $père, true, flags: JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR);
print "prénom du 1er petit-enfant : {$data['enfants'][0]['enfants'][0]['prénom']}\n";
// une chaîne jSON incorrecte provoque une exception [JsonException]
print "------------------------erreur\n";
try {
    json_decode('{"nom": "Bertholomé"', flags: JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR);
} catch (\JsonException $e) {
    print "Erreur : " . $e->getMessage() . "\n";
}
// sans [JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR], l'erreur est silencieuse
var_dump(json_decode('{"nom": "Bertholomé"'));
print "json_last_error_msg : " . json_last_error_msg() . "\n";

Results:

> php json-04.php
------------------------père
père={
    "nom": "Bertholomé",
    "prénom": "Dieudonné",
    "âge": 58,
    "enfants": [
        {
            "nom": "Bertholomé",
            "prénom": "Sylvain",
            "âge": 27,
            "enfants": [
                {
                    "nom": "Bertholomé",
                    "prénom": "Gaëtan",
                    "âge": 2,
                    "enfants": []
                },
                {
                    "nom": "Bertholomé",
                    "prénom": "Mathilde",
                    "âge": 1,
                    "enfants": []
                }
            ]
        },
        {
            "nom": "Bertholomé",
            "prénom": "Géraldine",
            "âge": 12,
            "enfants": []
        }
    ]
}
------------------------json_encode
{"nom":"Bertholomé","prénom":"Sylvain","âge":27,"enfants":[{"nom":"Bertholomé","prénom":"Gaëtan","âge":2,"enfants":[]},{"nom":"Bertholomé","prénom":"Mathilde","âge":1,"enfants":[]}]}
------------------------json_decode
prénom du 1er petit-enfant : Gaëtan
------------------------erreur
Erreur : Syntax error
NULL
json_last_error_msg : Syntax error

Comments

  • lines 10-12: construction of [$enfant1] and its two children through chained calls;
  • line 19: the father's [__toString] method produces a formatted JSON string containing all the descendants (lines 3-34 of the results). We have written no recursive code;
  • line 22: without [JSON_PRETTY_PRINT], the JSON string is compact (line 36 of the results);
  • line 25: the [json_decode] function performs the reverse operation: it transforms a JSON string into a PHP value. With a 2nd parameter set to [true], JSON objects become associative arrays. Note that we obtain arrays and not [Personne4] objects: rebuilding objects from a JSON string requires additional code (or a library such as Symfony's [Serializer] component). The named argument [flags:] avoids having to pass the 3rd parameter [depth];
  • line 30: the JSON string is incorrect (missing closing brace). With [JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR], a [JsonException] exception is thrown (line 40 of the results);
  • line 35: without [JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR], [json_decode] returns [null] without reporting anything (line 41). You must then remember to consult the [json_last_error_msg] function to find out whether an error occurred. This is why we will systematically use the [JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR] option in the rest of the course.

docs.title: 25. Conclusion
docs.text:
This document has presented the PHP 8 language through numerous scripts and a common thread, the income tax calculation, built in 13 versions:

  • versions 1 and 2 write the calculation with functions and text or JSON files;
  • version 3 writes it with classes, and version 4 organizes it in [dao] / [métier] / [console] layers, tested with [PHPUnit];
  • versions 5 to 7 fetch the tax data from a [MySQL] database, then a [PostgreSQL] one, then from either of them depending on a simple configuration file;
  • versions 8 to 11 turn the calculation into a web service, with a console client: authentication, sessions, logging, sending emails to the administrator, [Redis] cache, JSON then XML responses;
  • version 12 is an MVC web application that can respond in JSON, XML or HTML, with its console client;
  • version 13 protects the application's files by leaving only the [public] folder visible from the web.

Along the way, we have encountered most of what PHP 8 brings compared to PHP 7: strict typing and the types of parameters, return values and attributes; read-only classes and attributes, constructor parameter promotion, enumerations, property hooks and the asymmetric visibility of PHP 8.4; the [match] expression, the nullsafe operator, named arguments, the pipe operator of PHP 8.5; errors that have become exceptions; the new [PDO] and [DOM] APIs. Each time, we have also seen what PHP has abandoned: none of the scripts in this document displays a [Deprecated] message with PHP 8.5.

The architecture of the version 12 server (a main controller, secondary controllers, [métier] and [dao] layers, JSON, XML or HTML responses) is that of modern PHP web frameworks such as [Symfony] or [Laravel], some of whose components we have in fact used ([HttpFoundation], [HttpClient], [Mailer]). The reader who has followed this course has the foundations needed to tackle one of these frameworks.

The JSON web service of version 12 can also have clients other than the console client written in PHP: a JavaScript client run by a browser, a mobile application… This is the client / server architecture presented in the introduction of this document.

Serge Tahé's courses are available on the website https://stahe.github.io.

docs.title: 7. Exceptions and errors
docs.text:
When a method of a class encounters an unrecoverable error (non-existent file, database not connected, network connection down), it does not display an error on a console (file, database) but throws an exception. Exceptions extend the [\Exception] class. Besides exceptions, PHP's internal machinery also throws errors whose base class is the [\Error] class. Both classes implement the PHP interface [\Throwable].

PHP 8 profoundly changed error handling: many situations that in PHP 7 produced a mere warning (and an often absurd result) now throw an error that can be caught. We will see this throughout the examples.

docs.title: 7.1. The script tree
docs.text:
The scripts of this chapter are in the [scripts-console/exceptions] folder:

php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/exceptions
├── exceptions-01.php
├── exceptions-02.php
├── ...
├── exceptions-11.php
└── throwables.php

docs.title: 7.2. The [\Throwable] interface
docs.text:
The [\Throwable] interface is as follows (see the documentation):

interface Throwable extends Stringable
{
    public function getMessage(): string;
    public function getCode(): int;
    public function getFile(): string;
    public function getLine(): int;
    public function getTrace(): array;
    public function getTraceAsString(): string;
    public function getPrevious(): ?Throwable;
    public function __toString(): string;
}

The role of the interface's methods is as follows:

MethodRole[getMessage]returns the error message[getCode]returns the error code (an integer)[getFile]returns the name of the file where the object was created[getLine]returns the number of the line where the object was created[getTrace]returns the function call stack as an array[getTraceAsString]returns the function call stack as a string[getPrevious]returns the previous (wrapped) [Throwable] object, or [null][__toString]returns a string representation of the object

Note that the [Throwable] interface extends the [Stringable] interface encountered in the chapter on classes. A class cannot implement the [Throwable] interface directly: it must derive from [\Exception] or from [\Error].

docs.title: 7.3. Predefined exceptions and errors in PHP 8
docs.text:
The following [throwables.php] script displays the tree of predefined classes that implement the [Throwable] interface. We use it to get an exact list, that of PHP 8.5, rather than copying it from some documentation. The reader will lose nothing by not trying to understand its code, which uses PHP's reflection API (the [ReflectionClass] class lets you query PHP about a class: its name, its originating extension, its interfaces...) and a recursive function:

<?php

// respect strict des types déclarés des paramètres de fonctions
declare(strict_types=1);

// affiche l'arborescence des classes prédéfinies implémentant l'interface [Throwable]
// on se limite aux extensions toujours présentes dans PHP 8.5 :
// le noyau (Core), la bibliothèque standard, la bibliothèque SPL, jSON et Random
$extensions = ["Core", "standard", "SPL", "json", "random"];

// les classes prédéfinies de ces extensions qui implémentent [Throwable]
$classes = array_filter(
    get_declared_classes(),
    function (string $classe) use ($extensions): bool {
        $reflexion = new ReflectionClass($classe);
        return $reflexion->isInternal()
            && $reflexion->implementsInterface(Throwable::class)
            && in_array($reflexion->getExtensionName(), $extensions, true);
    }
);
sort($classes);

// affichage récursif des classes filles de la classe [$parent]
function afficher(?string $parent, array $classes, string $indentation): void
{
    // les filles directes de [$parent]
    $filles = array_values(array_filter(
        $classes,
        fn(string $classe): bool => (get_parent_class($classe) ?: null) === $parent
    ));
    foreach ($filles as $i => $fille) {
        $derniere = $i === count($filles) - 1;
        print $indentation . ($derniere ? "└── " : "├── ") . $fille . "\n";
        afficher($fille, $classes, $indentation . ($derniere ? "    " : "│   "));
    }
}

print "Throwable\n";
afficher(null, $classes, "");

Results:

> php throwables.php
Throwable
├── Error
│   ├── ArithmeticError
│   │   └── DivisionByZeroError
│   ├── AssertionError
│   ├── CompileError
│   │   └── ParseError
│   ├── FiberError
│   ├── Random\RandomError
│   │   └── Random\BrokenRandomEngineError
│   ├── TypeError
│   │   └── ArgumentCountError
│   ├── UnhandledMatchError
│   └── ValueError
└── Exception
    ├── ClosedGeneratorException
    ├── ErrorException
    ├── JsonException
    ├── LogicException
    │   ├── BadFunctionCallException
    │   │   └── BadMethodCallException
    │   ├── DomainException
    │   ├── InvalidArgumentException
    │   ├── LengthException
    │   └── OutOfRangeException
    ├── Random\RandomException
    ├── RequestParseBodyException
    └── RuntimeException
        ├── OutOfBoundsException
        ├── OverflowException
        ├── RangeException
        ├── UnderflowException
        └── UnexpectedValueException

Comments

  • line 13: the [get_declared_classes] function returns the list of all classes known at that moment, predefined or not;
  • lines 16-18: we keep only the predefined (internal) classes that implement the [Throwable] interface and belong to the extensions always present in PHP 8.5 (line 9). Other extensions add their own exceptions (for example [PDOException] for database access, which we will meet later);
  • lines 24-36: a recursive function that displays the direct child classes of the [$parent] class, then the children of each of them, and so on. The [get_parent_class] function returns [false] for a class without a parent: the [?:] operator then turns [false] into [null];
  • line 29: an arrow function (PHP 7.4), a short form of an anonymous function reduced to a single expression;
  • line 39: we start from the classes without a parent: [Error] and [Exception].

The results show two families:

  • the [Exception] family: these are the exceptions thrown by libraries and application code. It includes:
    • [ErrorException], which lets you turn a PHP warning into an exception (we will use it at the end of the chapter);
    • [JsonException] (PHP 7.3), thrown by [json_encode] and [json_decode] with the [JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR] option;
    • [Random\RandomException] (PHP 8.2), thrown by the random number generation functions;
    • the exceptions of the SPL (Standard PHP Library), a collection of classes and interfaces intended to solve problems frequently encountered by developers. They form two sub-families:
    • [LogicException] and its subclasses: programming errors, which a fix of the code should make disappear: invalid argument ([InvalidArgumentException]), value outside the expected domain ([DomainException]), non-existent method ([BadMethodCallException])...;
    • [RuntimeException] and its subclasses: errors that can only be detected at runtime: index out of bounds ([OutOfBoundsException]), unexpected value ([UnexpectedValueException]), capacity overflow ([OverflowException])...;
  • the [Error] family: these are the errors thrown by the PHP engine itself. It includes:
    • [TypeError]: a value does not have the expected type (function parameter, typed property, return value, operand of an operator...). Its subclass [ArgumentCountError] reports too few arguments;
    • [ValueError] (PHP 8.0): a value has the right type but an invalid value (for example a negative or zero length);
    • [ArithmeticError] and its subclass [DivisionByZeroError]: errors in arithmetic operations;
    • [UnhandledMatchError] (PHP 8.0): no arm of a [match] expression matches;
    • [AssertionError]: failure of an [assert] assertion;
    • [CompileError] and its subclass [ParseError]: syntax error in a file loaded by [require] or [include];
    • [FiberError] (PHP 8.1) and [Random\RandomError] (PHP 8.2): errors related to fibers and random generators, which we will not use.

The two families are not related in any way: a [catch (\Exception $e)] clause does not catch an [Error]. Only the [Throwable] interface brings them together.

docs.title: 7.4. Example 1
docs.text:
The first example [exceptions-01.php] shows both a PHP warning and an error:

<?php

// respect strict des types déclarés des paramètres de fonctions
declare(strict_types=1);

// affichage de toutes les erreurs
error_reporting(E_ALL);
ini_set("display_errors", "1");
// code --------
$var = [];
// clé inconnue
print $var["abcd"];
// division par zéro
$var = 7 / 0;
var_dump($var);
// tableau à bornes fixes
$array = new \SplFixedArray(5);
$array[1] = 2;
$array[4] = "foo";
// indice en-dehors des bornes
$array[5] = 8;

Comments

  • line 7: we ask PHP to report all errors. The parameter of the [error_reporting] function is the level of reported errors. It is a combination of the following constants (the main ones):
ConstantMeaning[E_ERROR]fatal runtime error: the script is stopped[E_WARNING]warning: the script continues[E_PARSE]syntax error detected at compile time[E_NOTICE]notice: something that could be an error[E_DEPRECATED]use of a deprecated feature, which will disappear in a future version[E_USER_WARNING], [E_USER_NOTICE], [E_USER_DEPRECATED]the same levels, triggered by the code with the [trigger_error] function[E_ALL]all levels
  • the [E_STRICT] constant, which no longer corresponds to any message since PHP 8.0, has been deprecated since PHP 8.4, as has the use of the [E_USER_ERROR] level with [trigger_error]: to report a fatal error, the code throws an exception;
  • line 8: we ask for errors to be displayed on the console. In production, we do the opposite: errors are written to a log file and not displayed;
  • line 12: we access a non-existent element of the [$var] array;
  • line 14: we perform a division by zero;
  • line 17: we create an instance of the [SplFixedArray] class of the SPL library. This class lets you create a fixed-size array with integer indices;
  • line 21: we access a non-existent element of the array.

Results:

> php exceptions-01.php

Warning: Undefined array key "abcd" in .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/exceptions/exceptions-01.php on line 12

Fatal error: Uncaught DivisionByZeroError: Division by zero in .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/exceptions/exceptions-01.php:14
Stack trace:
#0 {main}
  thrown in .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/exceptions/exceptions-01.php on line 14

Comments on the results

  • line 3: accessing a non-existent key of an array causes an [E_WARNING] level warning (it was a mere [E_NOTICE] in PHP 7). This does not interrupt the execution of the script;
  • lines 5-8: in PHP 7, dividing a number by zero caused an [E_WARNING] warning and returned the value [INF] (infinity). In PHP 8, the [/] operator throws an error of type [DivisionByZeroError]. Since it is not caught, it interrupts the execution of the script: it is a fatal error (Fatal error: Uncaught...). The message shows the call stack (Stack trace) at the time of the error;
  • the code following the division is not executed: the access to a non-existent index of the [SplFixedArray] array does not take place. We will come back to it in the following examples.

docs.title: 7.5. Handling exceptions
docs.text:
The [exceptions-02.php] script shows how to handle exceptions:

<?php

// respect strict des types déclarés des paramètres de fonctions
declare(strict_types=1);

// on affiche toutes les erreurs
error_reporting(E_ALL);
ini_set("display_errors", "1");
// on entoure le code par un try / catch
try {
    $var = [];
    // clé inconnue
    print $var["abcd"];
    // division par zéro
    $var = 7 / 0;
    var_dump($var);
    // tableau à bornes fixes
    $array = new \SplFixedArray(5);
    $array[1] = 2;
    $array[4] = "foo";
    // indice en-dehors des bornes
    $array[5] = 8;
    // vérification
    print "ce message ne sera pas affiché\n";
} catch (\Throwable $ex) {
    // \Throwable est l'interface implémentée par toutes les erreurs et exceptions
    // on affiche l'exception
    print "erreur, message : " . $ex->getMessage() . ", type : " . $ex::class . "\n";
}

Comments

  • the script is the one presented in the previous section. Only now, we have surrounded the code likely to cause errors with a [try / catch] structure: if the code of lines 11-24 causes (throws) an exception or an error, it will be handled by the [catch] clause of lines 25-29;
  • line 25: the parameter of the [catch] clause is the type of exception or error we want to handle. By using as type [\Throwable], which is an interface, we indicate that we want to handle any instance of a class implementing the [\Throwable] interface. Since all error and exception classes implement this interface, the [catch] clause here handles any error / exception;
  • line 15: the statement that triggers the error. As soon as an exception occurs, execution branches to the [catch] clause. The code that follows in the [try] is therefore not executed;
  • line 28: the notation [$ex::class] returns the name of the class of the [$ex] object.

Results:

> php exceptions-02.php

Warning: Undefined array key "abcd" in .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/exceptions/exceptions-02.php on line 13
erreur, message : Division by zero, type : DivisionByZeroError

Comments on the results

  • line 3: we find the [E_WARNING] level warning again. A warning is not an exception and is therefore not handled by the [catch] clause. We will see at the end of the chapter how to turn warnings into exceptions;
  • line 4: we have the error message written in the [catch] clause. So an exception derived from [\Exception] or an error derived from [\Error] occurred. We see here that it is the [DivisionByZeroError] class. The script ended normally.

docs.title: 7.6. Parameters of the [catch] clause
docs.text:
Let us examine the following [exceptions-03.php] script:

<?php

// respect strict des types déclarés des paramètres de fonctions
declare(strict_types=1);

// on affiche toutes les erreurs
error_reporting(E_ALL);
ini_set("display_errors", "1");

// un tableau à bornes fixes
$array = new \SplFixedArray(5);
try {
    // indice en-dehors des bornes
    $array[5] = 8;
} catch (\Throwable $ex) {
    // affichage message d'erreur
    print "Erreur 1 : " . $ex->getMessage() . " (" . $ex::class . ")\n";
}

try {
    // indice en-dehors des bornes
    $array[5] = 8;
} catch (\Exception $ex) {
    // affichage message d'erreur
    print "Erreur 2 : " . $ex->getMessage() . "\n";
}

try {
    // indice en-dehors des bornes
    $array[5] = 8;
} catch (\RuntimeException $ex) {
    // affichage message d'erreur
    print "Erreur 3 : " . $ex->getMessage() . "\n";
}

try {
    // indice en-dehors des bornes
    $array[5] = 8;
} catch (\OutOfBoundsException $ex) {
    // affichage message d'erreur
    print "Erreur 4 : " . $ex->getMessage() . "\n";
}

try {
    // division par 0
    intdiv(5, 0);
} catch (\Throwable $ex) {
    // affichage message d'erreur
    print "Erreur 5 : " . $ex->getMessage() . " (" . $ex::class . ")\n";
}

try {
    // division par 0
    intdiv(5, 0);
} catch (\DivisionByZeroError $ex) {
    // affichage message d'erreur
    print "Erreur 6 : " . $ex->getMessage() . "\n";
}

try {
    // division par 0
    intdiv(5, 0);
} catch (\ArithmeticError $ex) {
    // affichage message d'erreur
    print "Erreur 7 : " . $ex->getMessage() . "\n";
}

try {
    // division par 0
    intdiv(5, 0);
} catch (\Error $ex) {
    // affichage message d'erreur
    print "Erreur 8 : " . $ex->getMessage() . "\n";
}

try {
    // division par 0
    intdiv(5, 0);
} catch (\Exception $ex) {
    // affichage message d'erreur
    print "Erreur 9 : " . $ex->getMessage() . "\n";
}

Comments

  • lines 11-41: 4 different ways of handling the exception generated by using an incorrect index with the [\SplFixedArray] class. Execution shows that this error generates an exception of type [OutOfBoundsException] (line 2 of the results). In the PHP 7 course (and still in PHP 8.3), it was a [RuntimeException]. The change did not break existing code since the [OutOfBoundsException] class derives from the [RuntimeException] class;
    • line 15: handles an error of type [\Throwable]. This is valid since the [OutOfBoundsException] type derives from the [\Exception] type, which implements the [\Throwable] interface;
    • line 23: handles an error of type [\Exception]. This is valid since the [OutOfBoundsException] type derives from the [\Exception] type;
    • line 31: handles an error of type [\RuntimeException]. This is valid since the [OutOfBoundsException] type derives from the [\RuntimeException] type. It is a good choice: the code works whatever the PHP version;
    • line 39: handles the exact type of the generated exception;
  • lines 46-81: 5 different ways of handling the error generated by the [intdiv] function when it is passed a divisor equal to 0. The function [intdiv(int $dividend, int $divisor): int] performs the integer division [$dividend / $divisor]. When the divisor is zero, the [\DivisionByZeroError] error is thrown;
    • line 47: we catch any error implementing the [\Throwable] interface. This is valid;
    • line 55: we catch the exact type of the error: this is the preferred method;
    • line 63: we catch the [\ArithmeticError] type. This is valid since the [DivisionByZeroError] class extends the [ArithmeticError] class;
    • line 71: we catch the [\Error] type. This is valid since the [DivisionByZeroError] class derives from the [Error] class;
    • line 79: we catch the [\Exception] type. This is invalid because the [DivisionByZeroError] class has no relationship with the [\Exception] class.

Erreur 2 : Index invalid or out of range

Lines 11-15 of the results show that the [DivisionByZeroError] error was not caught by the last [catch (\Exception $ex)] clause: it is a fatal error.

docs.title: 7.7. The [finally] clause
docs.text:
The [try / catch] structure can have a third element and become a [try / catch / finally] structure. The code of the [finally] clause is executed in the following two cases:

  • the [try] clause does not throw an exception. It is then executed in full, then execution moves on to the [finally] clause, which is executed in full;
  • the [try] clause throws an exception. It is then executed up to the statement that throws the exception. Execution then moves on to the [catch] clause, which is executed in full. Then execution moves on to the [finally] clause, which is executed in full.

Ultimately, the code of the [finally] clause is always executed. This scenario is useful in the following case:

  • in the [try], the code has obtained resources (files, databases, network connections, queues). These resources are generally costly. They must then be released (most often we say closed) as soon as possible;
  • if the resources were acquired in the [try], their release will be placed in the [finally]. This ensures that in every case (error or not), the acquired resources are returned to the system.

The following script [exceptions-04.php] shows how the [finally] clause behaves in various situations:

<?php

// respect strict des types déclarés des paramètres de fonctions
declare(strict_types=1);

// on crée une instance d'exception
$e = new \Exception("Erreur...");

// premier test
try {
    print "Premier test\n";
    throw $e;
} catch (\Exception $ex1) {
    print $ex1->getMessage() . "\n";
} finally {
    print "Terminé\n";
}

// second test
try {
    print "Second test\n";
} catch (\Exception $ex1) {
    print $ex1->getMessage() . "\n";
} finally {
    print "Terminé\n";
}

// troisième test
try {
    print "Troisième test\n";
    return;
} catch (\Exception $ex1) {
    print $ex1->getMessage() . "\n";
} finally {
    print "Terminé\n";
}

Comments on the code

  • line 7: [$e] is an instance of the predefined [\Exception] class. We will throw it in various places;
  • lines 11-12: the [$e] exception is thrown in the [try] with the [throw] statement;
  • line 13: the [\Exception] exception is caught and its error message written to the console;
  • lines 15-16: the [finally] clause writes a message. According to what was said previously, this message should always be written, whether or not there is an error in the [try];
  • line 21: there is no error in the [try]. Here too we should go through the [finally];
  • line 31: there is a [return] statement in the [try] and no error. One may then wonder whether the [finally] clause will be executed. Execution shows that it is. Used outside a function, the [return] statement ends the script.

Results:

> php exceptions-04.php
Premier test
Erreur...
Terminé
Second test
Terminé
Troisième test
Terminé

Let us examine another case [exceptions-05.php]:

<?php

// respect strict des types déclarés des paramètres de fonctions
declare(strict_types=1);

// quatrième test
try {
    print "Quatrième test\n";
    exit;
} finally {
    print "Terminé\n";
}

Comments

  • line 9: the [exit] statement stops the execution of the script immediately: the [finally] clause is not executed;
  • lines 7-12: an example of [try / finally] without a [catch] clause. This is possible.

Results:

> php exceptions-05.php
Quatrième test

docs.title: 7.8. Creating your own exception classes
docs.text:
In a project of some size, it is useful to distinguish the various errors by wrapping them in different exception classes. In the previous scripts, we saw that any exception could be caught by a [catch (\Throwable $ex)] clause. This is advisable if we have no idea of the error being caught and the handling is the same for all errors. This is sometimes the case, but we often need to adapt the handling to the exact type of the error. We then need to distinguish the errors from one another.

Let us examine the following [exceptions-06.php] script:

<?php

// respect strict des types déclarés des paramètres de fonctions
declare(strict_types=1);

// on définit notre propre famille d'exceptions
class Exception1 extends \RuntimeException
{
}

class Exception2 extends \RuntimeException
{
}

// on utilise nos exceptions
$e1 = new Exception1("Erreur1...");
var_dump($e1);
$e2 = new Exception2("Erreur2...", 2);

// premier test
print "premier test\n";
try {
    // on lance un type Exception1
    throw $e1;
} catch (Exception1 $ex1) {
    print "Exception 1\n";
    print $ex1->getMessage() . "\n";
} catch (Exception2 $ex2) {
    print "Exception 2\n";
    print $ex2->getMessage() . "\n";
}

// second test
print "second test\n";
try {
    // on lance un type Exception2
    throw $e2;
} catch (Exception1 $ex1) {
    print "Exception 1\n";
    print $ex1->getMessage() . "\n";
} catch (Exception2 $ex2) {
    print "Exception 2\n";
    print $ex2->getMessage() . "\n";
}

// troisième test
print "troisième test\n";
try {
    // on lance un type Exception1
    throw $e1;
} catch (Exception1 | Exception2 $ex) {
    print "Exception 1 ou 2\n";
    print $ex->getMessage() . "\n";
}

// quatrième test
print "quatrième test\n";
try {
    // on lance un type Exception2
    throw $e2;
} catch (Exception1 | Exception2 $ex) {
    print "Exception 1 ou 2 : " . $ex::class . "\n";
    // les informations portées par l'exception
    print "message : " . $ex->getMessage() . "\n";
    print "code : " . $ex->getCode() . "\n";
    print "fichier : " . basename($ex->getFile()) . "\n";
    print "ligne : " . $ex->getLine() . "\n";
}

Comments

  • lines 7-9: we define two classes [Exception1] and [Exception2], both derived from the predefined [\RuntimeException] class. The body of these classes is empty. In other words, we use them only for their types: it is because they have different types that we will be able to distinguish these two exceptions in the [catch] clauses;
  • lines 16-18: we define two variables [$e1] and [$e2] of types [Exception1] and [Exception2] respectively. The constructor used is that of the [Exception] class, whose signature is [__construct(string $message = "", int $code = 0, ?Throwable $previous = null)]. For [$e2], we specified an error code;
  • lines 21-31: we have a [try / catch / catch] structure. This lets us handle different types of exception with different [catch] clauses. The first clause whose type matches is executed, the others are ignored;
  • line 25: catches exceptions of type [Exception1];
  • line 28: catches exceptions of type [Exception2];
  • line 51: catches exceptions of type [Exception1] or ([|]) [Exception2]. This syntax has existed since PHP 7.1;
  • line 62: the name of the class of the caught exception;
  • lines 64-67: the information carried by the exception, obtained through the methods of the [Throwable] interface. The [basename] function returns the name of a file without the path of its folder.

Results:

> php exceptions-06.php
object(Exception1)#1 (7) {
  ["message":protected]=>
  string(10) "Erreur1..."
  ["string":"Exception":private]=>
  string(0) ""
  ["code":protected]=>
  int(0)
  ["file":protected]=>
  string(76) ".../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/exceptions/exceptions-06.php"
  ["line":protected]=>
  int(16)
  ["trace":"Exception":private]=>
  array(0) {
  }
  ["previous":"Exception":private]=>
  NULL
}
premier test
Exception 1
Erreur1...
second test
Exception 2
Erreur2...
troisième test
Exception 1 ou 2
Erreur1...
quatrième test
Exception 1 ou 2 : Exception2
message : Erreur2...
code : 2
fichier : exceptions-06.php
ligne : 18

Comments on the results

  • lines 2-18: the "content" of an exception, displayed by [var_dump]:
    • lines 3-4: the error message;
    • lines 7-8: the error code;
    • lines 9-10: the name of the file in which the exception was created. The length shown (string(76)) is that of the full path of the file: it depends on the folder in which the script is located;
    • lines 11-12: the line at which the exception was created;
    • lines 13-15: the function call stack at the time the exception was created. It is empty here because the exception was created in the main script and not in a function;
    • lines 16-17: the previous exception. An exception can wrap another exception and thus define a stack of exceptions. The [previous] property will let us make use of this stack;
  • lines 29-33: note that the file and line of the exception are those of its creation by [new] (line 18) and not those of its throwing by [throw].

docs.title: 7.9. Rethrowing an exception
docs.text:
An exception can be thrown several times, as the following [exceptions-07.php] script shows:

<?php

// respect strict des types déclarés des paramètres de fonctions
declare(strict_types=1);

try {
    try {
        // on lance une exception
        throw new \Exception("test");
    } catch (\Exception $ex) {
        // on relance l'exception interceptée
        throw $ex;
    } finally {
        // on passera bien dans le finally
        print "finally 1\n";
    }
} catch (\Exception $ex2) {
    // on récupère bien l'exception initiale
    print $ex2->getMessage() . " dans try / catch / finally externe\n";
} finally {
    // on passera bien dans le finally
    print "finally 2\n";
}

Comments

  • line 9: we throw an exception;
  • line 10: we catch it;
  • line 12: we rethrow it. It then passes into the [try / catch / finally] structure of the enclosing level. This scenario is common: some code catches an exception to perform local processing (write a log, roll back a transaction...) then rethrows it so that the calling code is also notified;
  • line 17: we catch it again;
  • lines 13-15: execution shows that even after the [throw] of line 12, we do go through the [finally] clause of the inner [try / catch / finally].

Results:

> php exceptions-07.php
finally 1
test dans try / catch / finally externe
finally 2

docs.title: 7.10. Working with a stack of exceptions
docs.text:
An exception can wrap another exception, which itself can wrap another one, ultimately forming a stack of exceptions. Here is an example [exceptions-08.php]:

<?php

// respect strict des types déclarés des paramètres de fonctions
declare(strict_types=1);

// on définit notre propre famille d'exceptions
class Exception1 extends \RuntimeException
{
}

class Exception2 extends \RuntimeException
{
}

class Exception3 extends \RuntimeException
{
}

// on utilise nos exceptions
$e1 = new Exception1("Erreur 1...", 1, new Exception2("Erreur 2...", 2, new Exception3("Erreur 3...")));
var_dump($e1);
// exploitation de la pile d'exceptions
$e = $e1;
do {
    // message d'erreur de l'exception courante
    print $e::class . " : " . $e->getMessage() . "\n";
    // on passe à l'exception précédente (null s'il n'y en a pas)
    $e = $e->getPrevious();
} while ($e !== null);

Comments

  • lines 7-15: define three exception classes derived from the predefined [RuntimeException] exception;
  • line 20: an instance of the [Exception3] class is wrapped in an instance of the [Exception2] class, which itself is wrapped in an instance of the [Exception1] class. The constructor used here is the constructor of the [Exception] class: [__construct(string $message = "", int $code = 0, ?Throwable $previous = null)]. The 3rd parameter of the constructor lets you wrap an exception. This can be useful in the following scenario:
    • we define a method M that may generate an exception of type [Exception1] and only of this type, for reasons of compatibility with an interface, for example;
    • yet other types of exceptions may occur in method M. To report an error to the code calling method M, we will then wrap these exceptions in the [Exception1] type, which we will throw. This avoids losing the information contained in the wrapped exception, which was the original cause of the error;
  • lines 24-29: show how to walk through the stack of exceptions inside an exception. The [getPrevious] method returns the wrapped exception, or [null] if there is none. The [do ... while] loop executes its body at least once and then as long as the condition is true.
