  • lines 51-53: walking through the stack of exceptions.

docs.title: 7.11. PHP 7 warnings that became errors in PHP 8
docs.text:
We have seen that division by zero, which produced a warning in PHP 7, throws an error in PHP 8. This is not an isolated case: PHP 8 turned into errors many warnings after which execution continued with a wrong result. The [exceptions-09.php] script presents a few of them:

<?php

// respect strict des types déclarés des paramètres de fonctions
declare(strict_types=1);

// affiche le type et le message d'une erreur
function afficher(int $n, \Throwable $ex): void
{
    print "$n - " . $ex::class . " : " . $ex->getMessage() . "\n";
}

// une fonction à deux paramètres
function somme(int $a, int $b): int
{
    return $a + $b;
}

// 1 - variable non définie : un simple avertissement (Notice en PHP 7, Warning en PHP 8)
print "1 - [" . $inconnue . "]\n";
// 2 - modulo par zéro : avertissement + résultat faux en PHP 7, erreur en PHP 8
try {
    print 1 % 0;
} catch (\DivisionByZeroError $ex) {
    afficher(2, $ex);
}
// 3 - opération arithmétique sur un tableau
try {
    print [] + 1;
} catch (\TypeError $ex) {
    afficher(3, $ex);
}
// 4 - opération arithmétique sur une chaîne non numérique
try {
    print "abc" * 2;
} catch (\TypeError $ex) {
    afficher(4, $ex);
}
// 5 - mauvais type de paramètre pour une fonction prédéfinie
try {
    print strlen([1, 2]);
} catch (\TypeError $ex) {
    afficher(5, $ex);
}
// 6 - paramètre du bon type mais de valeur invalide
try {
    print_r(array_chunk([1, 2, 3], 0));
} catch (\ValueError $ex) {
    afficher(6, $ex);
}
// 7 - nombre d'arguments insuffisant
try {
    print somme(1);
} catch (\ArgumentCountError $ex) {
    afficher(7, $ex);
}
// 8 - expression [match] sans branche correspondante (PHP 8.0)
try {
    $jour = 8;
    print match ($jour) {
        6, 7 => "week-end",
        1, 2, 3, 4, 5 => "semaine",
    };
} catch (\UnhandledMatchError $ex) {
    afficher(8, $ex);
}
// 9 - méthode appelée sur null
try {
    $objet = null;
    $objet->methode();
} catch (\Error $ex) {
    afficher(9, $ex);
}
// 10 - l'opérateur nullsafe ?-> évite l'erreur précédente : le résultat est null
var_dump($objet?->methode());

Results:

> php exceptions-09.php

Warning: Undefined variable $inconnue in .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/exceptions/exceptions-09.php on line 19
1 - []
2 - DivisionByZeroError : Modulo by zero
3 - TypeError : Unsupported operand types: array + int
4 - TypeError : Unsupported operand types: string * int
5 - TypeError : strlen(): Argument #1 ($string) must be of type string, array given
6 - ValueError : array_chunk(): Argument #2 ($length) must be greater than 0
7 - ArgumentCountError : Too few arguments to function somme(), 1 passed in .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/exceptions/exceptions-09.php on line 52 and exactly 2 expected
8 - UnhandledMatchError : Unhandled match case 8
9 - Error : Call to a member function methode() on null
NULL

Comments

  • line 19: using an undefined variable remains a mere warning, but of level [E_WARNING] (it was an [E_NOTICE] in PHP 7). The variable is [null] and the script continues (lines 2-4 of the results);
  • line 22: modulo by zero throws a [DivisionByZeroError] error (line 5). This was already the case in PHP 7: only division [/] by zero produced a mere warning there;
  • line 28: an arithmetic operation on an array causes a [TypeError] error (line 6);
  • line 34: in PHP 7, an arithmetic operation on a non-numeric string caused the warning "A non-numeric value encountered" and the string was worth 0. In PHP 8, it is a [TypeError] error (line 7). A numeric string (["12" * 2]) is still accepted;
  • line 40: in PHP 7, passing a parameter of the wrong type to a predefined function caused a warning and the function returned [null]. In PHP 8, all predefined functions throw a [TypeError] error, like functions written by the developer (line 8). The message designates the parameter by its number and its name;
  • line 46: the parameter has the right type ([int]) but an invalid value (a length must be positive): it is a [ValueError] error, new in PHP 8.0 (line 9). In PHP 7, it was a warning;
  • line 52: the [somme] function expects two arguments and receives only one: [ArgumentCountError] error (line 10);
  • lines 59-62: the [match] expression has no arm for the value 8 and no [default] arm: [UnhandledMatchError] error (line 11). This is an important difference from the [switch] statement which, for its part, does nothing when no [case] matches;
  • line 69: calling a method on [null] is an [Error] error (line 12). This was already the case in PHP 7;
  • line 74: the nullsafe operator [?->] (PHP 8.0) returns [null] if the object is [null], instead of calling the method. This avoids writing an [if ($objet !== null)] test (line 13).

These changes make PHP 8 programs safer: an error interrupts processing instead of letting it continue with wrong data. They also force the developer to provide the corresponding [catch] clauses.

docs.title: 7.12. Multiple [catch], [catch] without a variable and [throw] expression
docs.text:
The [exceptions-10.php] script presents three PHP 8 conveniences and a common use of exception wrapping:

<?php

// respect strict des types déclarés des paramètres de fonctions
declare(strict_types=1);

// [throw] est une expression depuis PHP 8.0 : on peut l'utiliser après ?? ou dans une fonction fléchée
function lireAge(array $data): int
{
    $age = $data["age"] ?? throw new \InvalidArgumentException("L'âge est absent");
    return is_int($age) && $age >= 0 ? $age : throw new \DomainException("Âge [$age] invalide");
}

// une fonction fléchée qui ne fait que lancer une exception
$interdit = fn(string $operation) => throw new \LogicException("Opération [$operation] interdite");

// des données de test
$tests = [["age" => 48], [], ["age" => -4]];
foreach ($tests as $i => $data) {
    try {
        print "test $i : âge=" . lireAge($data) . "\n";
    } catch (\InvalidArgumentException | \DomainException $ex) {
        // une seule clause [catch] pour deux types d'exceptions
        print "test $i : " . $ex::class . " : " . $ex->getMessage() . "\n";
    }
}

try {
    $interdit("suppression");
} catch (\LogicException) {
    // depuis PHP 8.0, la variable de la clause [catch] est facultative
    print "l'opération a été refusée\n";
}

// encapsuler une exception de bas niveau dans une exception de l'application
class DaoException extends \RuntimeException
{
}

function lireConfiguration(string $json): array
{
    try {
        return json_decode($json, true, flags: JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR);
    } catch (\JsonException $ex) {
        // la cause originelle est passée en 3e paramètre : elle n'est pas perdue
        throw new DaoException("Configuration illisible", 10, $ex);
    }
}

try {
    lireConfiguration('{"dsn": "mysql:host=localhost"');
} catch (DaoException $ex) {
    print $ex::class . " : " . $ex->getMessage() . " (code " . $ex->getCode() . ")\n";
    print "cause : " . $ex->getPrevious()::class . " : " . $ex->getPrevious()->getMessage() . "\n";
}

Results:

> php exceptions-10.php
test 0 : âge=48
test 1 : InvalidArgumentException : L'âge est absent
test 2 : DomainException : Âge [-4] invalide
l'opération a été refusée
DaoException : Configuration illisible (code 10)
cause : JsonException : Syntax error

Comments

  • line 9: since PHP 8.0, [throw] is an expression and no longer just a statement. It can therefore be used where a value is expected: here, after the [??] operator. If the [age] key does not exist, the exception is thrown; otherwise [$age] receives its value;
  • line 10: [throw] used in a conditional expression [? :];
  • line 14: an arrow function whose body consists only of throwing an exception. Before PHP 8.0, this was impossible: an arrow function can only contain an expression;
  • line 21: a single [catch] clause for two types of exceptions (lines 3-4 of the results). Note that [InvalidArgumentException] and [DomainException] both derive from [LogicException]: a [catch (\LogicException $ex)] would have had the same effect;
  • line 29: since PHP 8.0, the variable of the [catch] clause is optional when we do not need the exception, only its type (line 5);
  • lines 35-37: an application-specific exception. In the following chapters, we will write data access layers (DAO, Data Access Object) that will throw only this type of exception, whatever the origin of the error (file, JSON, database);
  • lines 39-47: the [lireConfiguration] function decodes a JSON string. The low-level [JsonException] exception is caught and wrapped (line 45) in a [DaoException] exception. The original cause is passed as the 3rd parameter of the constructor;
  • line 53: the calling code knows only [DaoException], but it can retrieve the original cause of the error with the [getPrevious] method (lines 6-7 of the results).

docs.title: 7.13. Turning warnings into exceptions: [ErrorException]
docs.text:
Despite the progress of PHP 8, some anomalies remain mere warnings: non-existent array key, undefined variable, file that cannot be opened with [fopen]... These warnings cannot be caught by a [try / catch]. You can, however, install an error handler that turns them into [ErrorException] exceptions. This is what the [exceptions-11.php] script does:

<?php

// respect strict des types déclarés des paramètres de fonctions
declare(strict_types=1);

// gestionnaire d'erreurs : transforme les avertissements de PHP en exceptions [ErrorException]
set_error_handler(function (int $niveau, string $message, string $fichier, int $ligne): bool {
    throw new \ErrorException($message, 0, $niveau, $fichier, $ligne);
});

// une clé inconnue ne provoque plus un simple avertissement mais une exception
$personne = ["nom" => "Langevin"];
try {
    print $personne["prenom"] . "\n";
} catch (\ErrorException $ex) {
    print "Erreur : " . $ex->getMessage() . " (ligne " . $ex->getLine() . ")\n";
    print "niveau E_WARNING : " . var_export($ex->getSeverity() === E_WARNING, true) . "\n";
}
// idem pour l'ouverture d'un fichier inexistant
try {
    $flux = fopen(__DIR__ . "/inexistant.txt", "r");
} catch (\ErrorException $ex) {
    print "Erreur : " . $ex->getMessage() . "\n";
}
// on revient au gestionnaire d'erreurs de PHP
restore_error_handler();
print "fin\n";

Results:

> php exceptions-11.php
Erreur : Undefined array key "prenom" (ligne 14)
niveau E_WARNING : true
Erreur : fopen(.../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/exceptions/inexistant.txt): Failed to open stream: No such file or directory
fin

Comments

  • lines 7-9: the [set_error_handler] function installs an error handler: a function that PHP will call on each warning, notice or deprecation, instead of displaying its message. It receives the level of the error, its message, and the file and line where it occurred. Here, it throws an [ErrorException] exception that stores this information. The return type [bool] is the one specified by the documentation of [set_error_handler]: the function would return [false] to let PHP handle the error normally. It never returns anything here since it always throws an exception;
  • line 14: the [prenom] key does not exist. Instead of a warning, we get an [ErrorException] exception, which we catch (line 2 of the results);
  • line 17: the [getSeverity] method, specific to the [ErrorException] class, returns the level of the original error (line 3);
  • line 21: opening a non-existent file also becomes an exception (line 4);
  • line 26: restores the previous error handler, here PHP's own.

This technique is used by many PHP frameworks (Symfony, Laravel): in development, any warning becomes an exception, which forces you to fix the code. The [PHPUnit] testing tool that we will use later proceeds in a similar way: it can make a test fail if it produces a warning or a deprecation.

docs.title: 2. Installing a working environment
docs.text:
The scripts were written and tested in the following environment:

  • an [Apache] web server / [MySQL] DBMS / [PHP] 8.5 environment called [Laragon];
  • the [Visual Studio Code] editor and its [PHP Intelephense] extension;
  • the [Composer] dependency manager, shipped with [Laragon], which installs the PHP libraries used by the course.

Other tools (the [Mailpit] mail server, the [PostgreSQL] DBMS, the [Redis] server) are only useful in some chapters: their installation is described in the chapters concerned.

docs.title: 2.1. Installing Laragon
docs.text:
[Laragon] is a package for [Windows] that brings together several pieces of software:

  • an [Apache] web server. We will use it to write web scripts in PHP;
  • the [MySQL] DBMS (and also [PostgreSQL]);
  • the PHP scripting language, in several versions, including 8.5;
  • a [Redis] server implementing a cache for web applications;
  • the [Composer] tool;
  • a command terminal in which all these tools can be used directly.

[Laragon] can be downloaded from https://laragon.org/download/. It is free to use, with all its features; a window occasionally invites you to buy a license to support its development, which is optional. Installation presents no difficulty: accept the default choices. [Laragon] is then installed in the [C:\laragon] folder, which we will call <laragon> from now on:

C:\laragon
├── bin\        les logiciels : apache, mysql, php, redis, composer…
├── data\       les données des SGBD
├── etc\        des fichiers de configuration
├── tmp\
└── www\        la racine du serveur web Apache : http://localhost

Launching [Laragon] displays its main window:

  • the [Start All] button launches the [Apache] web server and the [MySQL] DBMS. The window then shows, for each of them, that it is running and which port it listens on: 80 for [Apache], 3306 for [MySQL];
  • the [Web] button displays the page [http://localhost], which corresponds to the [<laragon>/www] folder;
  • the [Database] button launches a database administration tool ([HeidiSQL], shipped with [Laragon]);
  • the [Terminal] button opens a command terminal in which [php], [composer], [mysql]… can be used directly;
  • the [Root] button opens the [Windows] file explorer on the [<laragon>/www] folder. This is where all the web applications served by [Laragon]'s [Apache] server must be placed;
  • a right-click in the window (or on the [Laragon] icon in the taskbar) opens the [Laragon] menu, which gives access to the configuration of each piece of software.

docs.title: 2.1.1. Choosing PHP 8.5
docs.text:
[Laragon] can contain several versions of PHP. The version used is chosen in its menu, under [PHP > Version]. Choose version 8.5 (the most recent of the 8.5 series). It is then used both by the [Apache] server and by the [php] command in the terminal.

For the [php] command to also be usable in [VS Code] terminals, the PHP folder must be in the [Windows] PATH. [Laragon] takes care of this: menu [Tools > Path > Add Laragon to Path]. Then open a new terminal (terminals that are already open do not see the change) and type:

> php -v

The command should display the PHP version, 8.5.x.

docs.title: 2.1.2. Configuring PHP for learning
docs.text:
PHP is configured by a text file [php.ini], accessible from the [Laragon] menu, under [PHP > php.ini]. While learning, PHP must report all errors, all warnings and all deprecations. Check that the file contains the following lines (or modify them):

error_reporting = E_ALL
display_errors = On
display_startup_errors = On
log_errors = On
error_log = C:/laragon/tmp/php_errors.log
date.timezone = Europe/Paris
  • [error_reporting = E_ALL]: PHP reports everything, including the [Deprecated] messages that announce features due to disappear. A production configuration often uses [E_ALL & ~E_DEPRECATED], which hides them: that is not what we want here;
  • [display_errors = On]: the messages are displayed in the script's output (the terminal, or the web page);
  • [log_errors = On]: the messages are also written to the error log;
  • [error_log]: the file of this log. Without this line, a console script writes its log to the terminal itself, and each message would appear there twice (once preceded by [PHP], once without);
  • [date.timezone]: the time zone used by the date functions.

The course also uses several PHP extensions. They are enabled in the [Laragon] menu, under [PHP > Extensions], or in the [php.ini] file with lines of the form [extension=nom]. The extensions used are: [curl], [mbstring], [openssl], [pdo_mysql], [pdo_pgsql], [fileinfo] and [zip] (the latter is used by [Composer] to unzip the libraries it downloads). After modifying the [php.ini] file, [Apache] must be restarted ([Laragon]'s [Reload] button); console scripts, on the other hand, reread the [php.ini] file each time they are executed.

The configuration can be checked in a terminal with the command [php --ini] (the [php.ini] file used) and [php -m] (the list of loaded extensions). The first script of the next chapter, [phpinfo.php], displays the whole configuration.

docs.title: 2.2. Installing VS Code
docs.text:
[Visual Studio Code] is a free editor from Microsoft, which can be downloaded from https://code.visualstudio.com/. Here it replaces the [NetBeans] IDE used by the PHP 7 course.

Once [VS Code] is installed, we add support for the PHP language: in the [Extensions] panel (Ctrl+Shift+X), search for and install the [PHP Intelephense] extension. It provides:

  • code completion: PHP functions, classes, their methods and their attributes are suggested as you type;
  • display of the documentation of a function or method when hovering over its name;
  • error detection as you type (undefined variable, wrong type, non-existent method…), underlined in the code and gathered in the [Problems] panel;
  • code navigation: a Ctrl+click on a class or function name opens its definition, including in the libraries of the [vendor] folder.

[Intelephense] must know the version of PHP used in order to know its new features: in the [VS Code] settings (Ctrl+comma), search for "intelephense php version" and enter 8.5.

You then work by opening the course code folder in [VS Code] (menu [File > Open Folder]). A terminal is opened with the menu [Terminal > New Terminal]: it is positioned on the open folder, and you type the [php], [composer], [curl]… commands in it. To execute a console script, go to its folder ([cd] command) and type [php nom-du-script.php].

docs.title: 2.3. Installing the course code
docs.text:
The course code forms a folder [php8-oct-2026], which can be downloaded at the beginning of this document. Place it in the [<laragon>/www] folder:

C:\laragon\www
└── php8-oct-2026
    ├── composer.json
    ├── phpunit.xml
    ├── scripts-console
    └── scripts-web

Its web scripts are then accessible at the URL [http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/...]. For example, once [Apache] is started, the URL [http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/composer.json] should display the [composer.json] file.

docs.title: 2.4. Installing the libraries with Composer
docs.text:
Like most languages, PHP has a dependency manager, [Composer], which downloads the libraries a project needs from the [packagist.org] repository. The libraries used by the course are declared in the [composer.json] file of the [php8-oct-2026] folder:

{
    "name": "stahe/php8-oct-2026",
    "description": "Codes du cours « Introduction au langage PHP 8 par l'exemple » (octobre 2026)",
    "type": "project",
    "license": "MIT",
    "require": {
        "php": ">=8.5",
        "symfony/http-foundation": "^8.0",
        "symfony/http-client": "^8.0",
        "symfony/mailer": "^8.0",
        "symfony/mime": "^8.0",
        "predis/predis": "^3.0",
        "zbateson/mail-mime-parser": "^3.0"
    },
    "require-dev": {
        "phpunit/phpunit": "^12.0"
    },
    "config": {
        "sort-packages": true
    }
}
  • line 6: the libraries needed to execute the scripts. Each one is designated by a name of the form [vendor/package] and a version constraint: [^8.0] means "any version 8.x from 8.0 on". Their role is presented in the chapters that use them;
  • line 7: the project requires PHP 8.5 or later;
  • line 15: the libraries needed only for development, here the [PHPUnit] testing framework.

To install these libraries, open a terminal in the [php8-oct-2026] folder (the [Laragon] terminal, or the [VS Code] one) and type:

> composer install

[Composer] then creates a [vendor] folder containing the libraries and their own dependencies, as well as a [vendor/autoload.php] file. A script that wants to use these libraries only has to include this file, which automatically loads their classes the first time they are used. The course scripts do this with a path relative to their own folder, for example:

require_once __DIR__ . '/../../vendor/autoload.php';

The [__DIR__] constant designates the folder of the script that uses it: the path therefore depends neither on the folder in which the script is executed nor on where the [php8-oct-2026] folder has been placed.

We check the installation by displaying the [PHPUnit] version:

> php vendor/bin/phpunit --version
PHPUnit 12.5.37 by Sebastian Bergmann and contributors.

Now that the working environment has been installed, we can tackle the basics of PHP.

docs.title: 6. Interfaces
docs.text: An interface is a structure that defines method prototypes. A class implementing an interface must define the code of all the interface's methods. An interface is a contract: it says what an object can do, without saying how it does it.

docs.title: 6.1. The script tree
docs.text:
The scripts of this chapter are in the [scripts-console/interfaces] folder:

php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/interfaces
├── ICalcul.php
├── IExemple.php
├── IExemple2.php
├── interface-01.php
├── interface-02.php
├── interface-03.php
└── interface-04.php

docs.title: 6.2. A first interface
docs.text:
We define an interface [IExemple] in a script [IExemple.php]. In this same script, we define two classes implementing the [IExemple] interface:

<?php

// respect strict des types déclarés des paramètres de fonctions
declare(strict_types=1);

// espace de noms
namespace Exemples;

// une interface
interface IExemple
{
    // les méthodes de l'interface
    public function ajouter(int $i, int $j): int;

    public function soustraire(int $i, int $j): int;
}

// implémentation 1 de l'interface IExemple
class Classe1 implements IExemple
{
    public function ajouter(int $a, int $b): int
    {
        return $a + $b + 10;
    }

    public function soustraire(int $a, int $b): int
    {
        return $a - $b + 20;
    }
}

// implémentation 2 de l'interface IExemple
class Classe2 implements IExemple
{
    public function ajouter(int $a, int $b): int
    {
        return $a + $b + 100;
    }

    public function soustraire(int $a, int $b): int
    {
        return $a - $b + 200;
    }
}

Comments

  • lines 10-15: the [IExemple] interface defines two methods: the [ajouter] function (line 13) and the [soustraire] function (line 15). The interface does not define the code of these methods. The classes implementing the interface will do that. The methods of an interface are necessarily public;
  • line 19: the [Classe1] class implements ([implements]) the [IExemple] interface. It therefore defines code for the methods [ajouter] (line 21) and [soustraire] (line 26). The parameter names may differ from those of the interface ([$a] instead of [$i]) but their types must be compatible. Be careful, however: with PHP 8 named arguments, a call [ajouter(i: 1, j: 2)] would not work with [Classe1]. It is therefore preferable to keep the interface's names;
  • lines 33-44: the same for the [Classe2] class.

We use the [IExemple] interface in the following [interface-01.php] script:

<?php

// respect strict des types déclarés des paramètres de fonctions
declare(strict_types=1);

// inclusion et déclaration des classes et interfaces utilisées par le script
require_once __DIR__ . "/IExemple.php";
use Exemples\Classe1;
use Exemples\Classe2;
use Exemples\IExemple;

// fonction
function calculer(int $a, int $b, IExemple $interface): void
{
    print $interface->ajouter($a, $b) . "\n";
    print $interface->soustraire($a, $b) . "\n";
}

// ------------------- main
// création de 2 objets de type Classe1 et Classe2
$c1 = new Classe1();
$c2 = new Classe2();
// appel de la fonction calculer
calculer(4, 3, $c1);
calculer(14, 13, $c2);
// une interface ne peut pas être instanciée
try {
    new IExemple();
} catch (\Error $e) {
    print "Erreur : " . $e->getMessage() . "\n";
}

Results:

> php interface-01.php
17
21
127
201
Erreur : Cannot instantiate interface Exemples\IExemple

Comments

  • lines 7-10: inclusion and declaration of the classes and interfaces used by the script. The [IExemple.php] file is included with the [require_once] statement: it will be included only once even if several scripts of the project include it;
  • lines 13-17: we define a function;
  • line 13: here we have declared the type of the three parameters. If at runtime the actual parameter is not of the expected type, a [TypeError] error is thrown. The 3rd parameter is of type [IExemple]. This means that the actual parameter must be an instance of a class implementing the [IExemple] interface, so in our example, an instance of the [Classe1] or [Classe2] classes. The [calculer] function does not know these classes: it only knows the interface. We will be able to pass it objects of classes written later, provided they implement the [IExemple] interface;
  • lines 15-16: we use the [ajouter, soustraire] methods of the [IExemple] interface;
  • line 24: the 3rd actual parameter is of type [Classe1], compatible with the [IExemple] type of the function's 3rd formal parameter;
  • line 25: the same for the [Classe2] class;
  • line 28: an interface cannot be instantiated: we get an error (line 6 of the results).

docs.title: 6.3. Extending an interface
docs.text:
In the same way that a child class can extend a parent class, a child interface can extend a parent interface.

Let us consider the [IExemple2] interface defined in the [IExemple2.php] file:

<?php

// respect strict des types déclarés des paramètres de fonctions
declare(strict_types=1);

// espace de noms
namespace Exemples;

// inclusion de la définition de l'interface IExemple
require_once __DIR__ . "/IExemple.php";

// une interface qui dérive de IExemple
interface IExemple2 extends IExemple
{
    // la méthode ajoutée par l'interface
    public function multiplier(int $i, int $j): int;
}

// implémentation de l'interface IExemple2
class Classe3 extends Classe2 implements IExemple2
{
    // [Override] vérifie que la méthode existe bien dans l'interface
    #[\Override]
    public function multiplier(int $a, int $b): int
    {
        return $a * $b;
    }
}

Comments

  • line 7: the [IExemple2] interface will be in the same namespace as the [IExemple] interface;
  • line 10: we include the file defining the [IExemple] interface;
  • lines 13-17: define the [IExemple2] interface, which extends ([extends]) the [IExemple] interface and adds a new method to it (line 16). An interface can even extend several interfaces: [interface I3 extends I1, I2];
  • lines 20-28: the [Classe3] class extends the [Classe2] class. Since the latter implements the [IExemple] interface, so will the [Classe3] class. Indeed, [Classe3] inherits all the public and protected methods of the [Classe2] class, and therefore the [ajouter] and [soustraire] methods. In addition, we state that [Classe3] implements the [IExemple2] interface. As such, it must also implement the [multiplier] method, which [Classe2] does not. This is what lines 24-27 do;
  • line 23: since PHP 8.3, the [#[\Override]] attribute, encountered in the previous chapter, also applies to a method that implements an interface method. If the [multiplier] method disappeared from the [IExemple2] interface, PHP would report it.

The [IExemple2] interface is used by the following [interface-02.php] script:

<?php

// respect strict des types déclarés des paramètres de fonctions
declare(strict_types=1);

// inclusion et déclaration des classes et interfaces nécessaires au script
require_once __DIR__ . "/IExemple2.php";
use Exemples\IExemple2;
use Exemples\Classe3;

// fonction
function calculer(int $a, int $b, IExemple2 $interface): void
{
    print $interface->ajouter($a, $b) . "\n";
    print $interface->soustraire($a, $b) . "\n";
    print $interface->multiplier($a, $b) . "\n";
}

// ------------------- main
// création d'1 objet de type Classe3 qui implémente IExemple2
$c3 = new Classe3();
// appel de la fonction calculer
calculer(4, 3, $c3);

Results:

> php interface-02.php
107
201
12

Comments

  • line 12: the 3rd parameter of the [calculer] function is of type [IExemple2];
  • lines 14-16: we use the three methods of the [IExemple2] interface: the two inherited from [IExemple] and its own;
  • line 23: we call the [calculer] function with, as 3rd parameter, an object of type [Classe3] which implements [IExemple2] (line 21).

docs.title: 6.4. Passing an interface as a function parameter
docs.text:
We saw in the previous chapter (section "Passing an object as a function parameter") that when the type expected for a function parameter is a class, the actual parameter can be an object of the expected type or of a derived type. The same holds for interfaces, as the following script [interface-03.php] shows:

<?php

// respect strict des types déclarés des paramètres de fonctions
declare(strict_types=1);

// inclusion et déclaration des classes et interfaces nécessaires au script
require_once __DIR__ . "/IExemple.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/IExemple2.php";
use Exemples\IExemple;
use Exemples\IExemple2;
use Exemples\Classe1;
use Exemples\Classe3;

// fonction
function calculer(int $a, int $b, IExemple $interface): void
{
    print $interface->ajouter($a, $b) . "\n";
    print $interface->soustraire($a, $b) . "\n";
}

// ------------------- main
// création d'1 objet de type Classe3 qui implémente IExemple2 et donc IExemple
$c3 = new Classe3();
// appel de la fonction calculer
calculer(4, 3, $c3);
// l'opérateur [instanceof] teste si un objet implémente une interface
foreach ([new Classe1(), $c3] as $objet) {
    print $objet::class . " : IExemple=" . var_export($objet instanceof IExemple, true)
        . ", IExemple2=" . var_export($objet instanceof IExemple2, true) . "\n";
}
// les interfaces implémentées par la classe Classe3
print_r(class_implements($c3));

Results:

> php interface-03.php
107
201
Exemples\Classe1 : IExemple=true, IExemple2=false
Exemples\Classe3 : IExemple=true, IExemple2=true
Array
(
    [Exemples\IExemple] => Exemples\IExemple
    [Exemples\IExemple2] => Exemples\IExemple2
)

Comments

  • line 15: the [calculer] function expects an [IExemple] type as its third parameter. This means that the actual parameter may be of type [IExemple] or of a derived type;
  • line 23: we instantiate an object [$c3] of type [Classe3], a class that implements the [IExemple2] interface, which itself extends the [IExemple] interface. So ultimately [$c3] implements the [IExemple] interface;
  • line 25: we call the [calculer] function with, as third parameter, the object [$c3] of type [Classe3]. Through the interplay of class inheritance and interface implementation, we saw that the object [$c3] implemented the [IExemple] type. We can therefore use it as the third parameter;
  • lines 27-30: the [instanceof] operator tests whether an object implements an interface. A [Classe1] object implements [IExemple] but not [IExemple2] (line 4 of the results). A [Classe3] object implements both (line 5);
  • line 32: the [class_implements] function returns the list of interfaces implemented by an object or a class, directly or through inheritance (lines 6-10 of the results).

docs.title: 6.5. Interface constants, multiple interfaces and intersection types
docs.text:
An interface can also declare constants, and a class can implement several interfaces. We define two interfaces [ICalcul] and [INommable] and two classes implementing them in the [ICalcul.php] file:

<?php

// respect strict des types déclarés des paramètres de fonctions
declare(strict_types=1);

// espace de noms
namespace Exemples;

// une interface peut déclarer des constantes
interface ICalcul
{
    // constante typée (PHP 8.3)
    public const int PRECISION = 2;

    public function calculer(float $a, float $b): float;
}

// une seconde interface
interface INommable
{
    public function getNom(): string;
}

// une classe peut implémenter plusieurs interfaces
final class Addition implements ICalcul, INommable
{
    #[\Override]
    public function calculer(float $a, float $b): float
    {
        return round($a + $b, self::PRECISION);
    }

    #[\Override]
    public function getNom(): string
    {
        return "addition";
    }
}

final class Division implements ICalcul, INommable
{
    #[\Override]
    public function calculer(float $a, float $b): float
    {
        // [ICalcul::PRECISION] et [self::PRECISION] désignent la même constante
        return round($a / $b, ICalcul::PRECISION);
    }

    #[\Override]
    public function getNom(): string
    {
        return "division";
    }
}

Comments

  • line 13: the [ICalcul] interface declares a constant. All classes that implement the interface inherit it. Since PHP 8.3, a class or interface constant can be typed (here [int]);
  • lines 19-22: a second interface, with a single method;
  • line 25: the [Addition] class implements both interfaces: the interface names are separated by commas. It must define the methods of both;
  • line 30: the constant inherited from the interface is reached through [self::PRECISION]. The [round] function rounds a number to the given number of decimal places;
  • line 46: the constant can also be designated by the interface name: [ICalcul::PRECISION].

These interfaces are used by the [interface-04.php] script:

<?php

// respect strict des types déclarés des paramètres de fonctions
declare(strict_types=1);

// inclusion et déclaration des classes et interfaces nécessaires au script
require_once __DIR__ . "/ICalcul.php";
use Exemples\ICalcul;
use Exemples\INommable;
use Exemples\Addition;
use Exemples\Division;

// le paramètre [$calcul] a une valeur par défaut : un objet créé par [new] (PHP 8.1)
function executer(float $a, float $b, ICalcul $calcul = new Addition()): float
{
    return $calcul->calculer($a, $b);
}

// type intersection (PHP 8.1) : [$operation] doit implémenter les deux interfaces
function afficher(float $a, float $b, ICalcul&INommable $operation): void
{
    print $operation->getNom() . "($a, $b)=" . $operation->calculer($a, $b) . "\n";
}

// ------------------- main
// constante de l'interface
print "précision : " . ICalcul::PRECISION . " décimales\n";
// valeur par défaut du 3e paramètre
print "executer(1.234, 2.345)=" . executer(1.234, 2.345) . "\n";
// paramètre explicite
print "executer(10, 3, new Division())=" . executer(10, 3, new Division()) . "\n";
// type intersection
afficher(10, 4, new Division());
afficher(10, 4, new Addition());
// les classes implémentent les deux interfaces
print_r(class_implements(Division::class));

Results:

> php interface-04.php
précision : 2 décimales
executer(1.234, 2.345)=3.58
executer(10, 3, new Division())=3.33
division(10, 4)=2.5
addition(10, 4)=14
Array
(
    [Exemples\ICalcul] => Exemples\ICalcul
    [Exemples\INommable] => Exemples\INommable
)

Comments

  • line 14: the 3rd parameter of the [executer] function is of type [ICalcul] and has a default value, an [Addition] object created with [new]. Up to PHP 8.0, the default value of a parameter could only be a constant. Since PHP 8.1, the [new] expression is accepted in parameter default values ("new in initializers"), as well as in the arguments of PHP attributes ([#[...]]), static variables and global constants. It remains forbidden in the default value of a class property. The object is created on each call that omits the parameter;
  • line 20: the type [ICalcul&INommable] is an intersection type (PHP 8.1): the actual parameter must implement both [ICalcul] and [INommable]. The function can then call the methods of both interfaces. It must not be confused with the union type [ICalcul|INommable] (one or the other);
  • line 27: the constant is accessible from outside through the interface name (line 2 of the results);
  • line 29: the 3rd parameter is omitted: an [Addition] object performs the calculation (line 3);
  • line 31: we explicitly pass a [Division] object (line 4). Note that the integers 10 and 3 are accepted for [float] parameters despite the [strict_types=1] declaration: converting an [int] to a [float] is the only automatic conversion allowed in strict mode;
  • lines 33-34: both classes implement both interfaces: they are accepted by the [afficher] function (lines 5-6);
  • line 36: the notation [Division::class] returns the fully qualified class name, here [Exemples\Division]. The [class_implements] function accepts a class name as well as an object.

Interfaces are ubiquitous in PHP itself. We have already encountered two of them in the previous chapter: [Stringable], implemented automatically by any class having a [__toString] method, and [JsonSerializable], which lets you control the JSON encoding of an object. In the next chapter we will meet the [Throwable] interface, implemented by all errors and exceptions. An enumeration can also implement an interface. Finally, we will see later in the course that interfaces are the foundation of the layered architecture of our applications: each layer knows only the interface of the neighbouring layer.

docs.title: 1. Introduction
docs.text:
The PDF of the document is HERE.

The code of the document is HERE.

This document is a product of Anthropic's AI, Claude. It is a rewrite, for the PHP 8 language, of the course Introduction to the PHP 7 language by example written by Serge Tahé in July 2019. It keeps that course's outline, examples and common thread, and changes its language:

  • the 2019 course used PHP 7.3. Since then, PHP has gone through six major versions: 8.0 (2020), 8.1 (2021), 8.2 (2022), 8.3 (2023), 8.4 (2024) and 8.5 (2025). This document uses PHP 8.5;
  • between these two versions, PHP has changed a great deal: many features have appeared (types, enumerations, read-only classes, [match], named arguments…), and many others have become deprecated: they still work, but PHP displays a [Deprecated] message each time they are used, to warn that they will disappear in a future version. The code in this document uses no deprecated feature: all the scripts were executed with PHP 8.5 configured to display all errors, all warnings and all deprecations, and no [Deprecated] message appears in their results;
  • the tools have changed too: the [VS Code] editor replaces the [NetBeans] IDE, the [PHPUnit] testing framework replaces [Codeception], the [curl] command replaces the [Postman] tool, the [Symfony Mailer] library replaces the abandoned [SwiftMailer], and the [Mailpit] mail server replaces [hMailServer], which has also been abandoned.

This document offers a series of PHP console scripts in various areas (language structures, classes, access to files, databases and the internet). Web programming is approached through web services. In this document, a web service is any web application that produces data (plain text, JSON, XML) rather than HTML pages. These are data servers, not servers of web pages mixing HTML, CSS and JavaScript. The document covers classic web concepts (the HTTP protocol, JSON or XML responses, session management, authentication) that are also used in classic web programming. The last part of the document also builds an HTML web application.

docs.title: 1.1. The place of PHP in a client / server application
docs.text:
Nowadays, web applications are often built in client / server mode:

  • in [1], the web browser displays web pages for a user. These pages contain JavaScript implementing a client of a data web service [2] as well as a client of a server of web page fragments [3]. JavaScript frameworks such as [Vue.js], [React] or [Angular] are designed for this;
  • in [2], the web server is a data server. It can be written in any language, for example PHP. It does not produce web pages in the classic sense (HTML, CSS, JavaScript), except perhaps the first time. But this first page can be obtained from a classic web server [3]. The JavaScript of the initial page then generates the application's various web pages by obtaining the data [4] to be displayed from the data server [2]. It can also obtain web page fragments [5] from the web page server [3] to dress up this data;
  • in [4], the user initiates an action;
  • in [6, 7], they receive data dressed up by a web page fragment.

In this document, we will write client / server applications in PHP with the following structure:

This is a client / server application written entirely in PHP. A console script [9] will query a data server [4]. What is learned here for writing the data service can be reused in a web application: the PHP data service can be kept and the PHP client replaced by a JavaScript client.

As the common thread of the document, we will build an income tax calculation service in 13 versions. Version 12 will have the following architecture:

The server's [web] layer will have an MVC (Model – View – Controller) architecture. It will be able to respond in JSON, XML or HTML. The whole course aims to build this version, which version 13 secures.

docs.text:
The examples were written and tested with the following tools (their installation is described in the next chapter):

  • [PHP] 8.5, configured to report all errors, all warnings and all deprecations;
  • the [Laragon] 8 package, which brings together under [Windows] PHP 8.5, the [Apache] 2.4 web server, the [MySQL] 8.4 and [PostgreSQL] DBMSs, the [Redis] server and the [Composer] dependency manager;
  • the [Visual Studio Code] (VS Code) editor and its [PHP Intelephense] extension;
  • the PHP libraries installed with [Composer]: [symfony/http-foundation], [symfony/http-client], [symfony/mailer], [symfony/mime] 8, [predis/predis] 3, [zbateson/mail-mime-parser] 3 and, for testing, [phpunit/phpunit] 12;
  • the [Mailpit] test mail server and, for the IMAP protocol, an IMAP server (a [Gmail] account, or a local server);
  • the [curl] command-line tool, shipped with [Windows], which displays raw HTTP exchanges;
  • a browser ([Chrome], [Firefox], [Edge]…).

The scripts in this document are commented and their console execution is reproduced. Additional explanations are sometimes provided. The document requires active reading: to understand a script, you need to read its code, its comments and its execution results. The screenshots of web pages were taken with a programmatically driven browser: they are real pages of the course's applications.
