docs.title: 10.1. Introduction
docs.text:
The scripts of this chapter are in the [scripts-console/troiscouches] folder:

php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/troiscouches
├── Dao1.php
├── Dao2.php
├── IDao.php
├── IMetier.php
├── main1.php
├── main2.php
├── Metier.php
└── Personne.php

We are now going to discover how to structure a PHP application in layers:

In this diagram, it is the left-hand layer that takes the initiative of using the right-hand layer. The role of the layers is as follows:

  • [1]: the layer called [dao] (Data Access Objects) handles exchanges with external data stores [4] (files, databases, web services…). This layer is sometimes called [DAL] (Data Access Layer), a term that better describes its role. This layer can read data [3] or write data [2]. It is called upon by the [métier] layer [6] and returns results to it [7];
  • [5]: a layer called [métier] (business) that groups together "business" procedures to which all the data they need is supplied. It is generally the most stable layer of a project because it does not depend on the way the data are acquired. The data have two sources:
    • [9]: the data supplied by the PHP script;
    • [6, 7]: the data requested from the [dao] layer;
  • [8]: the main script is the conductor. In a console application, it will:
    • create the [métier] and [dao] layers;
    • run the application's algorithm. This algorithm is that of a conductor: it contains no "business" or data-access code. The main script merely calls the procedures of the [métier] layer [9]. It knows nothing at all about the [dao] layer and the external data. It can supply data to the [métier] layer [9]. In a console application, these data may come from configuration files or from the user of the script. It receives results [10] from the [métier] layer. It may need to store some results: to do so it again uses the procedures of the [métier] layer, which in turn will address the [dao] layer, which will do the work;
    • among the results, the main script may receive exceptions. It is its role to handle the exceptions that propagate up from all the layers.

This layering is intended to make the application easier to evolve. To this end, each layer implements an interface. Suppose that:

  • the [dao] layer is implemented by a [Dao] class that implements an [IDao] interface;
  • the [métier] layer is implemented by a [Metier] class that implements an [IMetier] interface.

The procedures of the [métier] layer will then use the [IDao] interface rather than the [Dao] class. This makes it possible to evolve the [dao] layer without touching the [métier] layer. Suppose that in a version 1, the [Dao1] layer uses data from a database. Following a change, these data are now supplied by a web service in a version 2, [Dao2]. We will make sure that both classes [Dao1] and [Dao2] implement the same [IDao] interface and that they throw the same exceptions. If this holds, the [Metier] layer, which works with the [IDao] interface, will remain unchanged.

The same reasoning applies to the [métier] layer.

The application will implement the following layered structure:

docs.title: 10.2. Objects exchanged between layers
docs.text:
Normally, the layers exchange various objects. Here they will exchange objects of the following [Personne] class [Personne.php]:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// une personne : un objet immuable
final readonly class Personne
{
    // constructeur avec promotion de l'attribut [id]
    public function __construct(public int $id)
    {
    }

    // toString
    public function __toString(): string
    {
        return "[Personne($this->id)]";
    }
}

Comments

  • line 6: the objects exchanged between layers contain only data. We make them immutable objects ([readonly] class): a layer thus cannot inadvertently modify an object it has received from another layer;
  • line 9: the person has only one property, its identifier [$id], initialized by the constructor thanks to parameter promotion. We will assume that this identifier designates a unique person in a data store;
  • lines 14-17: the [__toString] method, which displays the person's identifier.

docs.title: 10.3. The [dao] layer
docs.text:
The [IDao] interface implemented by the [dao] layer is as follows [IDao.php]:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// couche [dao] ------------------------
interface IDao
{
    // récupération d'une personne dans un entrepôt externe
    // on passe l'identifiant de la personne
    public function get(int $id): Personne;

    // sauvegarde d'une personne dans un entrepôt externe
    public function save(Personne $p): void;
}

This interface is implemented by the following [Dao1] class [Dao1.php]:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

final class Dao1 implements IDao
{
    // sauvegarde d'une personne dans un entrepôt externe
    #[\Override]
    public function save(Personne $p): void
    {
        print "[Dao1] : Sauvegarde de la personne $p en base de données [locale]\n";
    }

    // récupération d'une personne dans un entrepôt externe
    #[\Override]
    public function get(int $id): Personne
    {
        print "[Dao1] : Récupération de la personne d'identité ($id) en base de données [locale]\n";
        return new Personne($id);
    }
}

Comments

  • line 5: the [Dao1] class implements the [IDao] interface. It is declared [final]: it is not meant to be extended;
  • the class does not interact with a data store. We simply display messages to follow the flow of the code (line 11, line 18);
  • line 8: the [#[\Override]] attribute indicates that the method implements a method of the interface. If we get its name wrong, PHP reports it;
  • line 19: we do return a person having the identifier passed as a parameter to the method.

We also implement the [IDao] interface with the following [Dao2] class [Dao2.php]:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

final class Dao2 implements IDao
{
    // sauvegarde d'une personne dans un entrepôt externe
    #[\Override]
    public function save(Personne $p): void
    {
        print "[Dao2] : Sauvegarde de la personne $p en base de données [distante]\n";
    }

    // récupération d'une personne dans un entrepôt externe
    #[\Override]
    public function get(int $id): Personne
    {
        print "[Dao2] : Récupération de la personne d'identité ($id) en base de données [distante]\n";
        return new Personne($id);
    }
}

The [Dao2] class is similar to the [Dao1] class except that we have changed the messages displayed.

docs.title: 10.4. The [métier] layer
docs.text:
The [métier] layer offers the following [IMetier] interface [IMetier.php]:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// couche [métier] ------------------------
interface IMetier extends IDao
{
    // on exploite une personne
    public function doSomething(Personne $p): void;
}

Comments

  • line 6: the [IMetier] interface extends the [IDao] interface. This is not at all mandatory. We do it here because the example is simple: the [métier] layer offers the main script the [get] and [save] methods of the [dao] layer, which it hides from it;
  • line 9: the [doSomething] method is specific to the [métier] layer.

The PHP 7 course named the interface [IMétier] and the class [Métier], with an accent. PHP accepts accented letters in identifiers, but a file named [Métier.php] causes problems with some tools (zip archives, file systems, class autoloading). From now on we stick to class and file names without accents.

The [IMetier] interface is implemented by the following [Metier] class [Metier.php]:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

final class Metier implements IMetier
{
    // la couche [dao] est injectée par le constructeur
    public function __construct(private readonly IDao $dao)
    {
    }

    // on exploite une personne
    #[\Override]
    public function doSomething(Personne $p): void
    {
        // traitement
        print "[Métier] : Traitement métier de la personne $p\n";
    }

    // sauvegarde de la personne
    #[\Override]
    public function save(Personne $p): void
    {
        print "[Métier] : Sauvegarde de la personne $p\n";
        // on demande à la couche [dao] de faire la sauvegarde
        $this->dao->save($p);
    }

    // récupération d'une personne
    #[\Override]
    public function get(int $id): Personne
    {
        print "[Métier] : Récupération de la personne d'identifiant $id\n";
        // on demande la personne à la couche [dao]
        return $this->dao->get($id);
    }
}

Comments

  • line 8: the [métier] layer must have a reference to the [dao] layer in order to use its methods. This reference is passed to it through its constructor and stored in the private read-only property [$dao] (parameter promotion). Note that the type of the parameter is the [IDao] interface. Thus the [métier] layer will be able to work with any class implementing the [IDao] interface. If we switch from a [Dao1] layer to a [Dao2] layer and both implement the [IDao] interface, the [métier] layer does not have to be rewritten;
  • this technique is called constructor dependency injection: the [Metier] class does not itself create the [dao] layer it depends on; it is supplied with it. The PHP 7 course used a [setDao] setter. Constructor injection is the rule today: a [Metier] object cannot exist without its [dao] layer, and the latter can no longer be changed afterwards ([readonly] property). This is also what PHP frameworks such as Symfony or Laravel do;
  • lines 14-18: implementation of [IMetier::doSomething];
  • lines 22-27: implementation of [IMetier::save]. This method must save a person in a data store. The [métier] layer does not know how to do that. It addresses the [dao] layer to perform this save (line 26);
  • lines 31-36: implementation of [IMetier::get]. This method must retrieve from a data store the person whose identifier is passed to it as a parameter. The [métier] layer does not know how to do that. It addresses the [dao] layer to do the work (line 35).

Conclusion: as soon as the [métier] layer needs to access the data stored in the data store, it must go through the [dao] layer, which was created to access these data.

docs.title: 10.5. Main script
docs.text:
We are going to write two conductor scripts for this application. The 1st, [main1.php], will use the [Dao1] layer, while the second, [main2.php], will use the [Dao2] layer. We want to show that this has no impact on the code of the [Metier] layer.

The [main1.php] script is as follows:

<?php

// respect strict des types déclarés des paramètres et des résultats des fonctions
declare(strict_types=1);

// inclusion des classes et interfaces
require_once __DIR__ . "/Personne.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/IDao.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/IMetier.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/Dao1.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/Metier.php";

// création des couches : la couche [dao] est injectée dans la couche [métier]
$métier = new Metier(new Dao1());
// utilisation de la couche [métier]
$personne = $métier->get(4);
$métier->doSomething($personne);
$métier->save($personne);

Comments

  • the [main1.php] script is the conductor of the application. It loads the files of the classes and interfaces (lines 7-11), creates the layered structure of the application (line 14) and then talks to the [métier] layer (lines 16-18);
  • line 14: it is here, and only here, that the implementation of the [dao] layer is chosen;
  • according to the diagram of the layered structure, the [main1.php] script must address only the [métier] layer. It must not address the [dao] layer, even though this is theoretically possible.

The results of the execution are as follows:

> php main1.php
[Métier] : Récupération de la personne d'identifiant 4
[Dao1] : Récupération de la personne d'identité (4) en base de données [locale]
[Métier] : Traitement métier de la personne [Personne(4)]
[Métier] : Sauvegarde de la personne [Personne(4)]
[Dao1] : Sauvegarde de la personne [Personne(4)] en base de données [locale]

Comments

  • line 16 of the code caused lines 2 and 3 of the results to be written;
  • line 17 of the code caused line 4 of the results to be written;
  • line 18 of the code caused lines 5 and 6 of the results to be written.

The [main2.php] script is as follows:

<?php

// respect strict des types déclarés des paramètres et des résultats des fonctions
declare(strict_types=1);

// inclusion des classes et interfaces
require_once __DIR__ . "/Personne.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/IDao.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/IMetier.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/Dao2.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/Metier.php";

// création des couches : la couche [dao] est injectée dans la couche [métier]
$métier = new Metier(new Dao2());
// utilisation de la couche [métier]
$personne = $métier->get(4);
$métier->doSomething($personne);
$métier->save($personne);

Comments

  • line 10 and line 14: the layered structure now uses the [Dao2] layer. These are the only differences from [main1.php].

The results of the execution are as follows:

> php main2.php
[Métier] : Récupération de la personne d'identifiant 4
[Dao2] : Récupération de la personne d'identité (4) en base de données [distante]
[Métier] : Traitement métier de la personne [Personne(4)]
[Métier] : Sauvegarde de la personne [Personne(4)]
[Dao2] : Sauvegarde de la personne [Personne(4)] en base de données [distante]

The [Dao1] layer simulates access to a local database, while the [Dao2] layer simulates access to a remote database. As long as these two layers comply with the [IDao] interface, we see that the code of the [Metier] layer did not have to be changed.

We are now going to apply what we have just learned to the tax calculation exercise that serves as our common thread.

docs.title: 16. Network functions
docs.text:
We now turn to PHP's network functions, which allow us to do TCP / IP (Transmission Control Protocol / Internet Protocol) programming. The scripts for this chapter are in the [scripts-console/inet] folder of the course code:

php8-oct-2026
└── scripts-console
    └── inet
        ├── http
        ├── imap
        ├── ip
        ├── mailpit
        ├── smtp
        └── utilitaires

docs.title: 16.1.1. General overview
docs.text:
Consider communication between two remote machines A and B:

When an application AppA on a machine A wants to communicate with an application AppB on a machine B on the Internet, it needs to know several things:

  • the IP (Internet Protocol) address or the name of machine B;
  • the port number used by application AppB. Machine B may host many applications that work over the Internet. When it receives information from the network, it must know which application that information is intended for. The applications on machine B access the network through counters, also called communication ports. This information is contained in the packet received by machine B so that it can be delivered to the right application;
  • the communication protocols understood by machine B. In our study, we will use only the TCP / IP protocols;
  • the dialogue protocol accepted by application AppB. Machines A and B are going to "talk" to each other. What they say will be encapsulated in the TCP / IP protocols. Nevertheless, when application AppB, at the end of the chain, receives the information sent by application AppA, it must be able to interpret it. This is similar to the situation where two people A and B communicate by telephone: their conversation is carried by the telephone. Speech is encoded as signals by telephone A, carried over telephone lines, and arrives at telephone B where it is decoded. Person B then hears words. This is where the notion of dialogue protocol comes in: if A speaks French and B does not understand that language, A and B will not be able to have a useful conversation.

So the two communicating applications must agree on the type of dialogue they will adopt. For example, the dialogue with an FTP service is not the same as with a POP service: these two services do not accept the same commands. They have a different dialogue protocol.

docs.title: 16.1.2. The characteristics of the TCP protocol
docs.text:
We will only study here network communications using the TCP transport protocol, whose main characteristics are as follows:

  • the process that wants to send data first establishes a connection with the process that is to receive the information it will send. This connection is made between a port on the sending machine and a port on the receiving machine. A virtual path is thus created between the two ports, which will be reserved for the two processes that made the connection;
  • all packets sent by the source process follow this virtual path and arrive in the order in which they were sent;
  • the information sent has a continuous character. The sending process sends information at its own pace. This information is not necessarily sent immediately: the TCP protocol waits until it has enough to send. It is stored in a structure called a TCP segment. Once filled, this segment is passed to the IP layer, where it is encapsulated in an IP packet;
  • each segment sent by the TCP protocol is numbered. The receiving TCP protocol checks that it receives the segments in sequence. For each segment correctly received, it sends an acknowledgement to the sender;
  • when the sender receives it, it notifies the sending process. The latter can thus know that a segment has arrived safely;
  • if, after a certain time, the TCP protocol that sent a segment has not received an acknowledgement, it retransmits the segment in question, thus guaranteeing the quality of the information delivery service;
  • the virtual circuit established between the two communicating processes is full-duplex: this means that information can travel in both directions. Thus the destination process can send acknowledgements even while the source process continues to send information. This allows, for example, the source TCP protocol to send several segments without waiting for an acknowledgement. If after a certain time it realizes that it has not received the acknowledgement for a certain segment no. n, it will resume sending segments from that point.

docs.title: 16.1.3. The client-server relationship
docs.text: Communication on the Internet is often asymmetric: machine A initiates a connection to request a service from machine B. It specifies that it wants to open a connection with service SB1 on machine B. Machine B accepts or refuses. If it accepts, machine A can send its requests to service SB1. These must comply with the dialogue protocol understood by service SB1. A request-response dialogue is thus established between machine A, called the client machine, and machine B, called the server machine. One of the two partners will close the connection.

docs.title: 16.1.4. Architecture of a client
docs.text:
The architecture of a network program requesting the services of a server application will be as follows:

ouvrir la connexion avec le service SB1 de la machine B
si réussite alors
    tant que ce n'est pas fini
        préparer une demande
        l'émettre vers la machine B
        attendre et récupérer la réponse
        la traiter
    fin tant que
finsi
fermer la connexion

docs.title: 16.1.5. Architecture of a server
docs.text:
The architecture of a program offering services will be as follows:

ouvrir le service sur la machine locale
tant que le service est ouvert
    se mettre à l'écoute des demandes de connexion sur un port dit port d'écoute
    lorsqu'il y a une demande, la faire traiter par une autre tâche sur un autre port dit port de service
fin tant que

The server program handles a client's initial connection request differently from its subsequent requests for a service. The program does not provide the service itself. If it did, it would no longer be listening for connection requests during the service, and some clients would then not be served. So it proceeds differently: as soon as a connection request is received on the listening port and accepted, the server creates a task responsible for providing the service requested by the client. This service is provided on another port of the server machine, called the service port. Several clients can thus be served at the same time.

A service task will have the following structure:

tant que le service n'a pas été rendu totalement
    attendre une demande sur le port de service
    lorsqu'il y en a une, élaborer la réponse
    transmettre la réponse via le port de service
fin tant que
libérer le port de service

Another way to serve several clients at once, without creating tasks, is to monitor the listening port and the service ports simultaneously with a function that waits until one of them has something to say. This is what the TCP server we are going to write will do, with PHP's [stream_select] function.

docs.title: 16.2.1. Introduction
docs.text:
Once a client has connected to a server, a dialogue is established between them. Its nature forms what is called the server's communication protocol. Among the most common Internet protocols are the following:

  • HTTP: HyperText Transfer Protocol - the protocol for dialogue with a web server (HTTP server);
  • SMTP: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol - the protocol for dialogue with an email sending server (SMTP server);
  • POP: Post Office Protocol - the protocol for dialogue with an email storage server (POP server). Here the point is to retrieve received emails, not to send them;
  • IMAP: Internet Message Access Protocol - the protocol for dialogue with an email storage server (IMAP server). This protocol has gradually replaced the older POP protocol;
  • FTP: File Transfer Protocol - the protocol for dialogue with a file storage server (FTP server).

All these protocols share the characteristic of being text-line protocols: the client and the server exchange lines of text. If we have a client capable of:

  • creating a connection with a TCP server;
  • displaying on the console the lines of text the server sends it;
  • sending to the server the lines of text a user types on the keyboard;

then we are able to talk to a TCP server that uses a text-line protocol, provided we know the rules of that protocol.

docs.title: 16.2.2. TCP utilities
docs.text:
The PHP 7 course provided two Windows utilities, [RawTcpClient] and [RawTcpServer], written in C#. Here we replace them with two PHP scripts, which we are going to read: this is an opportunity to discover PHP's network functions. They are in the [inet/utilitaires] folder:

utilitaires
├── clavier.php
├── tcp-client.php
└── tcp-server.php
  • [tcp-client.php] lets you connect to port P of a server S;
  • [tcp-server.php] lets you create a server that waits for clients on a port P;
  • [clavier.php] contains two functions used by the two previous scripts.

Note that there are also ready-made tools for this kind of test. On Windows, the PowerShell command [Test-NetConnection localhost -Port 80] simply checks that a service is responding on a port. The [curl] tool, which we will meet with the HTTP protocol, can talk to many servers, and its [-v] (verbose) option displays the client / server exchanges. Our two scripts, on the other hand, let us type the protocol commands ourselves.

docs.title: 16.2.2.1. The [tcp-server.php] server
docs.text:
The TCP server [tcp-server.php] is invoked with the syntax [php tcp-server.php port] to create a TCP service on port [port] of the local machine (the computer you are working on):

  • the server can serve several clients simultaneously;
  • the server executes the commands typed by the user on the keyboard. These are as follows:
    • list: lists the clients currently connected to the server. They are displayed in the form [id=x - nom=y]. The [id] field is used to identify clients;
    • send x [text]: sends text to client no. x (id=x). The brackets [] are not sent. They are required in the command. They serve to visually delimit the text sent to the client;
    • close x: closes the connection with client no. x;
    • quit: closes all connections and stops the service;
  • the lines sent by a client to the server are displayed on the console;
  • all exchanges with a client are recorded in a text file [logs/machine-port.txt] where [machine-port] identifies the client (its IP address and the port it uses).

The server code is as follows:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// serveur TCP générique
// syntaxe : php tcp-server.php port
// - attend des clients sur le port [port] de la machine locale et peut en servir plusieurs à la fois ;
// - affiche les lignes de texte envoyées par les clients ;
// - exécute les commandes tapées au clavier :
//   list : liste les clients connectés ;
//   send id [texte] : envoie [texte] (sans les crochets) au client n° id ;
//   close id : ferme la connexion avec le client n° id ;
//   quit : ferme toutes les connexions et arrête le serveur ;
// - enregistre les échanges avec chaque client dans le fichier [logs/machine-port.txt]
//   où [machine-port] identifie le client

require_once __DIR__ . "/clavier.php";

// analyse des arguments de la ligne de commande
if (count($argv) !== 2 || !ctype_digit($argv[1])) {
    print "Syntaxe : php tcp-server.php port\n";
    exit(1);
}
$port = $argv[1];

// ouverture du service sur toutes les interfaces réseau de la machine locale
$serveur = @stream_socket_server("tcp://0.0.0.0:$port", $numErreur, $erreur);
if ($serveur === false) {
    print "Impossible d'ouvrir le service sur le port [$port] : $erreur\n";
    exit(2);
}
print "Serveur à l'écoute sur le port [$port]\n";
print "Commandes : list, send id [texte], close id, quit\n";
if (!is_dir(__DIR__ . "/logs")) {
    mkdir(__DIR__ . "/logs");
}

// les clients connectés : id => [socket, nom, fichier de logs, tampon]
$clients = [];
$prochainId = 1;
// le clavier est lu par un processus fils
[$lecteur, $clavier] = lancerLecteurClavier();
$écho = !stream_isatty(STDIN);
$tamponClavier = "";

// boucle de service
$fini = false;
while (!$fini) {
    // on surveille : le port d'écoute, les clients et le clavier
    $lectures = [$serveur, $clavier, ...array_column($clients, "socket")];
    $écritures = $exceptions = null;
    stream_select($lectures, $écritures, $exceptions, null);
    foreach ($lectures as $flux) {
        if ($flux === $serveur) {
            // un nouveau client se connecte
            $socket = stream_socket_accept($serveur, 0, $nom);
            if ($socket !== false) {
                $id = $prochainId++;
                $log = fopen(__DIR__ . "/logs/" . str_replace(":", "-", $nom) . ".txt", "w");
                $clients[$id] = ["socket" => $socket, "nom" => $nom, "log" => $log, "tampon" => ""];
                print "Client n° $id [$nom] connecté\n";
            }
        } elseif ($flux === $clavier) {
            // une commande a été tapée au clavier
            $données = fread($clavier, 8192);
            if ($données === false || $données === "") {
                // fin de l'entrée standard : on arrête le serveur
                $fini = true;
                break;
            }
            foreach (extraireLignes($tamponClavier, $données) as $commande) {
                if ($écho) {
                    print "$commande\n";
                }
                if (exécuter($commande, $clients)) {
                    $fini = true;
                    break;
                }
            }
        } else {
            // un client a parlé
            $id = array_find_key($clients, fn(array $client): bool => $client["socket"] === $flux);
            if ($id === null) {
                // client fermé entre-temps par la commande [close]
                continue;
            }
            $données = fread($flux, 8192);
            if ($données === false || $données === "") {
                print "Le client n° $id a fermé la connexion\n";
                fermer($clients, $id);
                continue;
            }
            foreach (extraireLignes($clients[$id]["tampon"], $données) as $ligne) {
                print "<-- client n° $id [$ligne]\n";
                fwrite($clients[$id]["log"], "<-- [$ligne]\n");
            }
        }
    }
}
// arrêt du service
foreach (array_keys($clients) as $id) {
    fermer($clients, $id);
}
fclose($serveur);
proc_terminate($lecteur);
print "Serveur arrêté\n";

// --------------------------------------------------------------------------
// exécute une commande tapée au clavier - rend true si c'est la commande [quit]
function exécuter(string $commande, array &$clients): bool
{
    // send id [texte]
    if (preg_match('/^send\s+(\d+)\s+\[(.*)\]$/', $commande, $champs)) {
        $id = (int) $champs[1];
        if (!isset($clients[$id])) {
            print "Client n° $id inconnu\n";
        } else {
            fwrite($clients[$id]["socket"], "$champs[2]\r\n");
            fwrite($clients[$id]["log"], "--> [$champs[2]]\n");
        }
        return false;
    }
    // les autres commandes
    $mots = preg_split('/\s+/', trim($commande));
    switch ($mots[0]) {
        case "list":
            foreach ($clients as $id => $client) {
                print "id=$id - nom={$client["nom"]}\n";
            }
            return false;
        case "close":
            $id = (int) ($mots[1] ?? 0);
            if (!isset($clients[$id])) {
                print "Client n° $id inconnu\n";
            } else {
                fermer($clients, $id);
                print "Connexion avec le client n° $id fermée\n";
            }
            return false;
        case "quit":
            return true;
        default:
            print "Commande [$commande] inconnue. Commandes : list, send id [texte], close id, quit\n";
            return false;
    }
}

// --------------------------------------------------------------------------
// ferme la connexion avec le client n° [$id]
function fermer(array &$clients, int $id): void
{
    fclose($clients[$id]["socket"]);
    fclose($clients[$id]["log"]);
    unset($clients[$id]);
}

Comments:

  • line 17: we load the [clavier.php] file, which we will see later;
  • line 20: the [$argv] array contains the command-line arguments. [$argv[0]] is the script name, [$argv[1]] the first argument, here the port number. The [ctype_digit] function checks that the latter consists only of digits;
  • line 27: the [stream_socket_server] function opens a TCP service. Its first parameter is an address of the form [tcp://interface:port]. The interface [0.0.0.0] refers to all the machine's network interfaces: the server will be reachable both via [localhost] and via the machine's IP address on the local network. On failure (port already in use, for example), the function returns [false] and puts an error number and an error message in the two variables passed as the 2nd and 3rd parameters. The [@] operator prevents PHP from displaying its own warning: we display our own message;
  • line 39: the dictionary of connected clients. Each client is described by its socket (the connection linking it to the server), its name [adresse:port], its log file and a buffer whose role we will see;
  • line 42: the keyboard is read by a child process. We will see why with the [clavier.php] file. [$clavier] is a stream into which the lines typed on the keyboard arrive;
  • line 43: the [stream_isatty] function indicates whether standard input is the keyboard (a terminal) or not. If standard input has been redirected to a file ([php tcp-server.php 100 < commandes.txt]), the commands read are not displayed on the screen. The server will then display them itself;
  • lines 48-52: the service loop. On each iteration, the server waits until one of the streams it monitors has something to say to it: the listening port (a new client is connecting), the keyboard (a command has been typed) or one of the clients (it has sent text). The [...] operator spreads the array of client sockets (obtained with [array_column]) into the [$lectures] array;
  • line 52: the [stream_select] function waits until one of the streams in the [$lectures] array is readable. The last parameter [null] means: wait with no time limit. On return, the function has removed from the [$lectures] array the streams that have nothing to read. The 2nd and 3rd parameters concern the streams we want to write to and exceptional events: they are of no interest to us. As they are passed by reference, we must pass variables to them, here [$écritures] and [$exceptions], which are [null];
  • lines 54-60: a new client is connecting. The [stream_socket_accept] function accepts the connection. It returns the service socket linking the server to this client and puts the client's identity in [$nom] in the form [adresse:port]. The timeout 0 means we do not wait: [stream_select] has told us that a client was waiting;
  • lines 63-75: a command has been typed on the keyboard. The [fread] function reads what is available (at most 8192 bytes). An empty string means that the stream has been closed. The [extraireLignes] function splits what was read into complete lines;
  • lines 81-95: a client has sent text. The [array_find_key] function (PHP 8.4) returns the key of the first array element that satisfies the condition expressed by the arrow function [fn] passed as the 2nd parameter: this is how we find the client number from its socket. If [fread] returns an empty string, the client has closed the connection. Otherwise each line received is displayed and recorded in the client's log file;
  • lines 110-141: the [exécuter] function executes a command typed on the keyboard. The [send id [texte]] command is recognized by a regular expression. The text is sent to the client followed by the sequence \r\n: Internet protocols terminate lines of text with the two characters CR (\r) and LF (\n);
  • line 150: the [fermer] function closes the connection with a client and removes it from the [$clients] dictionary, passed by reference ([&]).

docs.title: 16.2.2.2. The [clavier.php] file
docs.text:
The [clavier.php] file is as follows:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// outils communs à [tcp-client.php] et [tcp-server.php]

// --------------------------------------------------------------------------
// lance un processus fils qui lit le clavier et nous renvoie chaque ligne tapée
// par une socket. Pourquoi ? Nos programmes doivent surveiller en même temps le
// réseau et le clavier avec la fonction [stream_select]. Or sous Windows, [stream_select]
// ne sait surveiller que des sockets, pas le clavier (STDIN).
// Le descripteur ['socket'] de [proc_open] (PHP 8.0) relie le processus fils au
// processus père par une socket, que [stream_select] sait surveiller sur tous les OS.
// rend le processus fils et la socket qui délivre les lignes tapées au clavier
function lancerLecteurClavier(): array
{
    $processus = proc_open(
        // le processus fils : un script PHP d'une ligne qui recopie son entrée sur sa sortie
        [PHP_BINARY, "-r", 'while (($ligne = fgets(STDIN)) !== false) { echo $ligne; }'],
        // son entrée est notre clavier, sa sortie est une socket
        [0 => STDIN, 1 => ["socket"], 2 => STDERR],
        $tubes
    );
    if ($processus === false) {
        throw new RuntimeException("Impossible de lancer le lecteur du clavier");
    }
    return [$processus, $tubes[1]];
}

// --------------------------------------------------------------------------
// ajoute les octets [$données] au tampon [$tampon] et en extrait les lignes complètes,
// rendues sans leur marque de fin de ligne (\n ou \r\n) ;
// la fin du tampon (une ligne incomplète) reste dans le tampon
function extraireLignes(string &$tampon, string $données): array
{
    $tampon .= $données;
    $lignes = explode("\n", $tampon);
    // le dernier élément est la ligne en cours, pas encore terminée
    $tampon = array_pop($lignes);
    return array_map(fn(string $ligne): string => rtrim($ligne, "\r"), $lignes);
}

Comments:

  • line 15: our two scripts must monitor both the network and the keyboard at the same time. On Linux or macOS, we could pass the [STDIN] stream (the keyboard) to [stream_select]. On Windows, this is not possible: there, [stream_select] can only monitor sockets. The workaround is to have the keyboard read by a second process that sends the typed lines back to us through a socket;
  • lines 17-22: the [proc_open] function launches a child process. Its 1st parameter is the command to execute, in array form: the current PHP interpreter ([PHP_BINARY]) with the [-r] option, which executes the PHP code passed as an argument. This code copies each line read from its input to its output. The 2nd parameter describes the child process's streams: its input (0) is our standard input (the keyboard), its output (1) is a socket created by PHP (descriptor [['socket']], available since PHP 8.0), its errors (2) go to our error output. The 3rd parameter receives the created streams: [$tubes[1]] is our end of the socket;
  • line 34: when [stream_select] signals that a stream is readable, [fread] returns what has arrived: this may be one line, several lines or part of a line. The [extraireLignes] function appends these bytes to the buffer [$tampon] (passed by reference), extracts the complete lines from it and keeps the unfinished line in the buffer. Note the arrow function [fn(string $ligne): string => rtrim($ligne, "\r")], which removes the final \r from lines terminated by \r\n.

We could have read the lines with the [fgets] function. But [fgets] reads data in blocks and keeps in a buffer internal to PHP the lines it has not yet returned. [stream_select], which only looks at the network, would not see them. Reading with [fread] and splitting the lines ourselves avoids this pitfall.

docs.title: 16.2.2.3. The [tcp-client.php] client
docs.text:
The TCP client [tcp-client.php] is invoked with the syntax [php tcp-client.php [--quit commande] [--tls] serveur port] to connect to port [port] of server [serveur]:

  • the lines typed by the user on the keyboard are sent to the server;
  • the lines sent by the server are displayed on the console as soon as they arrive;
  • all exchanges are recorded in a text file [logs/serveur-port.txt];
  • the [quit] command stops the client. The [--quit] option lets you choose another command;
  • the [--tls] option encrypts the connection. We will need it to talk to secure servers.

Its code is as follows:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// client TCP générique
// syntaxe : php tcp-client.php [--quit commande] [--tls] serveur port
// - se connecte au port [port] de la machine [serveur] ;
// - affiche les lignes de texte envoyées par le serveur dès qu'elles arrivent ;
// - envoie au serveur les lignes de texte tapées au clavier ;
// - enregistre tous les échanges dans le fichier [logs/serveur-port.txt]
// options :
// --quit commande : la commande qui arrête le client (par défaut [quit])
// --tls : la connexion est chiffrée (TLS) dès son ouverture

require_once __DIR__ . "/clavier.php";

// analyse des arguments de la ligne de commande
$quit = "quit";
$tls = false;
$arguments = [];
for ($i = 1; $i < count($argv); $i++) {
    match ($argv[$i]) {
        "--quit" => $quit = $argv[++$i] ?? $quit,
        "--tls" => $tls = true,
        default => $arguments[] = $argv[$i],
    };
}
if (count($arguments) !== 2 || !ctype_digit($arguments[1])) {
    print "Syntaxe : php tcp-client.php [--quit commande] [--tls] serveur port\n";
    exit(1);
}
[$serveur, $port] = $arguments;

// ouverture de la connexion avec le serveur
// avec --tls, on ne vérifie pas le certificat du serveur : c'est un outil de découverte
$contexte = stream_context_create(["ssl" => ["verify_peer" => false, "verify_peer_name" => false]]);
$transport = $tls ? "tls" : "tcp";
$connexion = @stream_socket_client("$transport://$serveur:$port", $numErreur, $erreur, 10,
    STREAM_CLIENT_CONNECT, $contexte);
if ($connexion === false) {
    print "Échec de la connexion au serveur [$serveur:$port] : $erreur\n";
    exit(2);
}
$client = stream_socket_get_name($connexion, false);
print "Client [$client] connecté au serveur [$serveur:$port]\n";
print "Tapez vos commandes ($quit pour arrêter) :\n";

// fichier de logs
if (!is_dir(__DIR__ . "/logs")) {
    mkdir(__DIR__ . "/logs");
}
$log = fopen(__DIR__ . "/logs/$serveur-$port.txt", "w");

// le clavier est lu par un processus fils
[$lecteur, $clavier] = lancerLecteurClavier();
// si l'entrée standard est un fichier (php tcp-client.php ... < commandes.txt),
// les commandes lues ne s'affichent pas à l'écran : on les affichera nous-mêmes
$écho = !stream_isatty(STDIN);
// tampons des lignes incomplètes reçues du serveur et du clavier
$tamponServeur = "";
$tamponClavier = "";

// boucle de dialogue avec le serveur
$fini = false;
while (!$fini) {
    // on attend que le serveur ou le clavier ait quelque chose à nous dire
    $lectures = $clavier !== null ? [$connexion, $clavier] : [$connexion];
    $écritures = $exceptions = null;
    // sans clavier (fin de l'entrée standard), on n'attend pas le serveur plus de 2 secondes
    if (stream_select($lectures, $écritures, $exceptions, $clavier !== null ? null : 2) === 0) {
        break;
    }
    // le serveur a parlé ?
    if (in_array($connexion, $lectures, true)) {
        $données = fread($connexion, 8192);
        if ($données === false || $données === "") {
            // le serveur a fermé la connexion
            if ($tamponServeur !== "") {
                afficher("<-- [$tamponServeur]", $log);
            }
            print "Perte de la connexion avec le serveur...\n";
            break;
        }
        foreach (extraireLignes($tamponServeur, $données) as $ligne) {
            afficher("<-- [$ligne]", $log);
        }
    }
    // une ligne a été tapée au clavier ?
    if ($clavier !== null && in_array($clavier, $lectures, true)) {
        $données = fread($clavier, 8192);
        if ($données === false || $données === "") {
            // fin de l'entrée standard
            $clavier = null;
            continue;
        }
        foreach (extraireLignes($tamponClavier, $données) as $commande) {
            if ($écho) {
                print "$commande\n";
            }
            // fin du client ?
            if ($commande === $quit) {
                $fini = true;
                break;
            }
            // on envoie la commande au serveur : les protocoles de l'internet
            // terminent les lignes par la séquence \r\n
            fwrite($connexion, "$commande\r\n");
            fwrite($log, "--> [$commande]\n");
        }
    }
}
// fermeture de la connexion, du fichier de logs et du lecteur du clavier
fclose($connexion);
fclose($log);
proc_terminate($lecteur);
print "Fin du client\n";

// --------------------------------------------------------------------------
// affiche une ligne reçue et l'enregistre dans le fichier de logs
function afficher(string $ligne, $log): void
{
    print "$ligne\n";
    fwrite($log, "$ligne\n");
}

Comments:

  • lines 21-26: parsing the arguments. The [match] expression (PHP 8.0) compares its argument with the values of its arms using the [===] operator and evaluates the matching arm. Here, each arm is an assignment. [$argv[++$i] ?? $quit] returns the argument following [--quit] if it exists, and [$quit] otherwise;
  • line 32: array destructuring: [$serveur] receives [$arguments[0]] and [$port] receives [$arguments[1]];
  • lines 36-39: the [stream_socket_client] function opens a connection with the service [tcp://serveur:port]. With the [--tls] option, the address becomes [tls://serveur:port]: PHP then encrypts the connection with the TLS (Transport Layer Security) protocol. The context created by [stream_context_create] specifies here that the server's certificate must not be verified: for a discovery tool, this avoids problems with test servers that have self-signed certificates. The 4th parameter is the maximum time (in seconds) allowed for opening the connection;
  • line 44: the [stream_socket_get_name] function returns the local (false) or remote (true) address of a connection, in the form [adresse:port];
  • lines 65-70: the dialogue loop. It has the same structure as the server's: [stream_select] waits until the server or the keyboard has something to say. When standard input is exhausted (the case of input redirected to a file), the client keeps displaying what the server sends, but does not wait for it for more than 2 seconds;
  • lines 73-85: the lines sent by the server are displayed, enclosed in brackets, and recorded in the log file. If the server closes the connection, the loop stops;
  • lines 88-108: each line typed on the keyboard is sent to the server, followed by the sequence \r\n, except the client's stop command;
  • line 115: at the end, we stop the child process that reads the keyboard.

docs.title: 16.2.2.4. An example
docs.text:
Let's look at an example. We open two terminals (in VS Code, the [+] button of the [Terminal] view opens a new one) and in each of them we move to the [inet/utilitaires] folder. In the first terminal, we start the server on port 100. In the second, we start the client, asking it to connect to port 100 of the local machine [localhost], then we type a line of text. We go back to the server, reply to client no. 1, ask for the list of clients, close the connection with client no. 1 and stop the server.

Here is what the server displays (the commands typed on the keyboard are the lines [send 1 ...], [list], [close 1] and [quit]):

> php tcp-server.php 100
Serveur à l'écoute sur le port [100]
Commandes : list, send id [texte], close id, quit
Client n° 1 [127.0.0.1:47966] connecté
<-- client n° 1 [hello from client]
send 1 [hello from server]
list
id=1 - nom=127.0.0.1:47966
close 1
Connexion avec le client n° 1 fermée
quit
Serveur arrêté
  • [Client n° 1 [127.0.0.1:47966] connecté]: a client has been detected. The server has given it the number 1. The client is using port 47966 of the machine with IP address 127.0.0.1. This address is that of [localhost], the local machine;
  • [<-- client n° 1 [hello from client]]: in brackets, the line received from the client;
  • [send 1 [hello from server]]: the response sent to client no. 1. Only the text between the brackets is sent, not the brackets themselves;
  • [list]: the list of clients and its response;
  • [close 1] then [quit]: we close the connection with client no. 1, then stop the server.

And here is what the client displays:

> php tcp-client.php localhost 100
Client [127.0.0.1:47966] connecté au serveur [localhost:100]
Tapez vos commandes (quit pour arrêter) :
hello from client
<-- [hello from server]
Perte de la connexion avec le serveur...
Fin du client
  • [hello from client]: the line typed on the keyboard;
  • [<-- [hello from server]]: the response received from the server. The text received is the one between brackets;
  • [Perte de la connexion avec le serveur...] (lost connection with the server): the client has detected that the server closed the connection.

Two log files have been created in the [utilitaires/logs] folder, one by the server and another by the client. The server's file is named after the client [127.0.0.1-47966.txt]:

<-- [hello from client]
--> [hello from server]

The client's file is named after the server [localhost-100.txt]:

--> [hello from client]
<-- [hello from server]

docs.title: 16.3. Getting the name or IP address of a machine on the Internet
docs.text:
Machines on the Internet are identified by an IP address (IPv4 or IPv6) and most often by a name. But ultimately only the IP address is used. So we sometimes need to know the IP address of a machine identified by its name. This is the role of the DNS (Domain Name System) service.

The [inet/ip/ip-01.php] script is as follows:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// adresses IP et noms de machines de l'internet

// les machines dont on veut l'adresse IP et le nom
const HÔTES = ["istia.univ-angers.fr", "www.univ-angers.fr", "www.ibm.com", "www.php.net", "yahoo.com", "localhost", "xx"];

// on ajoute la machine locale, dont le nom est donné par [gethostname]
foreach ([...HÔTES, gethostname()] as $hôte) {
    getIPandName($hôte);
}
// fin
print "Terminé\n";

// --------------------------------------------------------------------------
function getIPandName(string $nomMachine): void
{
    // $nomMachine : nom de la machine dont on veut l'adresse IP
    print "---------------\n";
    // nomMachine --> adresse IP
    $ip = gethostbyname($nomMachine);
    if ($ip === $nomMachine) {
        print "Erreur, machine [$nomMachine] non trouvée\n";
        return;
    }
    print "ip[$nomMachine]=$ip\n";
    // toutes les adresses IPv4 de la machine
    $ips = gethostbynamel($nomMachine);
    if ($ips !== false && count($ips) > 1) {
        print "toutes les adresses IPv4 de [$nomMachine] : " . implode(", ", $ips) . "\n";
    }
    // adresse IP --> nomMachine
    $nom = gethostbyaddr($ip);
    if ($nom === false || $nom === $ip) {
        print "Erreur, pas de nom pour l'adresse [$ip]\n";
    } else {
        print "name[$ip]=$nom\n";
    }
}

Comments:

  • line 8: the list of machines whose name and IP address we want. PHP accepts accented characters in identifiers;
  • line 11: we add to this list the name of the local machine, given by the [gethostname] function. The [...] operator copies the elements of the [HÔTES] array into the new array;
  • line 18: PHP's network functions are used in the [getIPandName] function;
  • line 23: the [gethostbyname($nom)] function gives the IPv4 address "ip3.ip2.ip1.ip0" of the machine named $nom. If machine $nom does not exist, the function returns $nom as its result;
  • line 30: a machine may have several IPv4 addresses. The [gethostbynamel] function returns them all in an array (or [false] on failure);
  • line 35: the [gethostbyaddr($ip)] function gives the name of the machine with address $ip. If address $ip has no name, the function returns $ip as its result, and [false] if the address is malformed.

The [gethostbyname] and [gethostbynamel] functions only know IPv4 addresses. To get a machine's IPv6 addresses, we would use the [dns_get_record] function with the [DNS_AAAA] type.

Results:

> php ip-01.php
---------------
ip[istia.univ-angers.fr]=193.49.144.41
name[193.49.144.41]=ametys-fo-2.univ-angers.fr
---------------
ip[www.univ-angers.fr]=193.49.144.41
name[193.49.144.41]=ametys-fo-2.univ-angers.fr
---------------
ip[www.ibm.com]=23.217.77.36
name[23.217.77.36]=a23-217-77-36.deploy.static.akamaitechnologies.com
---------------
ip[www.php.net]=107.150.176.1
name[107.150.176.1]=107-150-176-1.bunnyinfra.net
---------------
ip[yahoo.com]=98.137.11.163
toutes les adresses IPv4 de [yahoo.com] : 98.137.11.164, 98.137.11.163, 74.6.231.21, 74.6.143.25, 74.6.231.20, 74.6.143.26
name[98.137.11.163]=media-router-fp74.prod.media.vip.gq1.yahoo.com
---------------
ip[localhost]=127.0.0.1
name[127.0.0.1]=localhost
---------------
Erreur, machine [xx] non trouvée
---------------
ip[vm]=127.0.0.1
name[127.0.0.1]=localhost
Terminé
  • the machines [istia.univ-angers.fr] and [www.univ-angers.fr] have the same IP address. The name obtained from the IP address, called the canonical name, is yet another name;
  • the name [www.ibm.com] is carried by a machine belonging to Akamai, a company that hosts the websites of many businesses;
  • the machine [yahoo.com] has six IPv4 addresses: requests are spread over several servers;
  • [localhost] has the address 127.0.0.1, called the loopback address: it always refers to the local machine;
  • the machine [xx] does not exist;
  • the last machine is the local machine, named [vm] here. The results depend on the machine's configuration: on a Windows workstation, you will get your computer's name and, depending on the configuration, its address on the local network (192.168.x.y for example).

The results obtained for machines on the Internet change over time: you will probably not get the same ones.

docs.title: 16.4.1. Example 1
docs.text:
When a browser displays a URL, it is the client of a web server, or in other words of an HTTP server. It takes the initiative and begins by sending a number of commands to the server. For this first example:

  • the server will be the [tcp-server.php] utility;
  • the client will be a browser.

We first start the server on port 100, then with a browser we request the URL [http://localhost:100], i.e. we say that the HTTP server being queried is running on port 100 of the local machine. The browser waits for the response. Let's go back to the server window. There we see the lines sent by the browser. We then type on the keyboard a response in HTTP format, line by line, then close the connection and stop the server:

> php tcp-server.php 100
Serveur à l'écoute sur le port [100]
Commandes : list, send id [texte], close id, quit
Client n° 1 [127.0.0.1:45752] connecté
<-- client n° 1 [GET / HTTP/1.1]
<-- client n° 1 [Host: localhost:100]
<-- client n° 1 [Connection: keep-alive]
<-- client n° 1 [sec-ch-ua: "HeadlessChrome";v="141", "Not?A_Brand";v="8", "Chromium";v="141"]
<-- client n° 1 [sec-ch-ua-mobile: ?0]
<-- client n° 1 [sec-ch-ua-platform: "Linux"]
<-- client n° 1 [Upgrade-Insecure-Requests: 1]
<-- client n° 1 [User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) HeadlessChrome/141.0.7390.37 Safari/537.36]
<-- client n° 1 [Accept-Language: fr-FR]
<-- client n° 1 [Accept: text/html,application/xhtml+xml,application/xml;q=0.9,image/avif,image/webp,image/apng,*/*;q=0.8,application/signed-exchange;v=b3;q=0.7]
<-- client n° 1 [Sec-Fetch-Site: none]
<-- client n° 1 [Sec-Fetch-Mode: navigate]
<-- client n° 1 [Sec-Fetch-User: ?1]
<-- client n° 1 [Sec-Fetch-Dest: document]
<-- client n° 1 [Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate, br, zstd]
<-- client n° 1 []
send 1 [HTTP/1.1 200 OK]
send 1 [Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8]
send 1 [Connection: close]
send 1 []
send 1 [<h1>Bonjour du serveur TCP !</h1>]
close 1
Connexion avec le client n° 1 fermée
list
quit
Serveur arrêté
  • [Client n° 1]: the browser that connected;
  • then come the lines of text it sent:
    • [GET / HTTP/1.1]: this line has the format [GET URL HTTP/1.1]. It requests the URL / and asks the server to use the HTTP 1.1 protocol;
    • [Host: localhost:100]: this line has the format [Host: serveur:port]. The case of the [Host] header does not matter. Here the client reminds the server that it is querying a local server operating on port 100;
    • the [Connection] header indicates the desired connection mode: [keep-alive] indicates that the connection should be kept open after the response, for any further requests;
    • the [User-Agent] header gives the client's identity. Here, it is a Chromium browser. The [sec-ch-ua...] and [Sec-Fetch...] headers are specific to recent browsers. The exact values depend on the browser and system used;
    • the [Accept] header indicates which document types the client accepts;
    • the [Accept-Language] header indicates in which language the requested documents are preferred if they exist in several languages;
    • the [Accept-Encoding] header indicates that the client accepts compressed documents;
    • the client ends its commands with an empty line;
  • the [send 1 [...]] commands send the response to the browser: a 1st line [HTTP/1.1 200 OK], which indicates that the requested document was found, some headers, an empty line, then the document. The [Content-Type] header indicates the document type, here HTML encoded in UTF-8, and the [Connection: close] header that the server will close the connection at the end of the document;
  • [close 1]: closing the connection tells the browser that the document is complete.

The browser then displays the document received:

We have just written a web server "by hand"!

docs.title: 16.4.2. Example 2
docs.text:
Now that we know the commands a browser sends to request a URL, we are going to request a URL with our TCP client [tcp-client.php]. The Apache server of [Laragon] will be our web server: start it ([Start All] button of [Laragon]). The [inet/http/pages] folder contains a static HTML page [bonjour.html]:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="fr">
    <head>
        <meta charset="utf-8">
        <title>Bonjour</title>
    </head>
    <body>
        <h1>Bonjour !</h1>
        <p>Une page statique servie par le serveur web.</p>
    </body>
</html>

Since the [php8-oct-2026] folder is in the [<laragon>/www] folder, this page is available at the URL [http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/inet/http/pages/bonjour.html]. Let's request it with our TCP client, connected to port 80 of the [localhost] server, where the web server operates. We type the commands we discovered in the previous section:

> php tcp-client.php localhost 80
Client [127.0.0.1:59734] connecté au serveur [localhost:80]
Tapez vos commandes (quit pour arrêter) :
GET /php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/inet/http/pages/bonjour.html HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:80

<-- [HTTP/1.1 200 OK]
<-- [Date: Thu, 01 Oct 2026 15:32:51 GMT]
<-- [Server: Apache/2.4.58 (Ubuntu)]
<-- [Last-Modified: Thu, 01 Oct 2026 15:02:24 GMT]
<-- [ETag: "ec-65cc8b40e550d"]
<-- [Accept-Ranges: bytes]
<-- [Content-Length: 236]
<-- [Vary: Accept-Encoding]
<-- [Content-Type: text/html]
<-- []
<-- [<!DOCTYPE html>]
<-- [<html lang="fr">]
<-- [    <head>]
<-- [        <meta charset="utf-8">]
<-- [        <title>Bonjour</title>]
<-- [    </head>]
<-- [    <body>]
<-- [        <h1>Bonjour !</h1>]
<-- [        <p>Une page statique servie par le serveur web.</p>]
<-- [    </body>]
<-- [</html>]
quit
Fin du client
  • [GET ... HTTP/1.1]: the [GET] command with the path of the requested document;
  • [Host: localhost:80]: the [Host] header;
  • these are the only two essential commands. For the other headers, the web server will use default values;
  • the empty line that must end the client's commands;
  • below the empty line comes the response of the Apache web server:
    • [HTTP/1.1 200 OK]: the status line. Code 200 means that the document was found;
    • next come the HTTP headers of the response, up to an empty line. The [Content-Length] header gives the size of the document in bytes;
    • after the empty line comes the requested HTML document;
    • the [Server] header identifies the web server: here an Apache 2.4 server. With [Laragon], you will see the mention [(Win64)] and the OpenSSL and PHP versions;
  • [quit]: we type [quit] to end the client. The server, for its part, keeps the connection open for a few seconds (HTTP/1.1 keep-alive mode) waiting for another request, then closes it.

The log file [utilitaires/logs/localhost-80.txt] contains the exchanges:

--> [GET /php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/inet/http/pages/bonjour.html HTTP/1.1]
--> [Host: localhost:80]
--> []
<-- [HTTP/1.1 200 OK]
<-- [Date: Thu, 01 Oct 2026 15:32:51 GMT]
<-- [Server: Apache/2.4.58 (Ubuntu)]
<-- [Last-Modified: Thu, 01 Oct 2026 15:02:24 GMT]
<-- [ETag: "ec-65cc8b40e550d"]
<-- [Accept-Ranges: bytes]
<-- [Content-Length: 236]
<-- [Vary: Accept-Encoding]
<-- [Content-Type: text/html]
<-- []
<-- [<!DOCTYPE html>]
<-- [<html lang="fr">]
<-- [    <head>]
<-- [        <meta charset="utf-8">]
<-- [        <title>Bonjour</title>]
<-- [    </head>]
<-- [    <body>]
<-- [        <h1>Bonjour !</h1>]
<-- [        <p>Une page statique servie par le serveur web.</p>]
<-- [    </body>]
<-- [</html>]

We now have the basics to program a TCP client that would request a URL.

docs.title: 16.4.3. Example 3
docs.text:
The [inet/http/http-01.php] script is an HTTP client configured by the JSON file [config-http-01.json]. Its content is as follows:

{
    "localhost": {
        "port": 80,
        "GET": "/php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/inet/http/pages/bonjour.html",
        "Host": "localhost:80",
        "User-Agent": "client PHP",
        "Accept": "text/html",
        "Accept-Language": "fr",
        "Connection": "close",
        "endOfLine": "\r\n"
    }
}
  • line 2: the name of the machine hosting the web server to reach;
  • line 3: the port on which this web server operates;
  • line 4: the URL of the desired document;
  • line 5: the target machine in the form machine:port;
  • line 6: the identification of the HTTP client: you can put whatever you like;
  • line 7: the type of document accepted by the client, here HTML text;
  • line 8: the desired language for the requested document;
  • line 9: we ask the server to close the connection once the document has been sent. Without this header, an HTTP/1.1 server keeps the connection open for a few seconds waiting for another request, and our client, which reads until the connection is closed, would wait needlessly;
  • line 10: the end-of-line marker for the commands sent by the client. The HTTP protocol requires the sequence \r\n.

The [http-01.php] script is as follows:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// client HTTP basique : demande un document à un serveur web et l'enregistre dans un fichier
// le fichier de configuration peut être passé en argument (php http-01.php config.json)
$configFileName = $argv[1] ?? "config-http-01.json";

// on récupère la configuration
$config = json_decode(file_get_contents($configFileName), true);
// obtenir le texte HTML des URL du fichier de configuration
foreach ($config as $site => $protocole) {
    // lecture de l'URL du site $site
    $résultat = getURL($site, $protocole);
    // affichage résultat
    print "$résultat\n";
}

// --------------------------------------------------------------------------
function getURL(string $site, array $protocole, bool $suivi = true): string
{
    // lit l'URL $protocole["GET"] du site $site et la stocke dans le fichier output/$site.html
    // le dialogue client / serveur se fait selon le protocole $protocole
    //
    // ouverture d'une connexion sur le port $protocole["port"] de $site
    $connexion = @stream_socket_client("tcp://$site:{$protocole["port"]}", $numErreur, $erreur, 10);
    // retour si erreur
    if ($connexion === false) {
        return "Échec de la connexion au site [$site:{$protocole["port"]}] : $erreur";
    }
    // $connexion représente un flux de communication bidirectionnel
    // entre le client (ce programme) et le serveur web contacté
    // ce canal est utilisé pour les échanges de commandes et d'informations
    // le protocole de dialogue est HTTP
    //
    // création du fichier output/$site.html
    if (!is_dir("output")) {
        mkdir("output");
    }
    $html = fopen("output/$site.html", "w");
    if ($html === false) {
        fclose($connexion);
        return "Erreur lors de la création du fichier [output/$site.html]";
    }
    // le client va commencer le dialogue HTTP avec le serveur
    if ($suivi) {
        print "Client : début de la communication avec le serveur [$site] ----------------------------\n";
    }
    // les lignes envoyées par le client doivent se terminer par \r\n
    $endOfLine = $protocole["endOfLine"];
    // par simplification, on ne teste pas les cas d'erreur dans la communication client / serveur
    // le client envoie la commande GET pour demander l'URL $protocole["GET"]
    // syntaxe GET URL HTTP/1.1
    $commande = "GET {$protocole["GET"]} HTTP/1.1$endOfLine";
    if ($suivi) {
        print "--> $commande";
    }
    fwrite($connexion, $commande);
    // émission des autres entêtes HTTP
    foreach ($protocole as $verb => $value) {
        if (!in_array($verb, ["GET", "port", "endOfLine"], true)) {
            // on construit la commande
            $commande = "$verb: $value$endOfLine";
            if ($suivi) {
                print "--> $commande";
            }
            // on envoie la commande au serveur
            fwrite($connexion, $commande);
        }
    }
    // les entêtes (headers) du protocole HTTP doivent se terminer par une ligne vide
    fwrite($connexion, $endOfLine);
    //
    // le serveur va maintenant répondre sur le canal $connexion. Il va envoyer toutes
    // ses données puis fermer le canal (Connection: close). Le client lit donc tout ce
    // qui arrive de $connexion jusqu'à la fermeture du canal
    //
    // on lit tout d'abord les entêtes HTTP envoyés par le serveur
    // ils se terminent eux aussi par une ligne vide
    if ($suivi) {
        print "Réponse du serveur [$site] ----------------------------\n";
    }
    while (($ligne = fgets($connexion)) !== false) {
        // on enlève les espaces de fin de ligne (dont \r\n)
        $ligne = rtrim($ligne);
        // a-t-on la ligne vide qui termine les entêtes ?
        if ($ligne === "") {
            break;
        }
        // on affiche l'entête HTTP
        if ($suivi) {
            print "<-- $ligne\n";
        }
    }
    // on lit le document HTML qui suit la ligne vide et on le mémorise dans le fichier
    while (($ligne = fgets($connexion)) !== false) {
        fwrite($html, $ligne);
    }
    // le serveur a fermé la connexion - le client la ferme à son tour
    fclose($connexion);
    fclose($html);
    // retour
    return "Fin de la communication avec le site [$site]. Vérifiez le fichier [output/$site.html]";
}

Code comments:

  • line 7: the configuration file can be passed as an argument. We will use several configuration files;
  • line 10: the configuration file is used to create a dictionary:
    • the dictionary keys are the web servers to query;
    • the values set the HTTP protocol to follow;
  • line 12: we loop over the list of web servers in the configuration;
  • line 20: the [getURL($site, $protocole, $suivi)] function requests a document from website $site and stores it in the text file [output/$site.html]. By default, the client / server exchanges are displayed on the console ($suivi=true);
  • line 26: the [stream_socket_client] function creates a connection with a TCP / IP service running on port [port] of machine $site. Once the client / server connection is open, many TCP / IP services exchange lines of text. This is the case here with the HTTP protocol. The stream from the server to the client can then be handled like a text file read with [fgets]. The same goes for the stream from the client to the server, which can be written with [fwrite];
  • line 40: creation of the file [output/$site.html] in which we will store the HTML document received;
  • line 54: the client's first command must be the [GET URL HTTP/1.1] command. It means: "I want (GET) the page [URL] of the website I am connected to. I am working with HTTP protocol version 1.1";
  • lines 60-70: we send the other lines of the HTTP protocol [Host, User-Agent, Accept, Accept-Language, Connection]. Their order does not matter. The PHP 7 course tested the keys to exclude one by one; the [in_array] function with the 3rd parameter [true] (strict comparison) is more readable;
  • line 72: we send an empty line to the server to indicate that the client has finished sending its HTTP headers and is now waiting for the requested document;
  • lines 83-94: the server will first send a series of HTTP headers giving various pieces of information about the requested document. These headers end with an empty line. We read a line with [fgets], remove its trailing whitespace (including \r\n) with [rtrim] and check whether it is the empty line that marks the end of the headers. Otherwise the header is displayed;
  • lines 95-97: the lines of text of the document can be read line by line with a while loop and saved in the text file [output/$site.html]. When the web server has sent the whole document, it closes its connection with the client. On the client side, this will be detected as an end of file: [fgets] returns [false].

Let's run the script in a terminal opened in the [inet/http] folder. The console displays the following logs:

> php http-01.php
Client : début de la communication avec le serveur [localhost] ----------------------------
--> GET /php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/inet/http/pages/bonjour.html HTTP/1.1
--> Host: localhost:80
--> User-Agent: client PHP
--> Accept: text/html
--> Accept-Language: fr
--> Connection: close
Réponse du serveur [localhost] ----------------------------
<-- HTTP/1.1 200 OK
<-- Date: Thu, 01 Oct 2026 16:47:43 GMT
<-- Server: Apache/2.4.58 (Ubuntu)
<-- Last-Modified: Thu, 01 Oct 2026 15:02:24 GMT
<-- ETag: "ec-65cc8b40e550d"
<-- Accept-Ranges: bytes
<-- Content-Length: 236
<-- Vary: Accept-Encoding
<-- Connection: close
<-- Content-Type: text/html
Fin de la communication avec le site [localhost]. Vérifiez le fichier [output/localhost.html]

In our example, the [output/localhost.html] file received is as follows:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="fr">
    <head>
        <meta charset="utf-8">
        <title>Bonjour</title>
    </head>
    <body>
        <h1>Bonjour !</h1>
        <p>Une page statique servie par le serveur web.</p>
    </body>
</html>

It is indeed the [bonjour.html] document: it is also the one a browser displays.

docs.title: 16.4.4. Example 4
docs.text: In this example, we will show that the HTTP client we have written is not good enough.

docs.title: 16.4.4.1. The HTTPS protocol
docs.text:
Let's change the configuration file. The [config-http-01-https.json] file is as follows:

{
    "localhost": {
        "port": 443,
        "GET": "/php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/inet/http/pages/bonjour.html",
        "Host": "localhost:443",
        "User-Agent": "client PHP",
        "Accept": "text/html",
        "Accept-Language": "fr",
        "Connection": "close",
        "endOfLine": "\r\n"
    }
}

Here, we are going to request the [bonjour.html] document from port 443 of the [localhost] server. Port 443 is the port used by the secure HTTP protocol called HTTPS. In this protocol, the client / server dialogue begins with an exchange of information that will secure the link: it will be encrypted by the TLS protocol. The client must then speak the HTTPS protocol and not the HTTP protocol, which our client does not do.

The Apache server of [Laragon] can use the HTTPS protocol, but it is not active by default. It is activated through the [Laragon] menu: right-click in the [Laragon] window, then [Apache / SSL / Enabled]. The Apache server is then restarted and now listens on two ports: port 80 (HTTP) and port 443 (HTTPS). [Laragon] has generated a so-called self-signed certificate for it. We will come back to this point in the next chapter.

With this configuration file ([php http-01.php config-http-01-https.json]), the console results are as follows:

> php http-01.php config-http-01-https.json
Client : début de la communication avec le serveur [localhost] ----------------------------
--> GET /php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/inet/http/pages/bonjour.html HTTP/1.1
--> Host: localhost:443
--> User-Agent: client PHP
--> Accept: text/html
--> Accept-Language: fr
--> Connection: close
Réponse du serveur [localhost] ----------------------------
<-- HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
<-- Date: Thu, 01 Oct 2026 16:47:43 GMT
<-- Server: Apache/2.4.58 (Ubuntu)
<-- Content-Length: 438
<-- Connection: close
<-- Content-Type: text/html; charset=iso-8859-1
Fin de la communication avec le site [localhost]. Vérifiez le fichier [output/localhost.html]
  • [HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request]: the server replied that the client's request was incorrect.

The content of the [output/localhost.html] file is then as follows:

<!DOCTYPE HTML PUBLIC "-//IETF//DTD HTML 2.0//EN">
<html><head>
<title>400 Bad Request</title>
</head><body>
<h1>Bad Request</h1>
<p>Your browser sent a request that this server could not understand.<br />
Reason: You're speaking plain HTTP to an SSL-enabled server port.<br />
 Instead use the HTTPS scheme to access this URL, please.<br />
</p>
<hr>
<address>Apache/2.4.58 (Ubuntu) Server at 127.0.0.1 Port 443</address>
</body></html>

The server clearly says that we did not use the right protocol: "You're speaking plain HTTP to an SSL-enabled server port" (SSL is the former name of TLS).

docs.title: 16.4.4.2. Document sent in chunks
docs.text:
The [inet/http/pages] folder contains a second document, the PHP script [index.php]:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// une page envoyée en plusieurs fois : [flush] force l'envoi immédiat de ce qui a déjà été écrit
// le serveur ne connaît donc pas la taille totale du document au moment d'envoyer les entêtes
print "<!DOCTYPE html>\n<html lang=\"fr\">\n<head><meta charset=\"utf-8\"><title>Morceaux</title></head>\n<body>\n";
flush();
for ($i = 1; $i <= 3; $i++) {
    print "<p>morceau n° $i</p>\n";
    flush();
}
print "</body>\n</html>\n";
  • line 8: the [flush] function requests that what the script has already written be sent immediately to the client. The script thus sends its document in five parts. When sending the HTTP headers of the response, the server therefore does not know the total size of the document.

Now let's use the following configuration file [config-http-01-morceaux.json]:

{
    "localhost": {
        "port": 80,
        "GET": "/php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/inet/http/pages/",
        "Host": "localhost:80",
        "User-Agent": "client PHP",
        "Accept": "text/html",
        "Accept-Language": "fr",
        "Connection": "close",
        "endOfLine": "\r\n"
    }
}
  • line 4: we request the [pages/] folder. The Apache server then sends its default document, here [index.php].

The console results are then as follows:

> php http-01.php config-http-01-morceaux.json
Client : début de la communication avec le serveur [localhost] ----------------------------
--> GET /php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/inet/http/pages/ HTTP/1.1
--> Host: localhost:80
--> User-Agent: client PHP
--> Accept: text/html
--> Accept-Language: fr
--> Connection: close
Réponse du serveur [localhost] ----------------------------
<-- HTTP/1.1 200 OK
<-- Date: Thu, 01 Oct 2026 16:47:43 GMT
<-- Server: Apache/2.4.58 (Ubuntu)
<-- X-Powered-By: PHP/8.5.11
<-- Vary: Accept-Encoding
<-- Connection: close
<-- Transfer-Encoding: chunked
<-- Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8
Fin de la communication avec le site [localhost]. Vérifiez le fichier [output/localhost.html]
  • the [X-Powered-By] header indicates that the document was produced by PHP 8.5;
  • the [Transfer-Encoding: chunked] header indicates that the server is sending the document in chunks. There is no [Content-Length] header: the server does not announce the size of the document.

This results in numbers appearing in the stream sent to the client: each chunk is preceded by a line giving its size in hexadecimal, and the document ends with a chunk of size 0. Here is the [output/localhost.html] file:

63
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="fr">
<head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>Morceaux</title></head>
<body>

15
<p>morceau n° 1</p>

15
<p>morceau n° 2</p>

15
<p>morceau n° 3</p>

10
</body>
</html>

0
  • [63]: the size in hexadecimal of the 1st chunk, i.e. 99 bytes: the first four lines of the document;
  • [15]: the size of the next three chunks, i.e. 21 bytes (the [°] character takes two bytes in UTF-8);
  • [10]: the size of the last chunk, 16 bytes;
  • [0]: the chunk of size 0 that ends the document.

A correct HTTP client should not leave these numbers in the final document.

docs.title: 16.4.4.3. Redirection
docs.text:
Here is one last configuration file [config-http-01-redirection.json]:

{
    "localhost": {
        "port": 80,
        "GET": "/php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/inet/http/pages",
        "Host": "localhost:80",
        "User-Agent": "client PHP",
        "Accept": "text/html",
        "Accept-Language": "fr",
        "Connection": "close",
        "endOfLine": "\r\n"
    }
}

It looks like the previous example, but the requested URL does not end with the / character. These are not the same URLs. Running the HTTP client then gives the following console results:

> php http-01.php config-http-01-redirection.json
Client : début de la communication avec le serveur [localhost] ----------------------------
--> GET /php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/inet/http/pages HTTP/1.1
--> Host: localhost:80
--> User-Agent: client PHP
--> Accept: text/html
--> Accept-Language: fr
--> Connection: close
Réponse du serveur [localhost] ----------------------------
<-- HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently
<-- Date: Thu, 01 Oct 2026 16:47:43 GMT
<-- Server: Apache/2.4.58 (Ubuntu)
<-- Location: http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/inet/http/pages/
<-- Content-Length: 346
<-- Connection: close
<-- Content-Type: text/html; charset=iso-8859-1
Fin de la communication avec le site [localhost]. Vérifiez le fichier [output/localhost.html]
  • [HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently]: code 301 indicates that the requested document has permanently changed URL;
  • [Location: ...]: the new URL. Note this time the / character at the end: [pages] is a folder, and the Apache server asks the client to refer to it with a URL ending in /.

The [output/localhost.html] file is then as follows:

<!DOCTYPE HTML PUBLIC "-//IETF//DTD HTML 2.0//EN">
<html><head>
<title>301 Moved Permanently</title>
</head><body>
<h1>Moved Permanently</h1>
<p>The document has moved <a href="http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/inet/http/pages/">here</a>.</p>
<hr>
<address>Apache/2.4.58 (Ubuntu) Server at localhost Port 80</address>
</body></html>

An HTTP client should be able to follow redirections. Here it should automatically request the new URL [http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/inet/http/pages/].

docs.title: 16.4.5. Example 5
docs.text:
The previous examples have shown us that our HTTP client was not good enough. We will now present a tool called [curl] that retrieves web documents while handling the difficulties mentioned: the HTTPS protocol, documents sent in chunks, redirections… The [curl] tool ships with Windows (since Windows 10) and with [Laragon]. In a PowerShell terminal, you must type [curl.exe] and not [curl]: in PowerShell 5, [curl] is an alias of another command, [Invoke-WebRequest].

The [curl --help] command displays the main configuration options of [curl]. There are several dozen of them. We will use very few. To request a URL, simply type the command [curl URL]. This command will display the requested document on the console. If we also want the HTTP exchanges between the client and the server, we write [curl --verbose URL]. Finally, to save the requested HTML document in a file, we write [curl --verbose --output fichier URL].

To avoid cluttering the course folders, let's move to a working folder, for example [c:\temp\curl] (create it if it does not exist), and request the [bonjour.html] page:

  • the lines beginning with [>] are the lines sent by [curl] to the [localhost] server. We recognize the HTTP protocol;
  • the lines beginning with [<] are the lines sent in response by the server;

The [localhost.html] file contains the requested document. You can check this by loading the file into a text editor.

Now let's request the URL [https://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/inet/http/pages/bonjour.html]. To get this URL, the HTTP client must be able to speak HTTPS. The [curl] client can. The server's certificate is self-signed: [curl] would refuse to continue. The [--insecure] option tells it not to verify the certificate. The console results are as follows:
