These are "console" scripts: they run in a terminal, with the command [php nom-du-script.php], and write their results to that same terminal. Web scripts, executed by [Laragon]'s [Apache] server and displayed by a browser, will come later.

docs.title: 3.2. PHP configuration
docs.text:
PHP comes preconfigured by a text file [php.ini]. All these settings can be changed programmatically. The PHP configuration greatly influences the execution of scripts. It is therefore important to know it. The following script [phpinfo.php] lets us do so:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// affiche la configuration de PHP
phpinfo();

Comments:

  • line 3: this line will be present at the beginning of all the course scripts. We will explain it in the section devoted to type changes;
  • line 6: the [phpinfo] function displays the PHP configuration.

Let us open a terminal in the [scripts-console/bases] folder and execute the script. Here is an excerpt:

> php phpinfo.php
phpinfo()
PHP Version => 8.5.11
…
Server API => Command Line Interface
…
PHP API => 20250925
PHP Extension => 20250925
Zend Extension => 420250925
PHP Integer Size => 64 bits
Debug Build => no
Zend Memory Manager => enabled
IPv6 Support => enabled
…
display_errors => STDOUT => STDOUT
error_reporting => 30719 => 30719
memory_limit => 512M => 512M
max_execution_time => 0 => 0
…

The [phpinfo] function displays nearly 1,500 lines of configuration here. We will not comment on them, as most concern advanced use of PHP. Let us note a few of them:

  • [PHP Version]: the version of PHP used, here 8.5;
  • [Server API]: the way PHP was launched. [Command Line Interface] (CLI) designates the interpreter executed in a terminal. When PHP is executed by the [Apache] server, this line changes, and the configuration may be different;
  • [display_errors] and [error_reporting]: PHP displays all errors, all warnings (Warning) and all deprecation notices (Deprecated). The value 30719 is that of the [E_ALL] constant since PHP 8.4. This is the configuration you need while learning: a warning almost always signals a programming error.

An important line of the full output is the [Loaded Configuration File] line: it indicates which [php.ini] file was used to configure the PHP that executes your scripts. With [Laragon], it is a file such as [C:\laragon\bin\php\php-8.5.x-Win32-vs17-x64\php.ini]. It can also be obtained directly with the command [php --ini]. If you want to modify the PHP runtime configuration, this is the file you need to modify ([Laragon] gives access to it through its menu, under [PHP > php.ini]). Many comments in this file explain the role of the various settings.

docs.title: 3.3.1. The code
docs.text:
Below is a program [bases-01.php] presenting the first features of PHP:

<?php

// contrôle strict des types des paramètres et des résultats des fonctions
declare(strict_types=1);

// ceci est un commentaire
// variable utilisée sans avoir été déclarée
$nom = "dupont";
// un affichage écran
print "nom=$nom\n";
// un tableau avec des éléments de type différent
$tableau = ["un", "deux", 3, 4];
// son nombre d'éléments
$n = count($tableau);
// une boucle
for ($i = 0; $i < $n; $i++) {
    print "tableau[$i]=$tableau[$i]\n";
}
// initialisation de 2 variables avec le contenu d'un tableau
[$chaine1, $chaine2] = ["chaine1", "chaine2"];
// concaténation des 2 chaînes
$chaine3 = $chaine1 . $chaine2;
// affichage résultat
print "[$chaine1,$chaine2,$chaine3]\n";
// utilisation fonction
affiche($chaine1);
// le type d'une variable peut être connu
afficheType("n", $n);
afficheType("chaine1", $chaine1);
afficheType("tableau", $tableau);
// le type d'une variable peut changer en cours d'exécution
$n = "a changé";
afficheType("n", $n);
// une fonction peut rendre un résultat
$res1 = f1(4);
print "res1=$res1\n";
// une fonction peut rendre un tableau de valeurs
[$res1, $res2, $res3] = f2();
print "(res1,res2,res3)=[$res1,$res2,$res3]\n";
// on aurait pu récupérer ces valeurs dans un tableau
$t = f2();
for ($i = 0; $i < count($t); $i++) {
    print "t[$i]=$t[$i]\n";
}
// des tests
for ($i = 0; $i < count($t); $i++) {
    // n'affiche que les chaînes
    if (gettype($t[$i]) === "string") {
        print "t[$i]=$t[$i]\n";
    }
}
// opérateurs de comparaison == et ===
if ("2" == 2) {
    print "avec l'opérateur ==, la chaîne 2 est égale à l'entier 2\n";
} else {
    print "avec l'opérateur ==, la chaîne 2 n'est pas égale à l'entier 2\n";
}
if ("2" === 2) {
    print "avec l'opérateur ===, la chaîne 2 est égale à l'entier 2\n";
} else {
    print "avec l'opérateur ===, la chaîne 2 n'est pas égale à l'entier 2\n";
}
// une comparaison dont le résultat a changé avec PHP 8
if (0 == "abc") {
    print "avec l'opérateur ==, l'entier 0 est égal à la chaîne abc\n";
} else {
    print "avec l'opérateur ==, l'entier 0 n'est pas égal à la chaîne abc\n";
}
// d'autres tests
for ($i = 0; $i < count($t); $i++) {
    // n'affiche que les entiers > 10
    if (is_int($t[$i]) && $t[$i] > 10) {
        print "t[$i]=$t[$i]\n";
    }
}
// une boucle while
$t = [8, 5, 0, -2, 3, 4];
$i = 0;
$somme = 0;
while ($i < count($t) && $t[$i] > 0) {
    print "t[$i]=$t[$i]\n";
    $somme += $t[$i];   // $somme = $somme + $t[$i]
    $i++;               // $i = $i + 1
}
print "somme=$somme\n";

// fin programme
exit;

//----------------------------------
function affiche(string $chaine): void
{
    // affiche $chaine
    print "chaine=$chaine\n";
}

//----------------------------------
function afficheType(string $name, mixed $variable): void
{
    // affiche le type de $variable
    print "type[variable $" . $name . "]=" . gettype($variable) . "\n";
}

//----------------------------------
function f1(int $param): int
{
    // ajoute 10 à $param
    return $param + 10;
}

//----------------------------------
function f2(): array
{
    // rend 3 valeurs
    return ["un", 0, 100];
}

The results:

> php bases-01.php
nom=dupont
tableau[0]=un
tableau[1]=deux
tableau[2]=3
tableau[3]=4
[chaine1,chaine2,chaine1chaine2]
chaine=chaine1
type[variable $n]=integer
type[variable $chaine1]=string
type[variable $tableau]=array
type[variable $n]=string
res1=14
(res1,res2,res3)=[un,0,100]
t[0]=un
t[1]=0
t[2]=100
t[0]=un
avec l'opérateur ==, la chaîne 2 est égale à l'entier 2
avec l'opérateur ===, la chaîne 2 n'est pas égale à l'entier 2
avec l'opérateur ==, l'entier 0 n'est pas égal à la chaîne abc
t[2]=100
t[0]=8
t[1]=5
somme=13

Comments:

  • line 4: asks PHP to strictly check the declared types of function parameters and results. We will come back to this in the section devoted to type changes. For now, just remember that all the course scripts begin this way;
  • line 8: in PHP, variables are not declared. They have a dynamic type that can vary over time. [$nom] represents the variable with identifier [nom];
  • line 10: to write to the screen, you can use the [print] statement or the [echo] statement;
  • line 12: the [[...]] notation is used to define an array. The notation [$tableau[$i]] represents element no. [$i] of the array [$tableau], the first element having no. 0. The older notation [array("un", "deux", 3, 4)] is still accepted, but we will not use it;
  • line 14: the function [count($tableau)] returns the number of elements of the array [$tableau];
  • lines 16-18: a loop. Since it has only one statement, the braces are optional. In the rest of this document, we will always use braces whatever the number of statements;
  • line 17: strings are enclosed in double quotes " or single quotes '. Inside double quotes, variables [$variable] are evaluated (we also say "interpolated"), but not inside single quotes;
  • line 20: the elements of an array can be assigned to several variables in a single operation. Here [$chaine1="chaine1"] and [$chaine2="chaine2"]. This syntax, called destructuring, replaces the [list] function of older versions of PHP: [list($chaine1, $chaine2) = ...] is still accepted;
  • line 22: the . (dot) operator is the string concatenation operator;
  • lines 91-95: the [function] keyword defines a function. A function can be defined anywhere in the script, even after it is used. Here, [string $chaine] indicates that the parameter [$chaine] must be a string and [: void] that the function returns no result. These type declarations are optional in PHP, but we will use them systematically: they document the code and allow PHP (and the editor) to detect errors;
  • line 98: the [mixed] type (PHP 8.0) means "any type". The parameter [$variable] can receive an integer, a string, an array…;
  • line 101: the predefined function [gettype($variable)] returns a string representing the type of [$variable]. The results show that this type can change over time: [$n] is first an integer (integer) and then a string (string);
  • line 105: a function returns a result with the [return] statement. The type of this result is declared after the parentheses: [: int]. The calling code can ignore or retrieve the results of a function;
  • line 112: a function can return several values by gathering them in an array;
  • lines 53-62: the [===] operator compares two elements strictly: they must have the same type and the same value to be equal. The [] operator is less strict: two elements can be equal without being of the same type. In this case, the comparison is made after converting both elements to the same type. It is quite easy to "forget" these implicit conversions and thus end up with unexpected results, such as discovering that a condition is true when you expected it to be false. To avoid this pitfall, we will systematically use the comparison operator [=] (and its opposite [!==]);
  • lines 64-68: an example of these implicit conversions. In PHP 7, the string "abc" was converted to the number 0, and the expression [0 == "abc"] was true! Since PHP 8.0, when a number is compared to a string that does not represent a number, it is the number that is converted to a string, and the expression is false. The behavior of [] has therefore changed from one version to the next: all the more reason to prefer [=];
  • line 72: the [is_int] function returns [true] if its parameter is an integer. Likewise there are [is_string], [is_float], [is_bool], [is_array]… The [&&] operator is the logical AND. You can also use the logical operators [||] (OR) and [!] (NOT). PHP also knows the keywords [and] and [or], but their precedence, lower than that of assignment, holds surprises: we will not use them;
  • line 80: a [while] loop. It stops as soon as the condition is false, here as soon as the array has been traversed or a negative or zero element is encountered;
  • line 88: the [exit] statement stops the execution of the script. The functions that follow are not executed at this point, but they are known to the whole script.

Note that the script does not end with the [?>] tag that closes PHP code. It is not required. Moreover, in a web context, it can cause problems if it is followed by spaces or end-of-line marks, which are hard to detect because they are not visible in a text editor. The [PSR-12] recommendation in fact requires omitting it in files containing only PHP. So, in the rest of the document, we will always omit it.

Note: in this document, we will use the [print] keyword to display text on the console. Another way to do the same thing is to use the [echo] keyword. There are subtle differences between these two keywords, but in the context of this document there will be none. So if you prefer to use [echo], go ahead.

docs.title: 3.3.2. Using VS Code
docs.text:
To work on the course scripts, open the [php8-oct-2026] folder in [VS Code] (menu [File > Open Folder]). The file tree appears in the explorer, on the left of the window. To execute a script:

  • open an integrated terminal (menu [Terminal > New Terminal]). It opens in the [php8-oct-2026] folder;
  • go to the script's folder: [cd scripts-console/bases];
  • run the script: [php bases-01.php]. The results are displayed in the terminal. You can also, in the explorer, right-click on the [bases] folder and choose [Open in Integrated Terminal].

If the [php] command is not recognized, the PHP folder is not in the Windows PATH: [Laragon] adds it when you check the corresponding option of its [Tools > Path] menu. The command [php -v] should display version 8.5.

The [PHP Intelephense] extension analyzes the code as you type and reports problems with a wavy line under the faulty code. Hovering over this line with the mouse displays the message. All the problems of the folder are gathered in the [Problems] panel (menu [View > Problems]). Among the useful warnings:

  • [Undefined variable]: a variable is used without having been initialized. This is often a typo in a variable name;
  • [Undefined function]: a call to a function that does not exist, again often a typo;
  • [Expected type 'int'. Found 'string'.]: an actual parameter does not have the type declared by the function. This is one of the great benefits of type declarations: the error is reported even before execution;
  • [Expected 2 arguments. Found 1.]: the number of actual parameters does not match the definition of the function.

Hovering over a function name displays its signature (parameters, types, result) and its documentation, including for PHP's predefined functions. For [Intelephense] to know the recent features of the language, check in the [VS Code] settings (menu [File > Preferences > Settings], search for "intelephense php version") that the PHP version indicated is 8.5. While learning the language, it is advisable to fix all the warnings reported. You learn a lot that way.

[Intelephense] can also format a file (right-click, [Format Document]) according to the [PSR-12] coding recommendations. PSRs (PHP Standard Recommendations) are recommendations for producing standard code and thus facilitating the interoperability and maintenance of code written by different people. They are published by the [PHP-FIG] on the website www.php-fig.org. The [PSR-1] and [PSR-12] recommendations set the rules for writing code. Here are those of [PSR-1]:

ElementRuleClass constantsClass constants MUST be written in uppercase with the _ character as separator.E.g.: [const TAUX_TVA]MethodsMethod names MUST be written in camelCase.E.g.: [public function executeBatchImpots()]PropertiesProperty names SHOULD be written consistently within the same body of code, in StudlyCaps, camelCase or under_score.E.g.: [$SalaireAnnuel], [$salaireAnnuel], [$salaire_annuel]Side effectsA file SHOULD either declare new symbols (classes, functions, constants…) with no other side effect, or execute code with side effects, but SHOULD NOT do both.TypesType names (classes, interfaces…) MUST be written in StudlyCaps. Each type is in a file of its own and in a namespace of at least one level.E.g.: [class EtudiantBoursier]

The side-effects rule says that a PHP file should contain:

  • either the declaration of types (classes, interfaces), functions or constants;
  • or executable code without the declaration of new types.

For convenience, the examples of this chapter do not follow it: each script is a single file that defines its functions and uses them. Spreading the code over several files would be too cumbersome for basic examples. For the application presented as the common thread of this document, we will try, as soon as it is written with classes, to follow these recommendations as closely as possible.

docs.title: 3.4.1. Example 1
docs.text:
The script [bases-02.php] is as follows:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// portée des variables

function f1(): void
{
    // on utilise la variable globale $i
    global $i;
    $i++;
    $j = 10;
    print "f1[i,j]=[$i,$j]\n";
}

function f2(): void
{
    // on utilise la variable globale $i
    global $i;
    $i++;
    $j = 20;
    print "f2[i,j]=[$i,$j]\n";
}

function f3(): void
{
    // on utilise une variable locale $i
    $i = 4;
    $j = 30;
    print "f3[i,j]=[$i,$j]\n";
}

// tests
$i = 0;
$j = 0;  // ces deux variables ne sont connues d'une fonction f
// que si celle-ci déclare explicitement par l'instruction global
// qu'elle veut les utiliser
f1();
f2();
f3();
print "test[i,j]=[$i,$j]\n";

The results:

> php bases-02.php
f1[i,j]=[1,10]
f2[i,j]=[2,20]
f3[i,j]=[4,30]
test[i,j]=[2,0]

Comments:

  • lines 34-35: define 2 variables [$i] and [$j] of the main program. These variables are not known inside functions. Thus, line 12, the variable [$j] of function [f1] is a variable local to function [f1] and is different from the variable [$j] of the main program;
  • line 10: a function can access a variable [$variable] of the main program through the [global] keyword. Here, the statement designates the global variable [$i] of the main program;
  • line 28: function [f3] has not declared [$i] global: its variable [$i] is a local variable, unrelated to the one in the main program.

The use of [global] is not recommended: a function that modifies global variables is hard to understand and to test. It is preferable for a function to receive its data through its parameters and return its results with [return]. This is what we will do from now on.

docs.title: 3.4.2. Example 2
docs.text:
The script [bases-03.php] is as follows:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// la portée d'une variable est globale aux blocs de code
$i = 0;
{
    $i = 4;
    $i++;
}
print "i=$i\n";

The results:

> php bases-03.php
i=5

Comments:

In some languages, a variable defined inside braces has their scope: it is not known outside them. The results above show that this is not the case in PHP. The variable [$i] used line 8 inside the braces is the same as the one used line 6 and line 11 outside them.

docs.title: 3.5. Type changes
docs.text:
Variables in PHP do not have a constant type. It can change during execution according to the value assigned to the variable. In operations involving data of various types, the PHP interpreter performs implicit conversions to bring the operands to a common type. These implicit conversions, if the developer is unaware of them, can be a source of errors that are hard to track down. Below is a script [bases-04.php] showing implicit and explicit conversions. Let us start with its first part:

<?php

// types stricts dans le passage des paramètres
declare(strict_types=1);

// changements implicites de types
// type --> bool
print "Conversion vers un booléen------------------------------\n";
showBool("abcd", "abcd");
showBool("", "");
showBool("[1, 2, 3]", [1, 2, 3]);
showBool("[]", []);
showBool("null", null);
showBool("0.0", 0.0);
showBool("0", 0);
showBool("4.6", 4.6);
showBool("\"0\"", "0");

function showBool(string $prefixe, mixed $var): void
{
    print "(bool) $prefixe : ";
    // la conversion de $var en booléen se fait automatiquement dans le test qui suit
    if ($var) {
        print "true";
    } else {
        print "false";
    }
    print "\n";
}

Comments:

  • line 4: requests a strict check of the type of a function's parameters when it is specified (and of the type of its result). We explain this statement a little further on;
  • line 19: the purpose of the [showBool] function is to show the implicit (automatic) transformation the PHP interpreter performs when a value of any type must be transformed into a boolean (line 23);
  • line 19: the parameter [$prefixe] must be of type [string]. The parameter [$var] is of type [mixed]: the actual parameter can therefore be of any type. The [showBool] function returns no value ([void]);
  • line 23: in the statement [if ($var)], the value of [$var] must be transformed into a boolean for the [if] to be evaluated. Surprisingly, the PHP interpreter has an answer for any type of value you give it;
  • lines 9-17: the value of the parameter of the [showBool] function will successively be:
    • line 9: a non-empty string: result [true] (case does not matter, TRUE=true);
    • line 10: an empty string: result [false];
    • line 11: a non-empty array: result [true];
    • line 12: an empty array: result [false];
    • line 13: the value [null] (absence of value): result [false];
    • line 14: the real number 0: result [false];
    • line 15: the integer 0: result [false];
    • line 16: a real (or integer) number other than 0: result [true];
    • line 17: a trap: the string "0" is converted to [false], whereas any other non-empty string is converted to [true].

This is what the screen output shows:

Conversion vers un booléen------------------------------
(bool) abcd : true
(bool)  : false
(bool) [1, 2, 3] : true
(bool) [] : false
(bool) null : false
(bool) 0.0 : false
(bool) 0 : false
(bool) 4.6 : true
(bool) "0" : false

Let us continue with the script's code:

// changements implicites de type string vers un type numérique
// string --> nombre
print "Conversion chaîne vers nombre------------------------------\n";
showNumber("12");
showNumber("45.67");
showNumber("12abcd");
try {
    showNumber("abcd");
} catch (TypeError $erreur) {
    print "(abcd): erreur [" . $erreur->getMessage() . "]\n";
}

function showNumber(string $var): void
{
    $nombre = $var + 1;
    var_dump($nombre);
    print "($var): $nombre\n";
}

Comments:

  • line 43: the [showNumber] function accepts a parameter of type [string] and returns no result ([void]);
  • line 45: this parameter is used in an arithmetic operation, which will force the PHP interpreter to try to transform [$var] into a number:
    • line 34: will transform the string "12" into the integer 12;
    • line 35: will transform the string "45.67" into the real number 45.67;
    • line 36: the string "12abcd" begins with a number. PHP uses this number, 12, but emits a warning (Warning);
    • line 38: the string "abcd" contains no number. In PHP 7, it was transformed into 0 with a mere warning. Since PHP 8.0, the operation is impossible: PHP throws an error of type [TypeError] which, if it were not caught, would stop the script;
  • lines 37-41: the [try { ... } catch (TypeError $erreur) { ... }] structure makes it possible to catch this error and continue execution. [$erreur->getMessage()] is the error message. Exceptions will be studied in a later chapter; here it is enough to know that the code of the [catch] block is executed when the code of the [try] block causes a [TypeError] error.

Here are the execution results:

Conversion chaîne vers nombre------------------------------
int(13)
(12): 13
float(46.67)
(45.67): 46.67

Warning: A non-numeric value encountered in .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/bases/bases-04.php on line 45
int(13)
(12abcd): 13
(abcd): erreur [Unsupported operand types: string + int]

The [var_dump] function displays the type and value of its parameter: int(13) is the integer 13, float(46.67) the real number 46.67.

Note that the [declare(strict_types=1)] statement did not prevent the conversion of the string "12" into a number. This is an important point: strict mode only concerns the passing of parameters to functions and the results they return. It changes nothing in the conversions made by operators (+, ., ==…) nor in the one made by the [if]. Here is what it does change:

  • without [declare(strict_types=1)] (so-called "coercive" mode), if a function expects an [int] and is passed the string "12", PHP converts the string into the integer 12;
  • with [declare(strict_types=1)] (strict mode), the same call causes a [TypeError] error. The actual parameter must be exactly of the expected type. There is a single exception: an [int] is accepted where a [float] is expected.

The statement must be the first in the file and applies only to function calls made in that file. We will use it in all scripts: it turns silent, error-prone conversions into reported errors. We will see an example in the section devoted to parameter passing.

Let us continue the script's code with explicit type changes:

// changements explicites de type
// vers int
print "Conversion explicite vers int------------------------------\n";
showInt("12.45");
showInt(67.8);
showInt(true);
showInt(null);

function showInt(mixed $var): void
{
    print "paramètre : ";
    var_dump($var);
    print "résultat de la conversion : ";
    var_dump((int) $var);
}

Comments:

  • line 58: the [showInt] function receives a parameter of any type ([mixed]) and returns no result. It converts the parameter [$var] into an integer (line 63). In general, to change a variable [$var] into a type T, you write [(T) $var] where T can be: int, bool, float, string, array, object. The forms (integer), (boolean), (double) and (binary) of older versions of PHP are obsolete: PHP 8.5 reports them as deprecated. The form (real) was removed as early as PHP 8.0;
  • line 53: converts the string "12.45" into the integer 12;
  • line 54: converts the real number 67.8 into the integer 67 (the decimal part is lost);
  • line 55: converts the boolean [true] into the integer 1 (the boolean [false] into the integer 0);
  • line 56: converts the value [null] into the integer 0.

This is what the screen output shows:

Conversion explicite vers int------------------------------
paramètre : string(5) "12.45"
résultat de la conversion : int(12)
paramètre : float(67.8)
résultat de la conversion : int(67)
paramètre : bool(true)
résultat de la conversion : int(1)
paramètre : NULL
résultat de la conversion : int(0)

We continue the study of the script with the explicit conversion of values to the [float] type:

// vers float
print "Conversion explicite vers float------------------------------\n";
showFloat("12.45");
showFloat(67);
showFloat(true);
showFloat(null);

function showFloat(mixed $var): void
{
    print "paramètre : ";
    var_dump($var);
    print "résultat de la conversion : ";
    var_dump((float) $var);
}

Comments:

  • line 73: the [showFloat] function receives a parameter of any type and returns no result;
  • line 78: the value of this parameter is explicitly transformed into a [float];
  • line 68: the string "12.45" is transformed into the real number 12.45;
  • line 69: the integer 67 is transformed into the real number 67;
  • line 70: the boolean [true] is transformed into the real number 1 (the value [false] into the number 0);
  • line 71: the value [null] is transformed into the real number 0.

This is what the screen results show:

Conversion explicite vers float------------------------------
paramètre : string(5) "12.45"
résultat de la conversion : float(12.45)
paramètre : int(67)
résultat de la conversion : float(67)
paramètre : bool(true)
résultat de la conversion : float(1)
paramètre : NULL
résultat de la conversion : float(0)

We end the presentation of the script by studying conversions to the [string] type:

// vers string
print "Conversion explicite vers string------------------------------\n";
showString(5);
showString(6.7);
showString(false);
showString(null);

function showString(mixed $var): void
{
    print "paramètre : ";
    var_dump($var);
    print "résultat de la conversion : ";
    var_dump((string) $var);
}

Comments:

  • line 88: the [showString] function receives a parameter of any type and returns no result;
  • line 93: the value of the parameter is transformed into a [string] type;
  • line 83: the integer 5 will be transformed into the string "5";
  • line 84: the real number 6.7 will be transformed into the string "6.7";
  • line 85: the boolean [false] will be transformed into an empty string;
  • line 86: the value [null] will be transformed into an empty string.

Here are the screen results:

Conversion explicite vers string------------------------------
paramètre : int(5)
résultat de la conversion : string(1) "5"
paramètre : float(6.7)
résultat de la conversion : string(3) "6.7"
paramètre : bool(false)
résultat de la conversion : string(0) ""
paramètre : NULL
résultat de la conversion : string(0) ""

docs.title: 3.6.1. Classic one-dimensional arrays
docs.text:
There are two notations for arrays in PHP:

$tableau = ["un", 2, "trois"];
$contraires = ["petit" => "grand", "beau" => "laid", "cher" => "bon marché"];

Array 1 is called an array (or list) and array 2 a dictionary or associative array, in which the elements are written key => value. The notation [$contraires["beau"]] designates the value associated with the key "beau". Here it is therefore the string "laid". Array 1 is merely a variant of the dictionary and could be written:

$tableau = [0 => "un", 1 => 2, 2 => "trois"];

We thus have [$tableau[2]="trois"]. Ultimately, there are only dictionaries. In the case of a classic array of n elements, the keys are the integers of the interval [0,n-1].

The script [bases-05.php] shows operations for manipulating an array of values:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// tableaux classiques
// initialisation
$tab1 = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
// parcours - 1
print "tab1 a " . count($tab1) . " éléments\n";
for ($i = 0; $i < count($tab1); $i++) {
    print "tab1[$i]=$tab1[$i]\n";
}
// parcours - 2
print "tab1 a " . count($tab1) . " éléments\n";
foreach ($tab1 as $clé => $valeur) {
    print "tab1[$clé]=$valeur\n";
}
// ajout d'éléments
$tab1[] = $i++;
$tab1[] = $i++;
// parcours - 3
print "tab1 a " . count($tab1) . " éléments\n";
$i = 0;
foreach ($tab1 as $élément) {
    print "tab1[$i]=$élément\n";
    $i++;
}
// suppression dernier élément
array_pop($tab1);
// parcours - 4
print "tab1 a " . count($tab1) . " éléments\n";
for ($i = 0; $i < count($tab1); $i++) {
    print "tab1[$i]=$tab1[$i]\n";
}
// suppression premier élément
array_shift($tab1);
// parcours - 5
print "tab1 a " . count($tab1) . " éléments\n";
for ($i = 0; $i < count($tab1); $i++) {
    print "tab1[$i]=$tab1[$i]\n";
}
// ajout en fin de tableau
array_push($tab1, -2);
// parcours - 6
print "tab1 a " . count($tab1) . " éléments\n";
for ($i = 0; $i < count($tab1); $i++) {
    print "tab1[$i]=$tab1[$i]\n";
}
// ajout en début de tableau
array_unshift($tab1, -1);
// parcours - 7
print "tab1 a " . count($tab1) . " éléments\n";
for ($i = 0; $i < count($tab1); $i++) {
    print "tab1[$i]=$tab1[$i]\n";
}
// premier et dernier éléments (PHP 8.5)
print "premier élément : " . array_first($tab1) . ", dernier élément : " . array_last($tab1) . "\n";

The results:

> php bases-05.php
tab1 a 6 éléments
tab1[0]=0
tab1[1]=1
tab1[2]=2
tab1[3]=3
tab1[4]=4
tab1[5]=5
tab1 a 6 éléments
tab1[0]=0
tab1[1]=1
tab1[2]=2
tab1[3]=3
tab1[4]=4
tab1[5]=5
tab1 a 8 éléments
tab1[0]=0
tab1[1]=1
tab1[2]=2
tab1[3]=3
tab1[4]=4
tab1[5]=5
tab1[6]=6
tab1[7]=7
tab1 a 7 éléments
tab1[0]=0
tab1[1]=1
tab1[2]=2
tab1[3]=3
tab1[4]=4
tab1[5]=5
tab1[6]=6
tab1 a 6 éléments
tab1[0]=1
tab1[1]=2
tab1[2]=3
tab1[3]=4
tab1[4]=5
tab1[5]=6
tab1 a 7 éléments
tab1[0]=1
tab1[1]=2
tab1[2]=3
tab1[3]=4
tab1[4]=5
tab1[5]=6
tab1[6]=-2
tab1 a 8 éléments
tab1[0]=-1
tab1[1]=1
tab1[2]=2
tab1[3]=3
tab1[4]=4
tab1[5]=5
tab1[6]=6
tab1[7]=-2
premier élément : -1, dernier élément : -2

Comments:

  • line 15: the array is traversed with a [foreach]. This syntactic element makes it possible to traverse a dictionary, and therefore an array, with two syntaxes: [foreach ($dictionnaire as $clé => $valeur)] and [foreach ($tableau as $valeur)]. The first syntax returns a (key, value) pair at each iteration whereas the second returns only the value. The PHP 7 course used the [each] function here, already obsolete at the time: it was removed in PHP 8.0. [foreach] is the normal way to traverse an array;
  • line 19: the notation [$tableau[] = valeur] adds the element [valeur] as the last element of [$tableau]. Here, [$i] is 6 on exiting the first [for] loop: we add 6, then 7;
  • line 24: a traversal with the second [foreach] syntax. Note that variable names can contain accented characters;
  • line 29: the function [array_pop($tableau)] removes the last element of [$tableau];
  • line 36: the function [array_shift($tableau)] removes the first element of [$tableau]. The remaining elements are renumbered from 0;
  • line 43: the function [array_push($tableau, valeur)] adds [valeur] as the last element of [$tableau];
  • line 50: the function [array_unshift($tableau, valeur)] adds [valeur] as the first element of [$tableau];
  • line 57: the [array_first] and [array_last] functions, introduced in PHP 8.5, return the first and last element of an array (or [null] if the array is empty).

docs.title: 3.6.2. The dictionary or associative array
docs.text:
The script [bases-06.php] is as follows:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// dictionnaires
$conjoints = ["Pierre" => "Gisèle", "Paul" => "Virginie", "Jacques" => "Lucette", "Jean" => ""];
// parcours - 1
print "Nombre d'éléments du dictionnaire : " . count($conjoints) . "\n";
foreach ($conjoints as $clé => $valeur) {
    print "conjoints[$clé]=$valeur\n";
}
// tri du dictionnaire sur la clé
ksort($conjoints);
// parcours - 2
foreach ($conjoints as $clé => $valeur) {
    print "conjoints[$clé]=$valeur\n";
}
// liste des clés du dictionnaire
$clés = array_keys($conjoints);
for ($i = 0; $i < count($clés); $i++) {
    print "clés[$i]=$clés[$i]\n";
}
// liste des valeurs du dictionnaire
$valeurs = array_values($conjoints);
for ($i = 0; $i < count($valeurs); $i++) {
    print "valeurs[$i]=$valeurs[$i]\n";
}
// un tableau classique est-il une liste ? et un dictionnaire ?
print "valeurs est une liste : " . var_export(array_is_list($valeurs), true) . "\n";
print "conjoints est une liste : " . var_export(array_is_list($conjoints), true) . "\n";
// recherche d'une clé
existe($conjoints, "Jacques");
existe($conjoints, "Lucette");
existe($conjoints, "Jean");
// valeur par défaut si la clé n'existe pas : opérateur ??
print "conjoint de Lucette : " . ($conjoints["Lucette"] ?? "inconnu") . "\n";
// suppression d'une clé-valeur
unset($conjoints["Jean"]);
print "Nombre d'éléments du dictionnaire : " . count($conjoints) . "\n";
foreach ($conjoints as $clé => $valeur) {
    print "conjoints[$clé]=$valeur\n";
}
// fin
exit;

function existe(array $conjoints, string $mari): void
{
    // vérifie si la clé $mari existe dans le dictionnaire $conjoints
    if (isset($conjoints[$mari])) {
        print "La clé [$mari] existe associée à la valeur [$conjoints[$mari]]\n";
    } else {
        print "La clé [$mari] n'existe pas\n";
    }
}

The results:

> php bases-06.php
Nombre d'éléments du dictionnaire : 4
conjoints[Pierre]=Gisèle
conjoints[Paul]=Virginie
conjoints[Jacques]=Lucette
conjoints[Jean]=
conjoints[Jacques]=Lucette
conjoints[Jean]=
conjoints[Paul]=Virginie
conjoints[Pierre]=Gisèle
clés[0]=Jacques
clés[1]=Jean
clés[2]=Paul
clés[3]=Pierre
valeurs[0]=Lucette
valeurs[1]=
valeurs[2]=Virginie
valeurs[3]=Gisèle
valeurs est une liste : true
conjoints est une liste : false
La clé [Jacques] existe associée à la valeur [Lucette]
La clé [Lucette] n'existe pas
La clé [Jean] existe associée à la valeur []
conjoint de Lucette : inconnu
Nombre d'éléments du dictionnaire : 3
conjoints[Jacques]=Lucette
conjoints[Paul]=Virginie
conjoints[Pierre]=Gisèle

Comments:

The previous code applies to a dictionary what was seen earlier for a simple array. We comment only on the new features:

  • line 13: the [ksort] (key sort) function sorts a dictionary in the natural order of the key;
  • line 19: the function [array_keys($dictionnaire)] returns the list of the dictionary's keys as an array;
  • line 24: the function [array_values($dictionnaire)] returns the list of the dictionary's values as an array;
  • line 29: the [array_is_list] function (PHP 8.1) returns [true] if the array's keys are 0, 1, 2… in that order, that is, if the array is a list. The [var_export] function here returns the PHP representation of a value ("true" or "false");
  • line 46: the [existe] function receives an array ([array]) and a string ([string]);
  • line 49: the function [isset($variable)] returns [true] if the variable [$variable] exists and does not have the value [null], [false] otherwise. Applied to an array element, it tells whether a key exists. The function [array_key_exists($clé, $tableau)] does the same thing, but returns [true] even if the value associated with the key is [null];
  • line 36: the [??] ("null coalescing") operator returns its left operand if it exists and is not [null], its right operand otherwise. It is a concise way to obtain a default value for a missing key, without a warning;
  • line 38: the function [unset($variable)] deletes the variable [$variable], here an element of the dictionary.

docs.title: 3.6.3. Multidimensional arrays
docs.text:
The script [bases-07.php] is as follows:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// tableaux classiques multidimensionnels
// initialisation
$multi = [[0, 1, 2], [10, 11, 12, 13], [20, 21, 22, 23, 24]];
// parcours
for ($i1 = 0; $i1 < count($multi); $i1++) {
    for ($i2 = 0; $i2 < count($multi[$i1]); $i2++) {
        print "multi[$i1][$i2]=" . $multi[$i1][$i2] . "\n";
    }
}
// dictionnaires multidimensionnels
// initialisation
$multi = ["zéro" => [0, 1, 2], "un" => [10, 11, 12, 13], "deux" => [20, 21, 22, 23, 24]];
// parcours
foreach ($multi as $clé => $valeur) {
    for ($i2 = 0; $i2 < count($valeur); $i2++) {
        print "multi[$clé][$i2]={$multi[$clé][$i2]}\n";
    }
}

Results:

> php bases-07.php
multi[0][0]=0
multi[0][1]=1
multi[0][2]=2
multi[1][0]=10
multi[1][1]=11
multi[1][2]=12
multi[1][3]=13
multi[2][0]=20
multi[2][1]=21
multi[2][2]=22
multi[2][3]=23
multi[2][4]=24
multi[zéro][0]=0
multi[zéro][1]=1
multi[zéro][2]=2
multi[un][0]=10
multi[un][1]=11
multi[un][2]=12
multi[un][3]=13
multi[deux][0]=20
multi[deux][1]=21
multi[deux][2]=22
multi[deux][3]=23
multi[deux][4]=24

Comments:

  • line 7: the elements of the array [$multi] are themselves arrays;
  • line 11: inside a double-quoted string, the simple interpolation [$multi[$i1][$i2]] does not work: PHP would only evaluate [$multi[$i1]]. So we take the expression out of the string and use concatenation;
  • line 16: the array [$multi] becomes a (key, value) dictionary in which each value is an array;
  • line 20: another solution: inside a double-quoted string, the [{$expression}] notation makes it possible to evaluate a complex expression. We will meet it again in the next section.

docs.title: 3.7.1. Notation
docs.text:
The script [bases-08.php] is as follows:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// notation des chaînes
$chaine1 = "un";
$chaine2 = 'un';
print "[$chaine1,$chaine2]\n";
// entre apostrophes, les variables ne sont pas évaluées
print '[$chaine1,$chaine2]' . "\n";
// la notation {$...} délimite l'expression à évaluer
$personne = ["nom" => "dupont", "âge" => 34];
print "{$personne['nom']} a {$personne['âge']} ans\n";
// une chaîne sur plusieurs lignes (heredoc)
$texte = <<<FIN
    nom : $chaine1
    âge : {$personne['âge']}
    FIN;
print "$texte\n";

Results:

> php bases-08.php
[un,un]
[$chaine1,$chaine2]
dupont a 34 ans
nom : un
âge : 34

Comments:

  • lines 6-7: a string can be enclosed in double quotes or single quotes;
  • line 8: inside double quotes, variables are evaluated;
  • line 10: inside single quotes, they are not: the string is displayed as is. Likewise, [\n] does not designate an end of line there, hence the concatenation of ["\n"];
  • line 13: the [{$...}] notation makes it possible to evaluate, inside a string, expressions more complex than a simple variable, here elements of a dictionary. The [${variable}] notation of older versions of PHP has been deprecated since PHP 8.2: we will not use it;
  • lines 15-18: the [heredoc] syntax makes it possible to write a string over several lines. The string begins after [<<<FIN] and ends with the [FIN] marker (the name is free). Variables are evaluated in it as between double quotes. Since PHP 7.3, the closing marker can be indented: this indentation is then removed from all the lines of the string.

docs.title: 3.7.2. Comparison
docs.text:
The script [bases-09.php] is as follows:

<?php

// respect strict du type des paramètres des fonctions
declare(strict_types=1);

// fonction de comparaison
function compareChaines(string $chaine1, string $chaine2): void
{
    // compare chaine1 et chaine2
    if ($chaine1 === $chaine2) {
        print "[$chaine1] est égal à [$chaine2]\n";
    } else {
        print "[$chaine1] est différent de [$chaine2]\n";
    }
}

// tests de comparaisons de chaînes
compareChaines("abcd", "abcd");
compareChaines("", "");
compareChaines("1", "");

// recherche d'une sous-chaîne (PHP 8)
$fichier = "taxpayersdata.txt";
print "[$fichier] contient [data] : " . var_export(str_contains($fichier, "data"), true) . "\n";
print "[$fichier] commence par [tax] : " . var_export(str_starts_with($fichier, "tax"), true) . "\n";
print "[$fichier] se termine par [.json] : " . var_export(str_ends_with($fichier, ".json"), true) . "\n";
// position d'une sous-chaîne
print "position de [data] dans [$fichier] : " . strpos($fichier, "data") . "\n";
// longueur, majuscules
print "longueur de [$fichier] : " . strlen($fichier) . ", en majuscules : " . strtoupper($fichier) . "\n";
// attention : strlen compte des octets, mb_strlen des caractères
print "strlen(\"été\")=" . strlen("été") . ", mb_strlen(\"été\")=" . mb_strlen("été") . "\n";

Results:

> php bases-09.php
[abcd] est égal à [abcd]
[] est égal à []
[1] est différent de []
[taxpayersdata.txt] contient [data] : true
[taxpayersdata.txt] commence par [tax] : true
[taxpayersdata.txt] se termine par [.json] : false
position de [data] dans [taxpayersdata.txt] : 9
longueur de [taxpayersdata.txt] : 17, en majuscules : TAXPAYERSDATA.TXT
strlen("été")=5, mb_strlen("été")=3

Comments:

  • line 10: we could have used the [] comparator rather than [=]. The latter operator is more restrictive in that it requires both operands to be of the same type. Note that here it could have been replaced by the [] operator since the type of both parameters is fixed to [string]* in the function's signature. We will nevertheless keep the habit of using *[=];
  • line 24: the function [str_contains($chaîne, $sousChaîne)] (PHP 8.0) returns [true] if [$sousChaîne] is present in [$chaîne];
  • line 25: the [str_starts_with] function (PHP 8.0) tests the beginning of a string;
  • line 26: the [str_ends_with] function (PHP 8.0) tests the end of a string;
  • line 28: the function [strpos($chaîne, $sousChaîne)] returns the position of [$sousChaîne] in [$chaîne], the first character having position 0, and [false] if the substring is absent. Before PHP 8, the presence of a substring was tested with [strpos(...) !== false], a tricky form since position 0 is converted to [false]: [str_contains] is much more readable;
  • line 30: the [strlen] function returns the length of a string and [strtoupper] converts it to uppercase;
  • line 32: [strlen] counts bytes, not characters. The course files are encoded in UTF-8, where an accented character takes up two bytes: "été" has 3 characters but 5 bytes. The functions of the [mbstring] extension (mb_strlen, mb_substr, mb_strtoupper…), on the other hand, work on characters.

docs.title: 3.7.3. Links between strings and arrays
docs.text:
The script [bases-10.php] is as follows:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// chaîne vers tableau
$chaine = "1:2:3:4";
$tab = explode(":", $chaine);
// parcours tableau
print "tab a " . count($tab) . " éléments\n";
for ($i = 0; $i < count($tab); $i++) {
    print "tab[$i]=$tab[$i]\n";
}
// tableau vers chaîne
$chaine2 = implode(":", $tab);
print "chaine2=$chaine2\n";
// ajoutons un champ vide
$chaine .= ":";
print "chaîne=$chaine\n";
$tab = explode(":", $chaine);
// parcours tableau
print "tab a " . count($tab) . " éléments\n";
for ($i = 0; $i < count($tab); $i++) {
    print "tab[$i]=$tab[$i]\n";
} // on a maintenant 5 éléments, le dernier étant vide
// ajoutons de nouveau un champ vide
$chaine .= ":";
print "chaîne=$chaine\n";
$tab = explode(":", $chaine);
// parcours tableau
print "tab a " . count($tab) . " éléments\n";
for ($i = 0; $i < count($tab); $i++) {
    print "tab[$i]=$tab[$i]\n";
} // on a maintenant 6 éléments, les deux derniers étant vides

Results:

> php bases-10.php
tab a 4 éléments
tab[0]=1
tab[1]=2
tab[2]=3
tab[3]=4
chaine2=1:2:3:4
chaîne=1:2:3:4:
tab a 5 éléments
tab[0]=1
tab[1]=2
tab[2]=3
tab[3]=4
tab[4]=
chaîne=1:2:3:4::
tab a 6 éléments
tab[0]=1
tab[1]=2
tab[2]=3
tab[3]=4
tab[4]=
tab[5]=

Comments:

  • line 7: the function [explode($séparateur, $chaine)] retrieves the fields of [$chaine] separated by [$séparateur]. Thus [explode(":", $chaine)] retrieves, as an array, the elements of [$chaine] that are separated by the string ":";
  • line 14: the function [implode($séparateur, $tableau)] performs the reverse operation of the [explode] function. It returns a string made up of the elements of [$tableau] separated by [$séparateur];
  • line 17: the [.=] operator appends one string to the end of another. The results show that an empty field at the end of the string yields an empty element in the array returned by [explode].

docs.title: 3.7.4. Regular expressions
docs.text:
The script [bases-11.php] is as follows:

<?php

// type strict pour les paramètres de fonctions
declare(strict_types=1);

// expressions régulières en php
// récupérer les différents champs d'une chaîne
// le modèle : une suite de chiffres entourée de caractères quelconques
// on ne veut récupérer que la suite de chiffres
$modèle = "/(\d+)/";
// on confronte la chaîne au modèle
compareModele2Chaine($modèle, "xyz1234abcd");
compareModele2Chaine($modèle, "12 34");
compareModele2Chaine($modèle, "abcd");

// le modèle : une suite de chiffres entourée de caractères quelconques
// on veut la suite de chiffres ainsi que les champs qui suivent et précèdent
$modèle = "/^(.*?)(\d+)(.*?)$/";
// on confronte la chaîne au modèle
compareModele2Chaine($modèle, "xyz1234abcd");
compareModele2Chaine($modèle, "12 34");
compareModele2Chaine($modèle, "abcd");

// le modèle - une date au format jj/mm/aa
$modèle = "/^\s*(\d\d)\/(\d\d)\/(\d\d)\s*$/";
compareModele2Chaine($modèle, "10/05/97");
compareModele2Chaine($modèle, "  04/04/01  ");
compareModele2Chaine($modèle, "5/1/01");

// le modèle - un nombre décimal
$modèle = "/^\s*([+-]?)\s*(\d+\.\d*|\.\d+|\d+)\s*/";
compareModele2Chaine($modèle, "187.8");
compareModele2Chaine($modèle, "-0.6");
compareModele2Chaine($modèle, "4");
compareModele2Chaine($modèle, ".6");
compareModele2Chaine($modèle, "4.");
compareModele2Chaine($modèle, " + 4");

// fin
exit;

// --------------------------------------------------------------------------
function compareModele2Chaine(string $modèle, string $chaîne): void
{
    // compare la chaîne $chaîne au modèle $modèle
    // on confronte la chaîne au modèle
    $champs = [];
    $correspond = preg_match($modèle, $chaîne, $champs);
    // affichage résultats
    print "\nRésultats($modèle,$chaîne)\n";
    if ($correspond === 1) {
        for ($i = 0; $i < count($champs); $i++) {
            print "champs[$i]=$champs[$i]\n";
        }
    } else {
        print "La chaîne [$chaîne] ne correspond pas au modèle [$modèle]\n";
    }
}

Results:

> php bases-11.php

champs[0]=1234
champs[1]=1234

Résultats(/(\d+)/,12 34)
champs[0]=12
champs[1]=12

Résultats(/(\d+)/,abcd)
La chaîne [abcd] ne correspond pas au modèle [/(\d+)/]

Résultats(/^(.*?)(\d+)(.*?)$/,xyz1234abcd)
champs[0]=xyz1234abcd
champs[1]=xyz
champs[2]=1234
champs[3]=abcd

Résultats(/^(.*?)(\d+)(.*?)$/,12 34)
champs[0]=12 34
champs[1]=
champs[2]=12
champs[3]= 34

Résultats(/^(.*?)(\d+)(.*?)$/,abcd)
La chaîne [abcd] ne correspond pas au modèle [/^(.*?)(\d+)(.*?)$/]

Résultats(/^\s*(\d\d)\/(\d\d)\/(\d\d)\s*$/,10/05/97)
champs[0]=10/05/97
champs[1]=10
champs[2]=05
champs[3]=97

Résultats(/^\s*(\d\d)\/(\d\d)\/(\d\d)\s*$/,  04/04/01  )

Résultats(/^\s*(\d\d)\/(\d\d)\/(\d\d)\s*$/,5/1/01)
La chaîne [5/1/01] ne correspond pas au modèle [/^\s*(\d\d)\/(\d\d)\/(\d\d)\s*$/]

Résultats(/^\s*([+-]?)\s*(\d+\.\d*|\.\d+|\d+)\s*/,187.8)
champs[0]=187.8
champs[1]=

Résultats(/^\s*([+-]?)\s*(\d+\.\d*|\.\d+|\d+)\s*/,-0.6)

champs[1]=-
champs[2]=0.6

Résultats(/^\s*([+-]?)\s*(\d+\.\d*|\.\d+|\d+)\s*/,4)
champs[0]=4
champs[1]=

champs[1]=
